Title: API integrations fail on a date field, so write the spec first
Description: Jose Haro Peralta (microapis.io) at Conf42 Python 2021 on documentation-driven API development with OpenAPI, FastAPI, Prism and Dredd in CI
Body:
Jose Haro Peralta, founder of microapis.io and author of a Manning book on microservice APIs in Python, argued at Conf42 Python 2021 that most API integrations fail for boring reasons, like a client sending a date with slashes to a server that expects dashes. His fix is documentation-driven development: write the OpenAPI specification first, mock it for the frontend, generate models from it for the backend, and let a contract test in CI refuse anything that drifts from it.

The talk is a full worked example, a to-do API from spec to Heroku, so it is as practical as it gets.

## Why do API integrations fail so often?

The familiar story: one team builds the server, another builds the client, both ship, they get connected, and the integration breaks. He traces it to three habits. No documentation, only JSON examples that cover a fraction of the valid payloads. Documentation in Google Docs, SharePoint or Confluence in no standard format, which no tool can read. And no design stage at all, with the API as an afterthought of the backend and a messy collection of URLs as the result.

Proper documentation depends on the protocol: OpenAPI for REST, the schema definition language for GraphQL, protocol buffers for gRPC. Use the standard format and the tooling comes free. You may know the approach as design-first, API-first or contract-first: produce the specification before anyone writes a client or a server, build both against it, and validate both against it before release.

> "These kind of errors are very common and they lead to all sorts of problems in our API integrations."

Jose Haro Peralta said that at Conf42 Python 2021 about the slashes-versus-dashes date bug. The rest of the talk turns the spec-first idea into a pipeline.

## The client side: mock the spec, not the server

The example is an OpenAPI 3 YAML spec with five endpoints and schemas for tasks and errors, edited in Swagger Editor, which validates as you type and points at the broken line. For the frontend team he shows two mock servers. Prism, Stoplight's CLI, serves valid responses straight from the spec on your machine. His own microapis.io does the same in the cloud: paste a spec, get a base URL, no sign-up. Clients can then build against realistic payloads, and realistic latency, while the real endpoints are still being written.

## The server side: generate the models, don't type them

The backend is FastAPI with pydantic models. Rather than hand-writing the models, he runs datamodel-code-generator over the spec to translate its schemas into pydantic classes, then cleans up a couple of duplicated classes it produces. His advice is blunt: if you have a spec, don't write your data models manually, because the translation step is where mistakes creep in. The endpoints themselves are Flask-like decorators with a response_model for validation and serialisation, explicit status codes, and typed path parameters. FastAPI also generates its own OpenAPI document and Swagger UI, handy for clicking through the result.

## Dredd catches what your unit tests miss

Unit tests check behaviour. A contract test checks that the server speaks the spec. He runs Dredd against the live app, and the first run is instructive: five tests pass, three fail, all of them on single-item GET, PUT and DELETE. Dredd uses random IDs, so it tries to fetch a task that was never created. The fix is a hooks file, written in Python via dredd-hooks, that saves the ID from the POST and reuses it in the following requests. Eight out of eight.

Finally, a Travis CI config installs Dredd and the Python dependencies, runs the suite, and only then deploys to Heroku. A push to master goes through the contract test or nowhere.

## Who should watch

Backend and frontend developers who have lived through an integration that broke on day one, and teams starting a new service with FastAPI. If you already run contract tests in CI, the Dredd hooks trick is the part to take home.

Title: A context manager's real job is putting things back
Description: Mason Egger (DigitalOcean) at Conf42 Python 2021 on building context managers with __enter__, __exit__ and contextlib, and handling exceptions in them
Body:
Mason Egger, Developer Advocate at DigitalOcean, used his Conf42 Python 2021 talk to take apart the with statement: what a context manager is, how to write one as a class or as a generator function, and how it should behave when the code inside it blows up. The lesson that sticks is that setting things up is the easy half. The value is in guaranteed teardown, and that only works if you saved the original state before you changed it.

It is a focused, intermediate talk on one language feature, with every example on GitHub.

## What problem does with actually solve?

You have written with open(...) as f a hundred times. Mason Egger's definition is the one worth remembering.

> "Context managers essentially are a tool built into Python that guarantee that some operation is performed after a block of code, even in the case of exception, return or exit"

He said that at Conf42 Python 2021, and framed it as Python's tidier take on try/finally. The uses go well past files: sockets, database connections, locks, global state, mocking in tests, logging, and the PPB game engine, which he describes as basically one giant context manager that opens a display on the way in and tears it down on the way out.

## The class version, and a bug you can see

The class implementation needs two dunder methods. __enter__ takes only self, runs before the block, and whatever it returns lands in the variable after as. __exit__ runs after the block.

His demo is a YellingText class that hijacks sys.stdout.write so that everything prints in upper case. With an empty __exit__, the text inside the block yells, and so does the line printed after it, and every line after that. The context ended and the side effect did not. The fix is the line he stresses: in __enter__, stash the original sys.stdout.write on self, and in __exit__, put it back. If you modify anything system-wide and do not keep a copy, you have no way home.

## When should __exit__ swallow an exception?

__exit__ receives three arguments: the exception class, the exception instance and the traceback. Return True and the exception is suppressed. Return anything else and it propagates until something catches it or the program dies. His example checks for the generic Exception, prints a message and returns True, so execution carries on with the yelling switched off. He is quick to say that catching the parent of all exceptions is a little odd. In practice you would pick something specific, such as a file-not-found error, and decide whether a failed close is worth crashing the whole program over.

## Parameters go in __init__

Since __enter__ only takes self, arguments such as a filename and mode go through the constructor. The with statement calls __init__ first, then __enter__. He shows this by reimplementing open as a FileOpen class: store the name and mode, open the handle in __enter__ and return it, close it in __exit__. The calling code looks the same as the built-in.

## contextlib: yield is the dividing line

For something lighter than a class, decorate a generator with contextlib.contextmanager. Everything before the yield is the enter, the yielded value is what as receives, and everything after it is the exit. His mirror-image Whisper example lowercases stdout. Wrapping the yield in try/finally gives you the exception handling, and the demo shows a nice detail: the exception message printed inside the handler comes out lowercase, because the whisper is still active until the finally block restores the original writer.

## Who should watch

Python developers who use with every day but have never written their own, and anyone who has written test mocks that leak into the next test. If you know __exit__'s return value semantics by heart, you can skip it.

Title: 270 lines of CloudFormation YAML, or one line of Python
Description: Sohan Maheshwar (AWS) at Conf42 Python 2021 on infrastructure as code with the AWS CDK, from hand-clicked consoles to L3 constructs
Body:
Sohan Maheshwar, Developer Advocate at AWS, gave a beginner-to-intermediate introduction to infrastructure as code at Conf42 Python 2021, built around one number: a VPC with subnets, NAT gateways and route tables takes 270 lines of CloudFormation YAML, and one line of Python with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK). The point is less the line count than what comes with it: loops, conditionals, your own IDE and your existing code review all apply to infrastructure.

He says up front that the talk is aimed at people new to the cloud, and it is pitched that way. It is also an AWS advocate showing an AWS tool, so expect AWS.

## Why not just click it together in the console?

He climbs a ladder of IaC maturity. Level 0 is one heroic engineer building everything by hand in the console: manual, error prone, hard to audit, and not reproducible, the infrastructure equivalent of ask Alice, she knows. Level 1 is imperative IaC, a deploy script full of if-the-resource-exists branches. It automates the clicking but leaves you stuck when a step fails halfway, and it races when two people run it at once.

Level 2 is declarative IaC: a YAML or JSON file describing every resource, handed to AWS CloudFormation or HashiCorp Terraform. Reproducible, auditable, safe for teams, and in his view tedious, because you describe every CIDR block and availability zone yourself.

> "I find writing cloud infrastructure using Yaml or JSON fairly tedious. It's a lot of lines of code, but I know Python or JavaScript programming and I can get started straight away."

Sohan Maheshwar said that at Conf42 Python 2021, and the CDK is his level 3: infrastructure written in a general-purpose language. CDK supported TypeScript, JavaScript, Java, C# and Python, with Go in preview at the time.

## What does the CDK actually do?

Your app.py talks to the CDK, which synthesises CloudFormation and lets CloudFormation do the provisioning. Resources make up stacks, and stacks make up an app. Around that sit a construct library covering AWS's 200-plus services and the cdk CLI. The workflow is four commands: cdk init (optionally from a sample app), cdk synth to generate the template, cdk diff to see what would change, git-style, and cdk deploy.

## The demo: a VPC in one line

The prerecorded demo (CloudFormation takes a few minutes, and nobody needs to watch that live) starts with cdk init in Python, activates the virtualenv and installs requirements. Each service's construct is its own pip package, so you install only what you need, here the EC2 one. Then a single ec2.Vpc call with a name. cdk diff lists the VPC, subnets, route tables and NAT gateway that line implies. The slides spell out the default: 65,536 IPs split equally between four subnets. After cdk bootstrap (a staging S3 bucket) and cdk deploy, the CloudFormation console shows the change set marching to CREATE_COMPLETE.

## L1, L2, L3: how much opinion do you want?

The most useful part for anyone past hello world is the construct levels:

- **L1** constructs map one to one onto CloudFormation resources (CfnBucket and friends), generated automatically.
- **L2** constructs are the higher-level service classes used in the demo, with sensible defaults. His example wires an S3 read, a Lambda function and a DynamoDB table, with read and write grants, in 10 to 15 lines.
- **L3** patterns are opinionated, purpose-built stacks. A load-balanced Fargate service with its VPC and ECS task definition is 829 lines of YAML and four lines with an existing pattern.

He also points at CDK Patterns and the CDK Day community conference for constructs other people have already debugged.

## Who should watch

Python developers who have never provisioned anything and assume infrastructure means YAML. If you already write CDK daily, the construct-levels section is the only part you will find new.

Title: Your pandas dates are strings until you tell pandas otherwise
Description: Reuven M. Lerner (Lerner Consulting) at Conf42 Python 2021 on timestamps, timedeltas, the dt accessor and resampling in pandas, live in Jupyter
Body:
Reuven M. Lerner, full-time Python trainer at Lerner Consulting, spent his Conf42 Python 2021 talk with no slides at all, typing straight into a Jupyter notebook to show how pandas handles dates and times. The takeaway: once your date columns are real datetime64 values instead of strings, pandas turns into a time series tool, and a 10,000-row sample of 2015 New York taxi rides gives up its secrets (and its data quality problems) in a few lines.

It is a hands-on tutorial, and a good one to watch with your own notebook open.

## A point in time is not a length of time

He opens with the distinction that took him, by his own admission, a long time to internalise. A timestamp is a specific moment that never repeats. A timedelta is a span. Move a 1pm-2pm meeting back half an hour and both timestamps change, but the one-hour interval stays the same. In plain Python, subtracting one datetime from another gives you a timedelta, stored internally as days, seconds and microseconds.

Pandas has both concepts, and the rest of the talk builds on them.

## Why does df.info() say object?

Load the taxi CSV with read_csv and the pickup and drop-off columns come back as object, which in practice means strings. Pandas reliably guesses integers and floats and gives up on everything else. The fix is the parse_dates argument, after which df.info() reports 64-bit datetimes down to the nanosecond. He also points at the knobs you need when dates are ambiguous: is 1/2/2021 the first of February or the second of January? Set dayfirst=True for European-style dates, or hand date_parser a custom function.

## The dt accessor, and a dataset that lies

With real datetimes you get the dt accessor, the date-flavoured sibling of str. It gives you hour, day of week, month, year, leap years and quarter ends. Why quarter ends? Because pandas grew up at an investment firm, where Wes McKinney wanted Python to do what finance people did in Excel.

The best moment comes from running value_counts on the pickup hour. The sample is wildly lopsided, with lots of 11am trips and a handful at 4pm, so any conclusion about when New Yorkers ride is suspect. That is an honest lesson tucked inside a syntax tutorial.

> "If you're trying to make any sorts of assertions based on this data, they're probably going to be fundamentally flawed"

Reuven M. Lerner said that at Conf42 Python 2021, before computing Monday versus Sunday fares anyway and immediately doubting the result.

## Timedeltas you can compare with strings

Subtract pickup from drop-off and you get a trip_time column of timedeltas. Pandas will compare those against strings like 1 hour or 1 minute, converting them for you. The results are a data cleaning checklist on their own: 84 of the 10,000 rides took under a minute, a few took under a second, and one lasted twelve and a half hours, covered about one mile and cost about $11. Either the traffic was spectacularly bad, or the data is not to be trusted.

## Make time the index, then resample

The last act sets the pickup time as the index, which makes the frame a time series. He reassigns the result rather than using inplace=True, following the pandas core developers' advice. Then partial string indexing does the heavy lifting. A full timestamp matches the three trips that started at exactly 11:19:29 on 2 June 2015. Drop the seconds and you get 146 trips in that minute. Slices of timestamps include both ends, unlike integer slices.

Finally, resample('1H') buckets everything from the earliest to the latest timestamp into hourly windows, empty ones included, so a dropna is often the next call. Swap in any interval and any aggregation (min, max, mean, standard deviation, count) and you have the core of most time series reports.

## Who should watch

Analysts and engineers who already use pandas for numbers and text but convert dates by hand, or not at all. If you already resample in your sleep, skip ahead to the taxi outliers for the laughs.

Title: Cloud native will cost you more, and Jevons says that is good news
Description: Marco Coulter (Tech-Whisperer.com) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on why Jevons paradox makes microservice spend grow, and how to keep the sprawl useful
Body:
Moving to microservices means paying for less stack, so the bill should shrink. Marco Coulter, Technical Evangelist at Tech-Whisperer.com, used his Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 talk to argue the opposite: a 19th-century economist predicts you will spend more on cloud native than you expect, and that this is fine as long as the extra spend is controlled sprawl rather than accidental sprawl.

It is a short, economics-flavoured talk about what happens after the microservices are written and running in production, aimed at your opex rather than your code.

## Why would cheaper units mean a bigger bill?

Coulter grants every usual benefit first. A microservice is a small piece of code that new hires can understand, it can be rolled back on its own, it can fail without taking the application down, and teams can ship in parallel. In a pay-as-you-go cloud you pay for the code and the data, not the operating systems and hypervisors underneath.

Then he brings in William Stanley Jevons. James Watt's steam engine got the same work out of less coal, and the sensible prediction was that coal use would fall. It rose, for about a century. Jevons worked out in 1865 that with elastic demand, efficiency gains drive more consumption, not less. Coulter's variant for IT: the efficiency and agility of cloud native make people use so much more of it that usage outruns the savings.

## Hasn't IT seen this film before?

Several times, and he walks the reels. Mainframes ran one program at a time, so logical partitions arrived, and so did partition sprawl. That pushed work onto servers and physical server sprawl. Underused hardware led to virtual machines, VM sprawl and software licence sprawl inside every VM. VM overhead led to containers and container sprawl, and containers lead to microservices.

The VM chapter has the best war story: scripted ping sweeps to find unknown nodes, which got his team yelled at by security for setting off the DDoS sensors. He also cites research from a division of Deloitte: 67% of IT directors admitted they did not know the exact number of microservices used in their organisation. Marco Coulter said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021: "Do you know how many microservices you have in production today? No. Then you have sprawl."

## Why the old sprawl tools fall short

The tools from earlier cycles still help. Write processes and standards, which are good for onboarding. Make naming conventions that let a stranger guess who owns a thing and why it exists. He is gentle about the Rick and Morty server names, but useful beats fun. Run occasional audits, and lean on performance monitors to find orphans.

Microservices break the counting, though. You could count physical boxes and scan disks for VM image files, but a microservice only exists while it runs: a trigger arrives, the work happens, the taximeter stops. Because it is independent, it cannot check whether its trigger was valid. His example: a function called 10,000 times, where 1,000 are real customer calls and the other 9,000 come from a typo in some code that keeps calling it. That is a cost leak, and with the execution caps some providers set, it can crowd out real work like a self-inflicted denial of service.

## The fix is a mesh, and the happiness is philosophical

His answer: keep the standards and the monitoring, look inside the orchestrators (Kubernetes, VMware, Azure, Lambda) to find what exists, then add a service mesh as a layer 7 network for microservice APIs. He mentions Istio and Linkerd and the popular sidecar proxy pattern. A mesh gives you security, circuit breakers, layer 7 load balancing and, as a bonus, blue-green and canary deployments. Most of all it gives you one place to see what runs and why.

The last section is a detour through hedonic and eudaimonic happiness and the idea of regeneration: leave things better than you found them, and build for the next engineer who has to maintain your code. The cost argument lands there too. When you can tie each microservice back to its business value, spending more just means people found more uses for what you made efficient, which is Jevons paradox working in your favour.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering managers who have promised that the move to microservices will cut the cloud bill, and anyone starting a FinOps practice who wants the history behind the problem. Don't expect dashboards or tooling demos. It is an argument, told with steam engines.

Title: Cybersecurity scales with the size of the company, not the size of the threat
Description: Gordon Rudd (Stone Creek Coaching) at Conf42 Python 2021 on why company size and maturity, not a vendor list, should shape a cybersecurity program
Body:
Gordon Rudd, CEO of Stone Creek Coaching and a former CISO who started out writing Fortran, used his Conf42 Python 2021 talk to argue that there is no one-size-fits-all security program: a mom and pop shop and a trillion dollar corporation need different tools, different processes and a different idea of what enough looks like. The useful part is the scaffolding he hangs that on, from a five-level maturity model to the one question every board actually asks.

It is a management talk at a Python conference, and he knows it. Python shows up as the tool security teams reach for when they need to find one drop of bad data in a lake of logs, and as the reason programmers are part of the security team whether they signed up or not.

## Why is everyone still building castles?

His framing device is the castle doctrine: inner walls, watchtowers, limited entry, a DMZ. We have built defences that way for a thousand years and the model still holds. The layers are what matter. Take incoming email: three or four products may touch one message, so when one layer misses a bad actor, another catches it.

The first layer is the perimeter kit (web application security, content filtering, firewall, VPN, intrusion prevention). The second is threat intelligence, vulnerability assessment and patch management, which only work together if you know every asset on the network. The third is encryption: data, email and devices. On top he puts behavioural analytics, because a bad actor can sit on a network for roughly 280 days before exfiltrating anything. That is a long window to spot them, if something is watching.

## How big are you, really?

The spine of the talk is a capability maturity model mapped onto network size. Level one is the small shop with a router, wifi and a firewall, held together by what he calls competent people and heroic efforts. Level three brings standardised processes, log collection and a SIEM. Level four is the campus, with Active Directory in both its hosted and Azure flavours, and quantitative management. Level five is mergers, outsourced departments and walled-off teams for regulatory reasons.

Picking tools is then a matter of four points of alignment: economics, talent, existing equipment and function. He has seen plenty of organisations replace software that already did the job because nobody took the class. And the economics are blunt: an asset worth a dollar might deserve ten cents of protection, not a dollar.

## What does the board want to hear?

This is the section worth the price of admission. After years of governance committee meetings, his conclusion is short.

> "The bottom line is the men and women that make up your board of directors and your senior management team want to know one thing, are we safe?"

Gordon Rudd said that at Conf42 Python 2021, and the reporting cadence follows from it: the board or a board committee quarterly if not monthly, the CEO monthly or as needed, the C-suite and department heads with threats, vulnerabilities and patch status layered on. For the risk appetite, ask the CFO what counts as a material loss. At the bank where he worked, the answer was $25,000 in his first week and $300,000 in his last, which set the line for what needed mitigating.

## The war stories

The numbers he brings are vivid. A three to five billion dollar bank sees around 500 million bad actors pass its firewall a year. His first asset inventory at an 800-person company came back with something like 8 million assets, mostly every Adobe Reader since the dawn of time baked into the desktop image. He also admits clicking on his own team's phishing test during a crunch and getting sent straight to extra training, which is the correct outcome and a decent argument for running those tests at all.

He closes with a clock: justify technology every 18 months, train for five days every 90, a Monday 8am meeting where the team says what is on its calendar, daily vulnerability assessments, annual risk assessments. Programmers get a specific ask: learn the OWASP model, because everything grows a web interface eventually.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving toward security leadership, and Python developers who want to see their code from the CISO's chair. If you want exploits or code, this is not that talk.

Title: Java goes cloud native in one sitting, with no slides to hide behind
Description: Elder Moraes (Red Hat) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on making Java cloud-native live with Quarkus, Kubernetes, health checks, metrics and Kafka
Body:
Java has a reputation for slow starts and heavy containers, and Elder Moraes, Developer Advocate at Red Hat, spent his Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 session arguing against it with his keyboard. He builds a Java service from an empty project with Quarkus, ships it to a Kubernetes cluster on AWS, then bolts on a REST client, health probes, metrics and a Kafka stream, with hot reloads that land in about a second. The takeaway: the cloud-native checklist is mostly a list of Quarkus extensions now.

The format is the point. After a short intro he announces that the slides are done until the last one, and from then on it is terminal and editor. Elder Moraes said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021: "This is the beauty of the live coding session. We are able to debug the applications."

## What does cloud native look like before you write any code?

He opens with a demo rather than a definition. A blue and a green version of the same app sit behind a load balancer, the browser flipping between them on each request. He adds a canary version without downtime, then rewrites the routing YAML so Chrome users stick to green and Firefox users go to the canary. The same mechanism could route Android, iPhone or all mobile users to a version of their own.

That is the service mesh doing the work: a layer on top of the application that handles traffic, security and load balancing, so the code does not have to. It sets the bar for the rest of the session. Cloud native here means changing what runs in production while people keep using it.

## How fast is Java in dev mode, really?

Fast enough to make the demo work. With Quarkus dev mode running through Maven, every save is hot deployed. The base project started in about one second, a renamed REST endpoint went live in roughly 600 milliseconds, and most later changes took between 1.2 and 2.7 seconds to reload.

The first app manages fruits. He adds Hibernate with Panache over JDBC, a fruit entity and a REST resource, seeds data with an import SQL file, then writes a custom finder that lists fruits by season. All of it runs locally against the live-reloading process, so the feedback loop feels closer to a scripting language than to the Java most people remember.

## From laptop to Kubernetes with two extensions

Deployment is two more extensions: one builds the container image, the other generates and applies the Kubernetes resources. A Maven package with the Quarkus Kubernetes deploy flag set to true then builds the image, pushes it and deploys it. It did not work the first time. He had to log in to his registry and add a certificate trust setting, which is the most honest minute of the talk. Once it was through, the pod came up fast, because a Quarkus app starts fast, and the service answered on its first curl.

## Health checks, metrics, then reactive

The rest of the session walks the features an orchestrator expects:

- **REST client**: the fruits get carbohydrates and calories from the external Fruityvice API through a typed interface.
- **Health checks**: adding the extension alone exposes a health endpoint. He then writes a custom liveness probe and a readiness probe, explaining that Kubernetes restarts what is not live and waits for what is not ready.
- **Metrics**: Micrometer, now the Quarkus default, with MicroProfile Metrics still supported. A counted annotation on a method, a few calls, and the counter shows up on the metrics endpoint.
- **Reactive with Mutiny**: a beer service on Punk API, returning Mutiny types instead of plain objects.
- **Reactive streams with Kafka**: a wine price generator feeding Kafka, with Kafka and ZooKeeper started from a Docker Compose file, and an endpoint streaming priced wines back.

Fruit, then beer, then wine. Whatever else this talk is, it is a well-stocked menu.

## Who should watch

Java developers who still picture cloud native as something done to other languages, and teams weighing Quarkus who want to see the developer loop before reading the docs. He says up front that he skips the details to show the bigger picture, so treat it as a tour of what is possible, not a tutorial you can copy line by line.

Title: Terraform can't see the drift it doesn't manage
Description: Stephane Jourdan (CloudSkiff) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on infrastructure drift, three AWS stories Terraform missed, and IaC coverage with driftctl
Body:
A clean terraform plan says your code matches the resources Terraform knows about. It says nothing about the access key someone created by hand on a Saturday. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Stephane Jourdan](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Stephane_Jourdan_infrastructure_drift), CTO of CloudSkiff, co-author of the Infrastructure as Code Cookbook and co-founder of the open-source tool driftctl, told three short AWS stories where drift went unnoticed, and demoed how to measure it.

The talk grew out of user interviews: asked about their biggest pain with infrastructure as code, DevOps engineers, SREs and CTOs kept naming drift. Stephane Jourdan said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 that the one thing to remember is "almost everyone experienced infrastructure drift recently, and that drifts can have major consequences, including security."

## What counts as drift?

His definition: what happens when reality and expectations don't match. Your AWS account holds a set of actual resources. Terraform manages part of it. The difference is the drift. The usual sources: manual changes in the console, authenticated Lambdas, microservices and nightly scripts that create or modify resources, another team using another tool, a service your Terraform provider version doesn't support yet, and the new project on a new cloud that nobody had time to automate. The security problem is simple: you can't fix a misconfiguration on a resource you don't know exists.

## Three stories Terraform didn't catch

**The IAM key.** A weekend incident on a freshly deployed microservice. On-call deactivated its access key, created a new one, then attached a broader policy on top of the read-only one. It started working a few minutes later, and the report back on Monday never happened. Terraform applied cleanly forever after, because a new access key and a new policy attachment are new objects outside its state, not changes to managed ones. In the demo, driftctl scanned 59 resources and flagged the unmanaged key on that user.

**The security group.** Early in the pandemic, a couple of people couldn't reach the company network from home, and a manager with enough credentials added an all-traffic rule from anywhere, IPv4 and IPv6, to a group that only allowed SSH from the local network. He named it temp. Terraform ran in CI every hour or so and still reported nothing, because the way the rules were written, an added rule is a separate object. driftctl showed the unmanaged rule and IaC coverage dropping from 85% to 66%. The group stayed open for a very long time.

**The S3 bill.** A London team of about 100 developers uploaded hundreds of gigabytes of throwaway plugin builds to S3 every day. A compliance team in another country agreed not to enable versioning on that bucket, then ran a script whose exception list didn't work and enabled it everywhere. The bucket was declared in Terraform, yet terraform apply reported nothing, and the refresh quietly wrote versioning into the state. As the slides put it, only billing noticed.

## Measuring drift like test coverage

The useful idea is to treat drift like test coverage: a percentage of your cloud that your IaC actually describes. driftctl reports it and can emit JSON, so you can pull the coverage figure out with jq and graph it on a dashboard or a pull request. Filters (JMESPath expressions) narrow a scan to one resource type, such as security group rules. A .driftignore file, modelled on .gitignore, lets you park known unmanaged resources while you import or delete them, and you can bake it into your own image built on the official Docker image.

Once the first report is clean, run it in CI or as a cron job, every hour or so for a modest account. He has seen it used in two opposite places: after terraform apply, to catch the mess left by the scripts that run after it, or before apply, as a safety check so a refresh doesn't silently rewrite state. It also runs happily in parallel with terraform plan, since one looks inside Terraform's scope and the other outside it.

At the time of the talk driftctl was months old: written in Go, Apache 2.0, supporting AWS and GitHub, reading state locally, from S3 or over HTTP, with the next cloud provider chosen by community vote.

## Who should watch

Anyone running Terraform on an account humans can also log into, which is everyone. The demos are short and the stories are painfully familiar.

Title: How Honeycomb moved to Graviton2 by testing on its dogfood first
Description: Shelby Spees (Honeycomb.io) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on how SLOs and a dogfood environment made Honeycomb's Graviton2 migration safe and 40% cheaper
Body:
Honeycomb cut the AWS bill for its highest-volume service by 40% by moving it to ARM, and the interesting part is how they knew the move was safe. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Shelby Spees](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Shelby_Spees_graviton2_honeycomb_infra_spend_highestvolume_service), Developer Advocate at Honeycomb.io, told the story of one of the early production adoptions of AWS Graviton2: the measurement first, then a gradual A/B rollout, then one change that went wrong.

Her first rule is not to do it because it is new and shiny. Have a measurable outcome.

## Why would a startup risk changing CPU architecture?

Because, as she put it, infrastructure is Honeycomb's second biggest expense after people, and it scales with traffic. Landing large customers means more traffic, so cost per event matters. Shelby Spees said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021: "Technical decisions are business decisions."

But only if reliability holds. Honeycomb already ran on service level objectives (the home page loads quickly with data, queries return fast, ingested data is stored fast and successfully) with error budgets and burn-rate alerts. A stable stretch of SLOs is what gave them room to experiment, and the same SLOs are how they judged the experiment.

## Dogfood, then kibble, then prod

The setup is the best idea in the talk. Honeycomb runs the same git hash in three environments. Production takes customers' telemetry. Dogfood takes production's telemetry, so Honeycombers query real production data the way customers do; it is not staging. Kibble observes dogfood. The services are dog-themed too: Shepherd for ingest, Retriever for the columnar store and query engine, Poodle for the web front end.

They started with Shepherd: the highest traffic, stateless, scales on CPU only, optimised for throughput then latency. Being a Go shop helped. The port was mostly setting arm64 as a compile target and adding a build step to the CircleCI config. Her teammate Liz started it as a side project and saw compelling results within a few idle afternoons.

## What did the A/B test show?

One Graviton2 instance in the dogfood Shepherd autoscaling group, then more via Terraform as confidence grew. At 20% they let it sit for a couple of weeks. The Graviton instances had lower latency and less tail latency, with median latency about 10% faster. CPU utilisation topped out around 60% on the old architecture and closer to 85% on Graviton, so they got more work per vCPU. After the cutover and some tuning, the cost graph was, in her words, her favourite graph so far.

Production Shepherd followed with a similar saving. For Retriever, the goal was speed, not savings: they spent a little more to get double the cores, and with each arm64 core handling 50% more load than the Intel equivalent, ended up with triple the performance. Since then traffic on Retriever has approached triple, with P99 latency holding steady.

## The snags

Spot capacity ran out: scaling up in production used every available Graviton2 spot instance of the type they needed. They paused, reached out to the Graviton2 team, and capacity was shifted within a few hours.

The bigger lesson was Kafka, which sits between Shepherd and Retriever. They tried Graviton2 for Kafka before even Confluent had, while also moving to Confluent tiered storage and AWS Nitro. Shelby Spees said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021: "we ended up changing too many variables at once." They reverted it and published a blog post and a full incident report. At the time of the talk, four of the five biggest services were fully on Graviton2.

## Take care of the people running the migration

The closing section is about humans. Encourage people to escalate when they are tired, push them to take time off after off-hours incident work, and write the unspoken rules down. One that came out of these incidents: people handling incidents can expense meals for themselves and their families. "One of our values at honeycomb is that we hire adults, and adults have responsibilities outside of work." Isolate variables, keep feedback loops tight, and accept that some migrations, like Kafka, take longer than planned.

## Who should watch

Teams weighing an ARM migration, and anyone planning a big infrastructure change who wants a template for doing it safely. The dogfood-observes-prod setup alone is worth stealing.

Title: Moving HBase to Kubernetes meant fixing upgrades, leaders and DNS
Description: Dhiraj Hegde (Salesforce) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on running HBase and HDFS on Kubernetes in public cloud, with a custom StatefulSet controller
Body:
Kubernetes grew up running stateless web servers behind a load balancer. HBase is the opposite: clients that need to know exactly which server holds which data, and cache that knowledge. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Dhiraj Hegde](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Dhiraj_Hegde_hbase_hdfs_kubernetes_public_cloud), Architect at Salesforce, explained how his team moved HBase and the Hadoop file system from bare metal into Kubernetes on public cloud, and the four places where Kubernetes needed help.

The scale behind it: Salesforce ran HBase on thousands of machines in its own data centers, with petabytes of data and billions of queries a day, managed in place with Puppet and Ambari.

## Why Kubernetes for a database?

Three reasons. **Immutability:** in-place installs on thousands of hosts leave some half-upgraded, and engineers fixing an incident edit configs by hand and forget. A container restarts from its image, so drift disappears. **Availability and elasticity:** pods move off failed hosts and scale up and down, which is the point of being in the cloud. **Consistency across clouds:** they started on AWS but expected Azure and GCP. Dhiraj Hegde said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021: "Kubernetes is actually very opinionated." It dictates how compute, storage and network are managed, so deployment processes built for one cloud carry over to the others.

## StatefulSets get you most of the way

A StatefulSet gives each pod a stable name and DNS entry, and a persistent volume claim (a 1 TB SSD in his example) that follows the name. When a host dies, the pod comes back on another host with the same hostname and the same disk. The IP address, though, changes. Data servers and metadata servers each became a StatefulSet.

## Fix one, upgrades: a custom controller

The StatefulSet controller upgrades pods strictly from the highest ordinal down, one at a time. With hundreds of pods that each take around five minutes to boot and set up Kerberos keytabs, that is far too slow.

Kubernetes is extensible, so they wrote a custom controller that works alongside the stock one using the OnDelete update strategy. The custom controller decides which pods to delete next. The StatefulSet controller recreates them with the new spec. That gave them:

- **Batch upgrades**, deleting pods in groups instead of one by one.
- **Unhealthy pods first.** With a pod disruption budget of one and two pods already unhealthy, the default order would block forever, because replacing a healthy pod adds a third disruption. Replacing the broken pods first unblocks the rollout.
- **Leader last.** Kubernetes knows nothing about leader election, so a naive rollout can hit the leader again and again as it gets re-elected onto old pods. A sidecar in each pod publishes a leader label, and the controller upgrades the leader once, at the end.

## Fix two and three, DNS

Old Hadoop and HBase code grew up where IPs never changed. Dhiraj Hegde said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 that "there was a lot of bugs in this code base where it would resolve DNS hostname to IP address and cache that information for literally forever in its code." Data servers lost their metadata servers every time a metadata pod moved.

Rather than wait until every such bug was found, they put a Kubernetes service, a virtual load balancer with a static IP, in front of each metadata server pod, and fixed the bugs in parallel. Recreating the stateless pattern for just those servers bought them breathing room.

The second DNS problem is that clients usually live outside the cluster and use a global DNS, not the cluster's CoreDNS. The open-source ExternalDNS tool copies the records out, but it runs periodically, about once a minute. So a booting data server checks that its record is visible in global DNS before it declares itself ready for traffic.

## Fix four, surviving an availability zone

They spread pods across three availability zones with affinity and anti-affinity rules on zone labels. For the data, they reused Hadoop's rack topology: a script tells HDFS that each zone is a rack, so the three replicas of every block land in different zones. Metadata servers are spread the same way. Lose a whole zone to a power or network outage, and the software and its data keep serving.

## Who should watch

Anyone putting a mature stateful system, Cassandra, Kafka, ZooKeeper or HBase itself, onto Kubernetes. The problems are generic to software designed for static hosts, and the fixes are clear enough to reuse.

Title: Security teams can't be gatekeepers in a pipeline that ships hourly
Description: Matt Jarvis (Snyk) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on building security into every pipeline stage, from IDE to admission control, for code, containers and IaC
Body:
Most of the vulnerable code in your application was written by someone you have never heard of, two dependencies removed from anything you chose. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Matt Jarvis](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Matt_Jarvis_conunuous_security_pipelines), Senior Developer Advocate at Snyk, argued that a security review at the end of the deploy process cannot keep up with continuous delivery, and mapped where security checks belong instead.

His starting point is that application, container and infrastructure are now one thing, declared as code and owned by the same team. Security, in many organisations, still behaves as if it were an external step after deployment.

## What exactly are we securing?

Three classes of thing, and he gives each a number or an example:

- **Open source dependencies.** Modern apps are a small core of homegrown code on top of a huge tree of third-party modules. Matt Jarvis said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 that "typically over 70% of all security vulnerabilities are found in these indirect dependencies," the ones you have least control over. His example is an npm package from 2018 that claimed to parse HTTP headers and was actually about 40 lines of remote code execution, hidden behind other dependencies until it ended up under a widely downloaded mail parser.
- **Container images.** Upstream images and full-OS base images bring large numbers of vulnerabilities, and images that were clean at build time pick up new CVEs in production. The fixes are usually cheap: over 40% of Docker image vulnerabilities can be fixed by upgrading the base image, and around 20% just by rebuilding.
- **Infrastructure as code.** Kubernetes YAML, Helm charts and Terraform, often copied from public repos by people who don't fully know what each line does. Big breaches tend to combine an application bug with an infrastructure misconfiguration that widens the blast radius.

On Kubernetes he is blunt: "kubernetes really doesn't give you any guardrails. It's insecure by default." No resource limits by default, so one pod can starve a node. Containers allowed to run as root, with many public images built to do so. Writable root filesystems and the runtime's full set of Linux capabilities, most of which your app never needs.

## Where do the checks go?

He walks the pipeline from left to right:

1. **The developer's machine.** CLI tools and IDE integrations that report severity, exploitability and a fix, not just a list of CVEs, before code reaches a repo.
2. **Git.** Two-factor auth, key hygiene, keeping git updated, no unencrypted config in repos (even local ones), gitignore, strong reviews, pre-commit hooks.
3. **Pull requests and repos.** Automated scans on every PR, plus ongoing monitoring, because a dependency that was clean at commit time may not be today.
4. **Registries.** Use built-in scanning, and keep scanning images you haven't changed, since their base images have.
5. **CI/CD.** Scan in the build, catching upstream changes on every rebuild.
6. **Production.** Scan running containers, enforce policy at admission with Open Policy Agent (for example, refuse unscanned images), and watch the emerging runtime anomaly-detection tools.

## The new job description for security teams

The organisational point is the one worth the half hour. With deployment in developers' hands, Matt Jarvis said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, "security teams aren't gatekeepers anymore." Their role becomes advisor and toolsmith: pick tools that fit developer workflows with as little friction as possible, automate the checks at every stage, and let teams keep their velocity.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers designing a DevSecOps pipeline, and developers who want the reasoning behind the scanners they are asked to run. It is a vendor talk, and Snyk gets a mention at the developer stage and at the end, but most of the advice is tool-agnostic.

Title: Global active-active serverless works best as read local, write global
Description: Jorge Fonseca (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on a multi-region serverless reference architecture with CQRS, the saga pattern and async replication
Body:
Users in Europe calling a backend in Australia pay roughly 300 extra milliseconds on every dynamic request, and a CDN cannot cache that away. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Jorge Fonseca](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Jorge_Fonseca_global_activeactive_serverless), Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, built a multi-region active-active serverless architecture for one specific workload, layer by layer, and landed on a pattern that sidesteps most write conflicts.

He is upfront about the cost of the exercise. Jorge Fonseca said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021: "building and successfully running a multiregion active active architecture is hard."

## Why go multi-region at all?

Latency first. "Amazon has reported a drop of 1% in sales for each additional 100 milliseconds in load time," he notes, and games, banking and interactive apps cannot absorb an extra 300 ms. Other legitimate reasons: disaster recovery, data residency, and tenant isolation for SaaS.

He also lists the anti-patterns. High availability inside one region is a job for availability zones, not regions. And edge services are often enough to fix latency without the complexity. The talk assumes you have weighed those and still chose multi-region.

The use case is concrete: an HTTP API over relational data, heavy on reads, light on writes, with writes that must be transactional across several microservices, third-party services and on-premises systems.

## The network layer

- **AWS Transit Gateway** in each region, peered into a full mesh over the AWS backbone at up to 100 Gbps, encrypted and off the public internet.
- **AWS Direct Connect** from data centers to the nearest region for production, with site-to-site and client VPN as the internet-based alternatives.
- **Amazon CloudFront** in front of the APIs to accelerate dynamic calls and websockets, plus **Amazon Route 53** latency, geolocation and geoproximity routing to send each user to the nearest region under the same URL.

## Sync or async replication?

Synchronous replication keeps regions consistent but makes them depend on each other: one region fails, they all fail. Asynchronous replication survives regional outages but invites write conflicts. He picks async and then designs the conflicts out.

The data stores he weighs: DynamoDB global tables (he cites up to 10 trillion requests a day and peaks of 20 million requests per second, with single-digit millisecond replication), ruled out as the system of record because the use case is relational and transactional. Aurora Global Database, which can promote a secondary region in under a minute, giving an RTO of 1 minute and an RPO of 1 second. And S3 replication, with 99.99% of objects replicated within 15 minutes.

## CQRS and read local, write global

Command query responsibility segregation fits the read-heavy shape. Writes go to normalised relational models. A denormalised copy lands in DynamoDB in exactly the shape the API returns, so reads are cheap. He shows it with API Gateway and Lambda, an asynchronous variant with a queue plus websocket notifications when the write completes, and an AWS AppSync GraphQL version that gives real-time subscriptions straight from DynamoDB without code.

Across regions, reads are served locally from DynamoDB global tables, and mutations happen only in the primary region; secondaries forward their writes. "This pattern is called read local, write global," and it removes cross-region data conflicts at the cost of extra write latency from secondary regions, which barely matters for a read-heavy API.

## Transactions across microservices: the saga

For writes that span services, third parties and on-premises components, he uses the saga pattern on AWS Step Functions. His example is checkout: pre-authorise the card, then charge it, then update the customer record, each step with single responsibility while the orchestration and failure handling live in the state machine. Amazon EventBridge carries the asynchronous mutations.

## What happens when a region fails?

A secondary region fails: Route 53 health checks move its users elsewhere, they notice a bit more latency, and data resyncs automatically when the region returns. The primary region fails: the application drops to read-only. If the business can live with that for the expected outage, wait. If not, promote a secondary and run the disaster recovery procedure.

## Who should watch

Architects with a real reason to leave a single region. It is a dense, well-ordered reference architecture walkthrough, published on the AWS Architecture Center, with no live demo.

Title: Static stability means the capacity is already there when a zone dies
Description: Eduardo Janicas (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on static stability, why EC2 avoids control plane dependencies in recovery, and zonal services
Body:
If your plan for losing an availability zone is to autoscale in the other two, your recovery depends on the most complicated part of the cloud working perfectly during an outage. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Eduardo Janicas](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Eduardo_Janicas_stability_availability), Solutions Architect at AWS, explained static stability, the pattern AWS uses to avoid exactly that, and how Amazon EC2 itself is built around it.

The lesson he opens with is short. Eduardo Janicas said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 that one lesson AWS has learned is to "be ready for impairments before they happen."

## Control plane versus data plane

The whole talk rests on a split borrowed from networking. The control plane makes changes: for EC2, launching an instance means finding a physical server that respects placement groups and tenancy, allocating a network interface from the subnet, preparing an EBS volume, generating IAM role credentials, installing security groups and propagating all of it. The data plane is the daily business of resources that already exist: routing packets by VPC route tables, reading and writing EBS volumes.

The data plane is far simpler, runs at orders of magnitude higher volume, and matters more to customers. A running instance staying up is worth more to most people than the ability to launch a new one. The control plane has more moving parts, so it is statistically more likely to be impaired. Hence the rule: separate the two, and let the data plane keep its last known state and keep working when the control plane cannot reach it.

## Why is autoscaling into the surviving zones the weaker plan?

Not because you won't be able to launch instances, he says, but because recovery now takes an immediate dependency on the EC2 control plane plus everything your app needs to become useful: downloading config, registering with service discovery, fetching credentials. All of that has to work while something is already broken.

The statically stable version provisions ahead. Stateless fleets behind a load balancer run across three or more zones, overprovisioned so the remaining zones carry the load. As he put it, "when you use three availability zones, we over provision by 50%," which means each zone runs at only 66% of the level it was load tested for. When a zone fails, instances there fail health checks, the load balancer shifts traffic, and nobody does anything. Elastic Load Balancing itself is built this way, and the same pattern works for workers pulling from an SQS queue.

Stateful services get active-standby: Amazon RDS keeps a standby in a different zone and repoints DNS on failover, and leader-based clusters elect a new leader from a standby that is already running instead of launching a replacement just in time.

## The arithmetic behind zonal services

The best part is a probability argument. Take a regional service that calls another regional service, both spread over three zones, with one zone suffering a grey failure the load balancer cannot see. The request avoids the bad zone with probability 2/3 at each hop, so 4/9 over two hops: in his words, "the request has worse than even odds of steering clear of the event." With N regional services in the path it is (2/3) to the power of N.

If the downstream service is zonal, so each caller talks to the endpoint in its own zone, the odds stay at 2/3 however long the chain. That is why the EC2 NAT gateway is a zonal resource that customers create per zone rather than a regional, VPC-wide gateway: an impairment in one zone should stay in that zone.

EC2 applies the same independence to deployments. Software for servers, edge devices, DNS resolvers and the launch path follows a zonal deployment calendar, so two zones in a region get a given change on different days, after the usual one-box-then-more rollout. A bad deploy hits one zone and gets rolled back there.

## Which pattern should you pick?

Regional calling regional is the simpler default and the right choice for most external and internal services. AWS uses it for higher-level services such as Amazon API Gateway. Regional calling zonal, or zonal calling zonal, is for data path infrastructure, and it has a side benefit he mentions in passing: keeping traffic inside a zone has favourable network cost characteristics on AWS.

## Who should watch

Architects running multi-AZ workloads who have never written down what happens in the first ten minutes of a zone failure. It is a lecture, not a demo, and he points to the Amazon Builders' Library for more on the same ideas.

Title: Deep health checks need a fail-open escape hatch
Description: Andrew Robinson (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on deep health checks, soft dependencies with static fallbacks, and when a load balancer should fail open
Body:
A health check that only returns 200 tells you the process is up. A health check that also calls your dependencies tells you much more, and can take your whole fleet down when that dependency gets slow. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Andrew Robinson](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Andrew_Robinson_improving_reliability_health_check_dependency_management), Principal Solutions Architect on the AWS Well-Architected team, walked through both sides of that trade with a small Python web app and the load balancer setting that rescues it.

## The demo workload

The app is a recommendation engine: users come in through an internet gateway to an Elastic Load Balancer, which spreads requests over three EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group, one per availability zone. Recommendations come from an external API backed by Amazon DynamoDB, reached through NAT gateways, one per zone, so a network failure in one zone does not cut the others off. Moving the recommendation call outside the app is the first, simplest piece of loose coupling. Queues or streams would go further.

## From shallow to deep health checks

The shallow version answers the load balancer on a health check path with HTTP 200. It proves the instance and the application are running and nothing more.

The deep version sets an is-healthy flag to false first, then calls the recommendation service inside a try block as part of the check. Only a valid response flips the flag. Healthy returns 200 with some metadata. Anything else returns a 503 with the exception traceback, so whoever looks at the failure has something to go on. The load balancer marks that instance unhealthy and stops sending it traffic. Andrew Robinson said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021: "This is a behavior that we call fail closed."

## Why would you ever send traffic to unhealthy instances?

Because a deep check couples every instance to the same dependency. If that dependency is slow, instances start flapping, and the failure-count threshold that would replace a single bad host never trips cleanly. In his words, "you may end up with all of the instances flapping at the same time, all go unhealthy at the same time, and then your application isn't available."

So when every target in the pool fails its check, the load balancer fails open and sends requests to all of them. That is the safety net: automation handles single failures, and when everything looks broken at once, the system keeps serving and a human gets to diagnose it. He pairs it with rate-limited thresholds or circuit breakers to turn the automation off before it removes the whole fleet. Test both checks, the shallow and the deep one, and test the failure modes of each.

## Hard dependency, soft dependency, I Love Lucy

The same thinking applies to the request path. Calling the recommendation API directly makes it a hard dependency: if the call fails, the user gets a 502 or 503 and the page is dead. Wrapping it in a try block with a fallback makes it soft. When the call fails, the app serves a predetermined static answer, and his choice of default is excellent: "we'd recommend the tv show I love Lucy to them."

The page also tells the user the recommendation is not personalised right now and shows the error code. Nobody gets their perfect show, but everyone gets a working page, and in a larger application the rest of it keeps working too.

## The rules he leaves you with

- Components should keep working, degraded, when their dependencies are unhealthy. No dynamic answer, then a static one.
- Health checks belong at the application layer (the data plane), not on the underlying infrastructure.
- Fail closed for one bad instance, fail open when all of them fail.
- Use multiple layers of checks, from lightweight to deep, because servers and software fail for very different and very weird reasons.
- Put tracebacks in error responses to cut the cognitive load on the engineer on call.

## Who should watch

Anyone who owns a load balancer config or has written a health endpoint and wondered what it should actually check. The code is short and explained for non-developers. The full architecture and code live in the open-source AWS Well-Architected labs on GitHub, part of a collection of over 100 labs, and he points to the Amazon Builders' Library article on implementing health checks for more depth.

Title: A passed cloud audit means you convinced an auditor, not that you're secure
Description: Ashish Rajan (Cloud Security Podcast) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on how real cloud security assessments differ from the docs, and why CSPM alone falls short
Body:
Every cloud provider publishes a Well-Architected framework, and almost nobody's account looks like one. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Ashish Rajan](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Ashish_Rajan_Cloud_Security_Assessments_in_2021), producer and host of the Cloud Security Podcast and a former cloud security consultant, told the practitioner's version of running cloud security assessments. His real title for the talk, he admits, would have been documentation versus reality.

The sharpest line comes at the end. Ashish Rajan said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021: "a successful compliance certification doesn't really mean you're secure. It just does mean that you were able to convince an auditor that you are ticking all the boxes."

## What does the documentation assume?

The expected client, per the docs: one or two cloud providers, everything defined in CloudFormation or another code repository, cloud native services, several deploys a day, and nobody with SSH or RDP into production.

What he actually found as an auditor:

- **A single tenancy that hides hundreds of services.** A single network hosting many applications, a mix of containers, Kubernetes and VMs, monoliths carried over from a decade ago next to microservices.
- **A YAML file instead of access.** Teams deep into infrastructure as code who asked him to audit the template and gave him no access to the accounts.
- **Too much access.** A 25-person startup that handed him full admin out of trust. His advice: don't give admin access to an external auditor.
- **Account sprawl.** One business unit with 20+ accounts, because account separation was recommended and accounts are free.

The good counterexample: an enterprise with a central team that provisions every tenancy with security defaults, which gave him read-only access and asked him to bring his automation. He ran tools during the interviews and finished in about half the time.

So his first question in any engagement is which kind of migration this was, lift and shift or a real transformation, and how far along it is. And his warning about leaning only on the provider's own tooling: "don't just rely on cloud native and stop drinking the kool aid."

## Where does initial access come from?

He uses the MITRE ATT&CK cloud matrix but focuses on initial access, since everything else assumes it. The techniques collapse into three buckets: an exploited public-facing application (a bucket made public, a Kubernetes API open to the internet), stolen credentials (cloud IAM sharing the corporate password with no SSO or MFA, plus machine identities whose keys work while you sleep), and third parties, every CSPM, monitoring or other vendor you have handed a credential into your account.

## Point in time versus continuous

The argument he most wants to land is that you need both. Point-in-time assessments, by an auditor with a checklist or a practitioner with automation, produce an actionable backlog. Continuous tools, CSPM and CASB, give visibility against a standard such as CIS or NIST, but they are API-driven checklists without context. A public bucket that is meant to be public, or one covered by an account-level block, still shows up red. New services arrive in the tools later than in the console. The result is the wall of red that hides the real findings he would hand you on day one.

He points to Checkov from Bridgecrew and the infrastructure-as-code scanners as the next generation, catching problems at commit time. Open source tools come with the same lag on new services, so someone on the team has to keep them current. And hire an auditor who understands that cloud compute is ephemeral and IPs change under autoscaling.

## Who should watch

Anyone about to commission, run or survive a cloud audit, and CSPM owners staring at a dashboard full of alerts. It is opinionated and specific, from someone who has sat on both sides of the table.

Title: Your biggest cloud threat depends on how new you are to cloud
Description: Stuart Green (Check Point Software Technologies) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on how cloud maturity decides which threats bite, and why visibility comes first
Body:
Ask a cloud security architect what the biggest cloud threat is and the honest answer is unsatisfying. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Stuart Green](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Stuart_Green_loud_thread_landscape_2021), Cloud Security Architect at Check Point Software Technologies working with customers across the UK and Ireland, opened with exactly that. Stuart Green said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021: "I'll start with a vague answer, which is, it depends."

What it depends on, he argues, is the customer's maturity. Everyone faces the same risks, but in a different order, and the talk is a tour of the three kinds of customer he meets every week and what goes wrong for each.

One note on scope: the abstract promises Check Point Research findings and COVID-19 threat statistics. The talk itself is a field report from customer conversations, and he promises up front not to pitch any product. He keeps the promise.

## Three customers, three different problems

**The reluctant mover.** A traditional organisation, often public sector, with servers in a data center and a mandate from someone somewhere to go to the cloud. No education, no budget, no enthusiasm. They browse the console, find compute and databases, and recreate what they had. Expect misconfiguration.

**The square peg.** A business with a real driver, usually cost, that treats cloud as the fix for everything and lifts and shifts what it ran on premises. He is careful here: cloud can be more cost effective, but cheaper is a misconception. The typical failures are architectures that do not behave the way they did in the data center, and security controls that were left behind with a plan to add them later.

**The cloud native.** Teams that have never racked a server and never want to. For them it is all about native tools, APIs and the speed of the next change to production. A ticket for a firewall rule change is a blocker, and security that slows them down gets routed around.

His request to the experts in the audience: don't look down on the first group. You made the same mistakes when you were new.

## Who owns security when there is no perimeter?

The middle of the talk walks the maturity curve from data center to serverless and names what changes. Change rates go from one or two requests a week to dozens or hundreds a day. Control shifts from the network, firewall and security teams to the developer, who now writes the code, deploys it and hopefully thought about open ports and dependency scanning on the way. And the perimeter fragments: ask where the firewall goes in a serverless architecture and the answer is that it doesn't.

## Misconfiguration, IAM, visibility

His top three:

- **Misconfiguration**, mostly storage (S3, Azure storage accounts), networks and databases. He quotes Gartner moving its estimate from about 95% to up to 99% of cloud security failures being the customer's fault through 2025. Automation is his answer, with a warning from the field: one team automated storage permissions, got them wrong, and produced hundreds if not thousands of badly configured services at once. They caught it early and fixed it with the same templating.
- **IAM**, which he calls the area with no magic product. Attackers who got in through a vulnerable workload have used over-broad permissions to move laterally until they could get data out. Use groups rather than per-user grants, use AWS permissions boundaries, and use the MITRE ATT&CK framework to decide where to focus.
- **Visibility**, the one executives care about. Logging is often off by default because storage costs money, and multi-cloud multiplies the number of consoles to dig through. His line on it: "If you don't know what you've deployed in public cloud, you have pretty much no hope of securing it."

The agility that makes cloud attractive becomes a threat when security is parked for later, because later tends to arrive as someone else finding the deployment first. Stuart Green said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021: "Security needs to be a primary consideration when you're moving to cloud. It shouldn't be an afterthought."

## Who should watch

Security people who sell, advise or audit, and anyone who has to explain cloud risk to a mixed audience. It is a non-technical, people-first talk: no demos, plenty of pattern recognition.

Title: Before you move to the cloud, assume your network is hostile
Description: Vandana Verma (IBM) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on secure architecture reviews, threat modelling and shared responsibility before a cloud move
Body:
A pen test tells you whether the front door is locked. It does not tell you whether the house was designed with a door at all. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Vandana Verma](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Vandana_Verma_secure_architecture), Security Architect at IBM and a member of the OWASP global board of directors, made the case for a secure architecture review as the first step of any cloud move, and for starting that review from one uncomfortable premise.

Vandana Verma said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021: "the first thing that we have to understand that our network is hostile, completely hostile, before even moving to the cloud."

## Why bother with a review when you already pen test?

Her framing is the pandemic rush of 2020 and 2021: organisations that were still planning a cloud migration suddenly found themselves on one. Lift and shift was the default, and she is blunt about legacy applications copied into containers without changes. They carry their overhead with them, plus new budget and support questions.

The numbers she cites are from the IBM and Ponemon research of the time: security breaches up 11% since 2018 and 67% since 2014, an attack every 39 seconds on average, and an average of 206 days to identify a breach in 2019. A regular pen test gives some assurance, she argues, but it does not look at the overall architecture design, and that is where an open bucket or database credentials committed to a public repo come from. Her point on the second one: change the password all you like, the code that was public stays cached.

## What does the review actually cover?

The methodology is a sequence rather than a checklist:

- **Data flow diagrams** first, to map the high-level cloud architecture and draw the trust boundaries.
- **Threat modelling** on top of them. She names STRIDE, PASTA and Trike, and says she has been working with STRIDE a lot. The tooling matters less than you think: "the tool is less important than the data recorded."
- **A risk-based plan** for what moves, what gets protected and where it lands.
- **Gap analysis** for visibility into your own environment, because many teams moving to the cloud do not know what they run today.

And for the threat modelling sessions themselves, her preference is refreshingly low-tech: "Whiteboarding is my favorite."

## The tenant analogy for shared responsibility

The shared responsibility model gets the most airtime. Her analogy: moving to the cloud is like renting out a house. The tenant calls you when something breaks, but you still own the house, so read the agreement, and get lawyers or auditors who understand its language. Whatever the service model, IaaS, PaaS or serverless, the data is always yours to protect, and so is your application code and its repositories.

Concrete items she lists for the plan: boundary protection and a WAF for internal applications too (HR tools and learning portals get attacked as well), MFA for everyone rather than only privileged users, least privilege, encryption at rest and in transit with proper key management, and audit logging with a decided retention and protection story. She also asks about the right to audit your provider, which many providers answer with their own reports instead.

On credentials she tells a story from an older project where developers were working with the cloud root credentials. Her summary of why that keeps security people awake: "cloud is like, if I get your credentials, especially root credentials, I can own your network."

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering leads planning a migration, or living with one that happened in a hurry. This is a methodology and checklist talk, not a tool demo, and it closes with a nudge toward zero trust and a cloud access security broker (CASB) at the cloud edge for shadow IT and SaaS monitoring.

Title: The bug that owns your container is usually in code you didn't write
Description: Brian Vermeer (Snyk) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on Docker image security, shown by hacking an outdated ImageMagick and a vulnerable Spring Data REST
Body:
Putting an application in a container doesn't seal it off from the world; the container ships its own operating system, binaries and dependencies, and each one is attack surface. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Brian Vermeer](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Brian_Vermeer_containers_breaking_in), Developer Advocate at Snyk and Java Champion, went through Docker image best practices and proved the point twice by getting remote code execution in apps whose own code was fine.

## Why isn't a container a safe box?

A real-world container, a soda can or a lunch box, keeps the outside out. Software containers need two-way traffic: a UI, a database connection, incoming requests. And everything inside is your responsibility. His slides put Docker Hub at 1 billion container image downloads a week, so the defaults people start from matter.

## Start from less

Tip one: prefer minimal base images. In Snyk's late-2019 research, all ten of the most popular free images on Docker Hub had known vulnerabilities by default. The untagged node image, for example, sat on a full Debian install. Switching Debian to Debian slim already removes a pile of issues; Alpine or Fedora may remove more. For OpenJDK 11, the default image was Ubuntu-based with 25 known vulnerabilities, mostly from the OS rather than the JDK. "What you do not have in your container cannot harm you," Brian Vermeer said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021.

## Don't run as root, and check whether a user already exists

Least privilege: create a system user with no password, home directory or shell, give it ownership of the app folder only, and switch to it with a USER line, because creating the user without switching still runs everything as root. The node image already ships a node user; many people never call it. Security is a chain of attacks, he says, so each link you harden limits how far the next step goes.

## Scan, rebuild, monitor

Most teams scan their application and forget the OS layer they ship. He shows the Snyk CLI testing a node 10 image and suggesting a better base image, then a monitor command that snapshots the image and alerts daily on new vulnerabilities and fixes. Two numbers from the slides: 44% of Docker image vulnerabilities can be fixed with newer base images, and 20% just by rebuilding. FROM ubuntu:latest today isn't the latest in three weeks, so rebuild regularly with no cache, even if your code hasn't changed a character.

## What can go wrong? Demo one: ImageTragick

A small Node.js app resizes uploaded pictures for Twitter using ImageMagick, an outdated version with improper input validation. A crafted file named like a JPEG breaks out of a URL with a pipe and runs touch; an empty file appears in the container. A second payload fetches a script from the host via host.docker.internal, downloads and unpacks a Netcat tarball, and opens a reverse shell to his machine. The application code did nothing wrong; the binary shipped with the image did.

## Your dependencies are in the container too

Lint the Dockerfile itself: he uses hadolint, which catches things like ADD where COPY belongs. Then look at the app: most of the binary is frameworks and libraries, and most of their vulnerabilities sit in indirect dependencies several levels deep.

## Demo two: the grocery list that runs commands

A Spring Boot grocery list (beans for 50 cents, milk for $1.09) uses Spring Data REST to turn a CRUD repository into endpoints. In the vulnerable version, a PATCH request to the item endpoint carries a JSON body that the server evaluates as Spring Expression Language, so he gets the runtime, executes a command and reads /etc/passwd back. Run that container as root and an attacker can read and write a lot more.

## Build big, ship small

Multi-stage builds separate the factory from the car: build with a Maven and JDK image, then copy only the jar into a JRE-on-Alpine image. His example went from 631 MB to 132 MB. It also keeps build-time secrets out of production; a registry token used during a node 12 build stays in the build stage instead of lingering in the layer history.

## Who should watch

Developers who write Dockerfiles and have never tried attacking their own images. The demos make the case better than any checklist. Snyk is his employer and the scanner on screen, and he notes the tooling shown can be used for free.
