Title: Kubernetes security is more locks on the bike, never a safe bike
Description: Mofizur Rahman (IBM) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on a Kubernetes security starter map, from base images and RBAC to admission webhooks and scanners
Body:
The strongest padlock you can buy off the shelf took a YouTube lock-picker about four minutes. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Mofizur Rahman](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Mofizur_Rahman_kubernetes_security_jumpstart), Developer Advocate at IBM, used that to set up his main point: security is a spectrum, and the job is to make your Kubernetes cluster more secure layer by layer, with the right tool at each layer, until breaking in isn't worth anyone's time.

He is clear that this is a jumpstart, not an in-depth tutorial: a checklist of what to worry about and which tools exist, with a few short demos.

## Why is security a spectrum?

His opening is a slideshow of real-world security theatre: a door with the code written on it, a turnstile next to a wide gap, a camera blocked by a sign. Then the padlock that was declared the strongest in the world, beaten by a lock-picker in about four minutes. "Things can be more secure or less secure. Never just secure," Mofizur Rahman said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021. Software is worse off than doors because, once it touches the internet, everything on the internet is an adversary.

## What should you lock down first?

He walks the stack in order:

- **Application**: follow the best practices of your language and runtime. Common sense, he notes, is not that common.
- **Container**: no unknown base images, and never latest. A specific tag is good; a digest SHA is best, because it pins exactly what you tested. Rebuild to pick up vulnerability fixes. Prefer Alpine over Debian, and scratch images for compiled languages such as Go, C, C++, Rust, or Java with GraalVM.
- **Image**: least privilege. Run as an unprivileged user, never root. "Root is the root of all evil," as he puts it: a root container that escapes is root on the host.
- **Infrastructure**: don't expose nodes. He cites the Tesla cryptojacking case, where an unauthenticated Kubernetes dashboard leaked AWS credentials. Treat metadata such as node IPs as valuable, harden nodes (no SSH), and keep both OS and Kubernetes versions current.
- **Network**: by default any pod can talk to any pod. Use network policies, for example back end accepts traffic only from front end.

## What about the cluster at runtime?

- **RBAC**: can subject verb object, scoped to the cluster or a namespace. His example lets user Jane get, watch and list pods in default, so kubectl get pods works and delete pod fails.
- **Resource quotas and limits**: a compromised pod can't starve the cluster, the scheduler packs better (he cites 70 to 80% utilisation), and equal requests and limits give the Guaranteed QoS class, so the pod is evicted last.
- **Central logging and monitoring**, outside the cluster, because pods are ephemeral and so are their logs.
- **Admission webhooks**: mutate requests to add a default quota, or reject anything without one, or with privilege escalation, or without an SELinux profile.
- **Encrypt etcd at rest**. Kubernetes secrets are only base64-encoded, so use a KMS from your cloud or HashiCorp Vault and inject secrets at runtime.

## Which tools did he show?

He stresses none of it is an endorsement. For image scanning: Anchore, Clair, Dockle, Snyk and Trivy. The demos run Dockle on a deliberately bad test image (credentials in environment variables, uncleared apt caches) and Trivy on golang:latest, a long list of CVEs; both can fail a CI build. For runtime: Falco from Sysdig, SELinux and seccomp. For networking, your overlay's own policies (IBM Cloud uses Calico). For image provenance: Grafeas, in-toto and Portieris, which has an admission webhook that only admits images from allowed sources.

For auditing, kube-bench from Aqua Security checks a running cluster, while kubeaudit and kubesec check YAML before deploy. kubeaudit flags the demo deployment for no AppArmor, the default service account, a missing security context, no run-as-non-root and unset privilege escalation; kubesec gives it a score of 4 and suggests the same fixes. OPA gets a mention as the most flexible option, too big to demo here. Service meshes (Istio, Linkerd, Kuma) add mTLS between services and traffic visibility.

## Who should watch

Developers and new platform engineers who need the whole map before going deep. Security specialists will know the list; the value is in its order and the CI-ready tools.

Title: RBAC can't enforce your trusted-registry rule. Gatekeeper can
Description: Ara Pulido (Datadog) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on policy-as-code for Kubernetes with OPA, Gatekeeper and its reusable policy library
Body:
RBAC answers who can do what to which resource. It has no opinion on whether that pod has the labels your organisation requires or pulls from a registry you trust. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Ara Pulido](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Ara_Pulido_poilcyascode_kubernetes_opa_gatekeeper), Technical Evangelist at Datadog, showed how OPA Gatekeeper fills that gap, and how far you get with its community policy library before writing a line of Rego yourself.

The talk is a compact introduction with two live demos on Minikube. If you have never used Gatekeeper, it is a good place to start.

## Why isn't RBAC enough?

She defines policy as the rules that govern what you can and cannot do with a software service. RBAC covers one slice: subject, Kubernetes API resource, verb, as in user ara may create, get and watch pods in a namespace. Authorisation is only a subset of the rules teams want, though. Images only from approved registries, mandatory labels on deployments and pods, digests on container images, CPU and memory limits on every container: none of that is expressible as RBAC.

## Where do OPA and Gatekeeper fit?

The Open Policy Agent, a CNCF project, decouples policy decisions from enforcement. It takes a JSON query, evaluates it against rules written in Rego plus any stored data, and returns a JSON decision. That's all it does; integrations handle enforcement, and Gatekeeper is the one for Kubernetes.

Gatekeeper embeds OPA and plugs into the API server's request path. A request goes through authentication, then authorisation (usually RBAC), then admission controllers, which can validate or mutate it. Gatekeeper registers as a validating admission webhook, with mutation in progress at the time, and blocks requests that violate a policy.

It is also Kubernetes native: policies are CRDs, reconciled by a controller. A ConstraintTemplate holds the Rego and declares parameters; a Constraint instantiates it. One required-labels template becomes namespaces must carry a gatekeeper label and, separately, pods in default must carry do-not-delete. Because they're ordinary objects, they live in Git with the rest of your cluster config.

## Do you have to learn Rego first?

No, and that's the main message. The common rules are the same everywhere; only the values change. The Gatekeeper Library, part of the OPA organisation, ships tested templates (HTTPS-only ingresses, required labels, allowed registries) with sample constraints and objects that should fail them. "The goal of this talk is for you to see the opportunity for gatekeeper to be used straight away, even if you don't know Rigo," Ara Pulido said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021. (The transcript's spelling; she means Rego.)

## What does it look like in a cluster?

Demo one installs Gatekeeper from the default manifest: four CRDs, a gatekeeper-system namespace with a three-replica controller and an audit pod. She applies the required-labels template from the library and adapts the sample constraint so every pod needs a conf42 label key. A typo bites first (the kind must be Pod, singular), which is the most realistic thing in the demo.

The audit pod then reports violations on existing objects without deleting them, here 14 pods, so you can roll out a new rule and clean up gradually. A new NGINX pod without the label is rejected with a clear message; add the label and it goes through.

Demo two needs context beyond the object itself: every ingress host must be unique. A Config object tells Gatekeeper to sync ingress objects into OPA's data. The first ingress is admitted, a second with the same host is rejected.

## Can you see what it's doing?

Gatekeeper exposes metrics out of the box: template and constraint counts, webhook request counts and latency, violations. Datadog's agent autodiscovered the pods and filled a ready-made dashboard, including those 14 violations. That's her employer's product; the metrics themselves come from Gatekeeper.

## Who should watch

Platform teams that have outgrown RBAC and want guardrails without building admission webhooks by hand. Rego experts can skip it.

Title: A cost-only utility function says deploy nothing. Melodic does better
Description: Paweł Skrzypek and Alicja Reniewicz (7bulls.com) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on Melodic, open source autonomous multi-cloud deployment and optimisation
Body:
Model your application once, declare what good looks like, and let the platform pick the clouds, size the resources and keep resizing them while it runs. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Paweł Skrzypek](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Pawe_Skrzypek_Alicja_Reniewicz_autonomous_multicloud_serverless_deployment), CTO of 7bulls.com, presented Melodic, an open source multi-cloud deployment platform he co-authors, and Full Stack Engineer Alicja Reniewicz showed it scaling a Spark genome-analysis job on AWS against a 60-minute deadline.

It is the authors presenting their own platform, and Paweł Skrzypek says so upfront. The demo is the part that earns the time.

## What is Melodic?

A single platform that deploys one cloud-agnostic application model to Azure, AWS, Google Cloud and OpenStack providers, covering virtual machines, containers, serverless functions and big data frameworks such as Spark. You don't learn each provider's tooling; you write a model, and Melodic decides which providers and how much of what to use. He calls it your smart, autonomic DevOps operator.

## How do you tell it what good looks like?

The model is written in CAMEL, the Cloud Application Modelling and Execution Language. It builds on TOSCA ideas but goes further: components, connections and security rules, plus requirements, constraints and a utility function that defines the best deployment.

The utility function is where the thinking is. Cost alone fails. "If we have only the cost as a goal or as utility function, then the best solution is just simply to not deploy anything because in that case the cost will be zero," Paweł Skrzypek said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021. So the utility is a trade-off between cost and business metrics (average response time, workload, a deadline), fed by custom sensors rather than CPU and memory figures.

## What happens after you press the button?

Only the modelling is manual, and only once. Then the loop: Melodic fetches offers from the selected providers, generates a constraint problem from the model, solves it, deploys, and starts collecting metrics. When a metric crosses a threshold it reasons again and reconfigures the running deployment in place, adding, removing or replacing resources rather than redeploying from scratch.

Internally it is microservices orchestrated as a BPM process in Camunda, with Mule ESB for integration and ActiveMQ with Esper for monitoring. They evaluated point-to-point, queue-based and ESB integration (three ESBs and four BPM engines in total) before settling on that pair, and the comparison is documented for anyone building something similar. The upside of BPM: changing the logic is a drag-and-drop edit, not a code change.

## What did the demo show?

Alicja Reniewicz uploads the genome application's CAMEL model (converted to XMI) through the UI. AWS credentials stay out of the model as placeholders filled from a secure store. A simulation mode lets you set metric values by hand and see which solution Melodic would pick, without starting any virtual machines; she turns it off for a real run on AWS only.

Melodic resolves the constraint problem (one to ten Spark workers allowed) and starts with a single worker in Dublin. A Grafana dashboard tracks the deadline with a traffic light: time left against estimated time, and cores needed against cores running. Within minutes the light goes red, the estimate needs four to seven cores against the one available, and a reconfiguration process kicks in and adds a second worker, which shows up in the Spark master UI. The cycle continues: add workers while the job is behind, remove them near the end once finishing on time is safe.

The second use case in the talk, a serverless image classifier fed by augmented reality glasses, is described rather than demoed.

## Who should watch

Teams that run batch or bursty workloads with a business deadline and want to see constraint-solving autoscaling across clouds in practice. If you want a general multi-cloud overview, this is one specific platform. Melodic is released under the Mozilla Public License 2.0, and the team was continuing the work in the Morphemic project.

Title: Your app thinks it's talking to S3. It's talking to Google Cloud
Description: Lawrence Finn (Cloud Sidecar) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on breaking vendor lock-in by translating AWS API calls to Google Cloud in a sidecar
Body:
The usual answer to a make-us-multi-cloud mandate is an abstraction library per service per language, which is a lot of libraries. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Lawrence Finn](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Lawrence_Finn_multicloud_breaking_cloud_sidecar), author of Cloud Sidecar, showed the opposite approach: leave the application alone, point its AWS SDK at a local sidecar, and let the sidecar translate S3, SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB and Redshift calls into their Google Cloud equivalents.

It is the author presenting his own open source project, so expect enthusiasm, but it comes with a working demo and a production story.

## Why go multi-cloud at all?

The talk opens with a CTO who read an article over breakfast and wants multi-cloud by the end of the half. Past the joke, Larry Finn gives real reasons: rising cloud bills and the leverage of being able to move; redundancy when your provider's status page says everything is fine and half the internet disagrees (though he says multi-region in one cloud is the sensible first step); picking each cloud's best service; and customers who won't work with you because of who hosts you, such as an ad tech prospect that won't touch a vendor on Google Cloud.

He splits the job in two. Infrastructure is mostly solved with Terraform or Kubernetes. Software is the hard part.

## Why not just write an abstraction layer?

Because it multiplies. Wrapping boto and google-cloud-storage behind one interface is fine for one Python app. Now add Go, Scala, Node.js, Java and something esoteric, and services like S3, SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB and Redshift: n languages times m services worth of wrappers. Then roll that out across 1,500-plus microservices, each using the SDKs slightly differently.

## How does Cloud Sidecar work?

It runs next to the application in the sidecar pattern, on localhost on an EC2 box or as a sidecar container in a Kubernetes pod. The app's own cloud library is configured to talk to localhost. An HTTP router exposes each API on its own port and sends requests to a handler (S3, SQS, Kinesis), which either passes the call through to AWS or translates it to Google Cloud and dresses the response back up as AWS. Because it translates wire APIs, it works with any language that has a cloud library.

He wrote it in Go for a small memory and CPU footprint. "It's not like JVM, which will eat all the memory on your machine," Lawrence Finn said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, adding that Go's simplicity also makes the project easier for contributors.

## What does the demo show?

A PNG-to-JPG converter: a Scala Play front end uploads to S3 and drops a message on SQS; a Python worker reads SQS, converts the image and writes the result to S3. Both talk to the sidecar on localhost. With the sidecar pointed at AWS, both files land in the S3 bucket. Restart the sidecar with a GCP config (it can reload config live, the restart is for the demo) and the next upload goes to Google Cloud Storage through Pub/Sub, without touching the Scala app or the worker.

## Where do the clouds disagree?

The interesting part is the gaps. S3 multipart upload has no GCS equivalent, so the sidecar mimics it with GCS compose (combine). Going the other way, GCS resumable upload and combine are faked using S3 primitives. SQS is a worker queue, Kinesis is offset-based like Kafka, and Pub/Sub sits in between with topics feeding many subscriptions. DynamoDB has both query and scan where Datastore has one call, and its nested JSON filter and update syntax has no direct match. For big data the sidecar speaks the Postgres wire protocol, so a JDBC client aimed at Redshift can be translated to BigQuery SQL, with stored-procedure-style plugins for queries that don't translate well.

The community edition covers S3/GCS both ways, SQS and Kinesis to Pub/Sub, plugins and middleware; DynamoDB, Redshift and StatsD/Datadog metrics were in the enterprise edition at the time.

## Does anyone run it?

Yes. His day job is at ActionIQ, a customer data platform that ran on AWS until customers asked for Google Cloud. The sidecar let them support both with very little code change, and they shipped multi-cloud before the deadline. It had been in production for many months by the time of the talk.

## Who should watch

Teams with heavy AWS SDK usage across many services facing a second-cloud requirement. The translation caveats are the real value even if you never run the tool.

Title: Write the pipeline before the feature, like you write the test first
Description: Ricardo Miranda (Closer Consulting) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on building CI/CD, infrastructure as code and test automation from day one
Body:
If your deployment automation gets built in the last sprint, it gets tested for the first time in production. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Ricardo Miranda](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Ricardo_Miranda_automation_is_where_a_project_starts), Big Data Consultant at Closer Consulting, made a short, sharp argument: treat automation the way TDD treats tests, and start it before the first line of feature code.

It is a brief talk, about ten minutes, and an opinion piece rather than a demo. That's a feature: the whole argument fits in one sitting.

## Why do services need more automation than a monolith?

He starts with the trade. A monolith tends to turn into a big ball of mud: tightly coupled, slow to change, and a newcomer can take years to really understand it. Its one advantage is that calls are cheap: no latency, no transport security, no service discovery. And it scales up, onto a bigger machine, which is slow, expensive, and sometimes impossible because the bigger machine doesn't exist.

Services flip that. Each one does one thing, a newcomer gets it in days, and you can rewrite one and benchmark it against the old version. Each scales out and in on its own. The complexity moves to coordination: contracts, discoverability, secure communication and a much harder deploy.

His wish list follows: loosely coupled services you can develop, maintain, test and deploy independently. The catch is the code that wish list demands. "The amount of code that you need to develop for your application increases much more than the functional requirements," Ricardo Miranda said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021.

## What does the toolchain look like?

Nothing exotic, and that's the point:

- **Git** for everything, with one repository per service, the approach he says has worked best for his teams.
- **An automation server** such as Jenkins for builds, tests and deploys.
- **Artifactory** to store versioned artifacts.
- **Infrastructure as code**, such as Terraform, for everything from virtual machines to databases, tables and VPNs.

The flow: every merge to main publishes a new artifact version, and deploying is a script call that says which version goes to which environment. Testing goes well beyond unit tests: integration, acceptance, performance and security tests all have to be automated before anything reaches production.

## Humans are gatekeepers, not operators

His hard line is that no task belongs to a person. A human may approve a production deploy, but never performs it. The upside is that the works-on-my-machine anti-pattern disappears, because nothing runs on your machine but the IDE. Pipelines run the builds and tests; a red pipeline gives you a report, a green one means it's ready for production.

## Why start on day one?

Because automation is incremental, exactly like TDD's write a test, make it pass, refactor loop. On day one you might only need a build script and a little infrastructure code; as the application grows you add test stages, deployment stages and more infrastructure. He gives two reasons this beats bolting it on later. Coverage: building incrementally means nothing gets left behind, and the effort is far smaller than a big push at the end. And confidence: the automation layer is itself exercised against production from the start, so by the time the stakes are high it has, in his words, gained muscle.

## Who should watch

Tech leads kicking off a new service, and anyone who needs a short, quotable case for putting pipeline and infrastructure work in sprint one. If your team already ships everything through CI/CD from the first commit, this will confirm what you do rather than teach you something new.

Title: Stop patching your database and pick the one built for the job
Description: Akanksha Sheoran (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on moving off self-managed databases to managed, purpose-built AWS engines like Aurora and DynamoDB
Body:
One relational database doing every job for every service is the last monolith in a lot of microservice architectures. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Akanksha Sheoran](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Akanksha_Sheoran_save_grow_innovate_databases), EMEA Business Development Manager at AWS, made the case for two moves: hand the undifferentiated database work to a managed service, and replace the one-size-fits-all database with engines picked per access pattern.

To be clear about scope: this is an AWS portfolio talk from AWS, a tour of the managed database line-up and the migration tooling around it, with no demo. If you want a map of which AWS database fits which workload, it delivers that in about 25 minutes.

## What's driving the change?

She names three trends. Data from phones, watches and IoT devices, which by AWS's own estimate grows 10x every five years. Microservices, because applications now need to reach millions of users globally with millisecond responses, and small teams want to ship without taking the whole site down. And DevOps, which pushes code to production faster through CI/CD. Together, she argues, they create demand for purpose-built databases rather than a single shared engine.

## Why stop running your own?

The self-managed list will be familiar to anyone who has carried a database pager: installing hardware and software, patching, making sure backups exist and actually restore, and capacity planning months ahead, where you overbuy to be safe or underbuy and eat downtime. "Many dbas don't even know how the databases will handle an instance failure until it actually happens," Akanksha Sheoran said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021.

Her pitch for the managed model is that AWS takes patching, minor upgrades, backups, failover and storage scaling, and the DBA's time goes to schema design, query optimisation and access control instead.

## Which engine for which job?

AWS counted 15 purpose-built database engines at the time. She walks through the families:

- **Relational**: Amazon RDS with seven engines (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle and others), and Aurora.
- **Key-value**: DynamoDB, for shopping carts and product catalogues.
- **Document**: DocumentDB, MongoDB-compatible, for catalogues and mobile apps.
- **In-memory**: ElastiCache for Redis and Memcached, for caching and gaming.
- **Wide-column**: Keyspaces, Cassandra-compatible.
- **Graph**, for social networks and fraud detection; **time series**, for monitoring; and **ledger**, an immutable cryptographic log for finance, HR and invoicing.

## What do Aurora and DynamoDB actually promise?

The numbers she gives for Aurora: MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible, three to five times the throughput when you lift and shift MySQL or PostgreSQL onto it, storage in 10 GB segments each replicated six ways across availability zones, writes surviving the loss of two of six copies and reads surviving three. She also positions it as the licence-free exit from commercial databases and their audits.

For DynamoDB: more than 10 trillion requests per day across the service, peaks above 20 million requests per second, encryption at rest by default, point-in-time recovery, and Lambda triggers on item-level changes. DocumentDB gets MongoDB compatibility, CloudWatch metrics and up to 15 read replicas.

## How do you get there?

The migration section is the most practical part. The Database Freedom programme offers advice, workshops and partners for leaving Oracle, SQL Server, Netezza, Teradata, Cassandra or MongoDB. Free migration playbooks walk through common hurdles. The Database Migration Service (DMS) handles both homogeneous moves (MySQL to MySQL) and heterogeneous ones (a commercial engine to Aurora), and the Schema Conversion Tool translates schemas, stored procedures and embedded SQL in application code.

## Who should watch

Teams weighing a move from self-managed or commercial databases onto AWS, and architects splitting a shared database along service lines. If you already run Aurora and DynamoDB in production, you'll know most of this; the purpose-built framing is still a useful checklist to hold your current schema up against.

Title: Instance 42 shouldn't have a different config than instance 1
Description: Ismael Hommani and Joachim Rousseau (WeScale) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on the configuration layer pattern, shown with Lightbend Config and HOCON
Body:
Cloud native patterns get written for services and data, and configuration is left to whoever writes the deploy script. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Ismael Hommani and Joachim Rousseau](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Ismael_Hommani_Joachim_Rousseau_cloud_application_configuration), Cloud Native Developer and Coding Architect at WeScale, argue for a third way between baking config into the artifact and scattering getenv calls everywhere: a configuration layer that ships the model with the code and pulls the values from the environment.

## Why is config a cloud native problem?

Their definition is the twelve-factor one: configuration is whatever is likely to vary between deploys. They split it in two: application configuration you control (third-party service locations, identifiers, algorithm settings) and values the platform hands you (IP address, port).

The cloud part is scale and churn. You run hundreds or thousands of ephemeral instances and still want them to behave as one logical service, so the same input gets the same output on any of them. Statelessness handles the request-history half of that. "What if my instance 42 contain a different configuration than the instance one? I won't have the same result for sure," Ismael Hommani said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021. And there's no operator SSHing in to fix a file anymore; some instances you can't even connect to.

## What's wrong with the two usual approaches?

**Config baked into the artifact.** Developers like it: one central model, values right there. Operators don't: the artifact is now tied to an environment, the dev build can't go to staging, traceability between deploys breaks, and you're back to it works on my machine.

**Twelve-factor, factor three: config in environment variables.** One artifact, which is good. But the code reads the environment directly, getenv calls spread through the codebase, and nobody has a single view of what the application needs to start.

## What is the configuration layer?

One artifact that carries the configuration model without the values. The values live in the environment, and the layer fetches them and exposes them to the application, which never touches the environment directly. They stress it is a concept, an association of libraries and patterns, not a product. Values can come from environment variables or from a config server such as Spring Cloud Config, backed by a Git repository, a blob store or Vault.

They show it on a client's PHP estate. Before: an in-house CLI synced the code repo to servers and symlinked files from a second repo holding every application's config, exposing far too much and hiding the model from developers. Step one moved the templates into the source code and rendered them in a CI/CD pipeline with values fetched from Spring Cloud Config (still one package per environment). Step two moved the rendering into a Kubernetes init container that writes the config to a volume before the application starts.

## What does it look like in code?

Joachim Rousseau's demo is a Scala app on Lightbend Config, using the HOCON format (JSON-compatible, with dot paths, durations like 30 seconds, references and includes), in three layers:

1. **reference.conf** in the jar: defaults only, under your own namespace, since all reference.conf files on the classpath get merged.
2. **A fixed application file** in the jar, loaded as a fallback: values tied to this version of the artifact, such as business and algorithm parameters, optionally referencing environment variables.
3. **A runtime file** outside the artifact, passed with a JVM system property and mounted as a volume: hostnames, ports, sizing.

JVM system properties override everything. A client ID built from the app name and an instance ID that only exists when an environment variable is set means a missing variable throws at load time, and the app refuses to start. "If the configuration is not consistent, we won't start," Joachim Rousseau said. PureConfig then maps the merged tree onto a typed Kafka consumer/producer model, so no code checks types at the moment of use. The debug output shows which file every value came from.

## Who should watch

JVM teams with config sprawl across environments, and anyone whose Helm values files have quietly become the real source of truth. The pattern isn't JVM-only, but the demo is.

Title: Microservices are supposed to be Dory. Most real apps are Marlin
Description: Mary Grygleski (IBM) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on keeping state in cloud native microservices with sagas, LRA, JCache and Open Liberty on Kubernetes
Body:
The twelve-factor app says processes should be stateless, and then your users want to stay logged in. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Mary Grygleski](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Mary_Grygleski_stateful_microservices_open_liberty_kubernetes), Developer Advocate at IBM, walked through where state lives once a system becomes a set of cloud native microservices: in the infrastructure (StatefulSets, persistent volumes, cookie affinity), in patterns (sagas and MicroProfile Long Running Actions), and in a distributed session cache, which she demoed with Open Liberty, JCache and Hazelcast.

She is upfront that this is exploratory: a new topic for her, and examples that are not production level yet. Treat it as a map of the options, with one worked example.

## Why does a stateless platform need stateful services?

Her framing device is Finding Nemo. Dory forgets everything, which makes her fast and fearless (she happily bounces on jellyfish); Marlin remembers, which makes him careful and slow. Stateless computing is Dory: easy to scale out, trivial to recover after a crash. Stateful computing is Marlin: every new node must sync with the others, and recovery means rebuilding the state the system had before it fell over.

"Realistically, we actually live in a stateful world and we really cannot survive if we are living statelessly," Mary Grygleski said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021. A logged-in session that doesn't make you reauthenticate on every request is already state.

## How did we do this before the cloud?

In the client-server era the database carried most of the weight, with stateful Enterprise JavaBeans and servlet HTTP sessions on top, and cookies or tokens on the client. She contrasts the two auth styles: a cookie hands the server a session ID it has to look up, while a JWT can carry the session information itself, saving the lookup. The mechanisms haven't changed much; the topology has.

## Where does state go in a cloud native system?

She sorts the answers into layers:

- **Infrastructure**: Kubernetes StatefulSets, persistent volumes and cookie affinity, which take the burden off the application.
- **Caching**: still valid, now distributed.
- **Patterns**: sagas, so a transaction can span services without falling back to two-phase commit. Choreography sagas pass events (order placed, then payment checks the card); orchestration sagas put a coordinator in the middle. She points to Chris Richardson's microservices.io as the reference.
- **MicroProfile LRA** (Long Running Actions): a newer spec, supported in Open Liberty, built on a compensator model. There is no rollback in the database sense; a compensator works out what failed and reinstates the earlier state.

## What does the demo show?

The worked example is the Open Liberty guide on caching HTTP session data with JCache and Hazelcast. A small cart application with JAX-RS endpoints keeps its session in a Hazelcast-backed cache, so the data survives across instances. She runs it with Maven's Liberty dev mode (hot deploy on every change) on OpenJ9 with AdoptOpenJDK 15, then uses the OpenAPI UI to add bananas for $2 and read the cart back.

The demo also shows the usual live-coding weather: the IDE run fails, the fix is running from the right directory in a terminal. Her advice when tooling misbehaves is to drop to the command line. A second repo, a stateful Kubernetes demo with NGINX and Hazelcast by her colleague Graham Charters, is left as homework.

## Who should watch

Java developers moving session-heavy applications into Kubernetes, and anyone who has been told microservices must be stateless and suspects it isn't the whole story. If you already run sagas in production, the theory half will be familiar; the Open Liberty guide is the practical takeaway.

Title: Five languages, one trace, and the blank SSL credentials nobody mentions
Description: Michael Sickles (Honeycomb.io) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021 on porting Google's polyglot microservices demo from OpenCensus to OpenTelemetry
Body:
OpenTelemetry has a "hello world" for every language and very few examples where five languages share one trace. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, [Michael Sickles](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Michael_Sickles_telemetry_polyglot_environment), Solutions Architect at Honeycomb.io, took the CNCF/Google microservices demo (Go, Java, Node.js, .NET and Python on Kubernetes), ripped out its OpenCensus code and rebuilt the instrumentation in OpenTelemetry until a single checkout showed up as one trace across every service. The takeaway: auto-instrumentation gets you moving, but trace propagation breaks in small, language-specific ways, and you only find them in a real polyglot system.

## Why bother with OpenTelemetry at all?

His pitch is the lock-in argument. Vendor-specific agents mean every tool switch is a rewrite; OpenTelemetry means you instrument once and point the exporter at one vendor, or several, and compare. The demo app was a good target because it already used OpenCensus, and OpenCensus and OpenTracing merged into OpenTelemetry, so most concepts map across. In the Java service the change was close to search-and-replace: put attribute became set attribute, add annotation became add event.

He also lays out the vocabulary before the code: a span is a timed unit of work, span attributes carry context like user and session IDs, span events are point-in-time logs such as exceptions, a trace is the set of spans for one user action, OTLP is the wire format, and exporters decide where the data goes.

## How did each language behave?

He worked front end to back end, one hop at a time.

- **Go** (front end and three other services): wrap the gorilla/mux router with the OpenTelemetry middleware, add the gRPC wrapper, set up an OTLP-over-gRPC exporter with a batch span processor. Then copy and paste into the other Go services and change the service name.
- **Java** (ad service): the agent hooks into the JVM and instruments Spring, HTTP, databases and Kafka from a few environment variables. The WithSpan annotation plus Span.current let him enrich auto-created spans without starting and stopping them by hand.
- **Node.js** (payment and another service): a tracing.js loaded at startup with gRPC and HTTP plugins. The docs said the plugins would load automatically; they didn't, so he listed them explicitly. Node wasn't GA yet, and the API was already shifting from plugins to instrumentations.
- **.NET** (cart service): built on Microsoft's own diagnostics libraries, so the naming differs, but the startup wiring was straightforward.
- **Python** (email service and another): thinner documentation and a gRPC server interceptor to pick up the upstream trace ID.

## What broke?

Two things stand out. First, in Go, Node.js, .NET and Python a secure endpoint needed explicitly empty SSL credentials passed to the gRPC exporter; Java didn't, and he only found that by reading the libraries' source. Second, trace context didn't propagate until he added the automatic gRPC instrumentation in Go. "The short answer is yes. The long answer is it took me a couple of tries," Michael Sickles said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, on whether the grand trace finally worked.

There was also a Kubernetes casualty: with OpenTelemetry added, pods started too slowly for their readiness health checks and kept crashing, so he removed the checks for now.

## Auto-instrumentation is the floor, not the ceiling

The part worth stealing is the manual layer. On the front end he added email, zip code, state, country and session ID as span attributes, so a support ticket with a session ID turns into a query for that one user's checkout. "Auto instrumentation is good, definitely to get up and going. It's not going to be the end, be all," he said. Since then he has added baggage, so the session ID propagates to every downstream span instead of living only at the edge.

His to-do list is honest: more manual instrumentation, health checks back in, upgrades to GA versions, and injected slowness so the demo can show a tracing tool finding a bottleneck.

## Who should watch

Anyone instrumenting more than one runtime with OpenTelemetry, especially teams migrating from OpenCensus. The OpenTelemetry versions have moved on since 2021, so treat the specific API calls as history, but the propagation and TLS gotchas are the kind that still bite. His fork of the demo is linked from the talk.

Title: The best code review ends with the reviewer reverting his own fixes
Description: Victor Rentea at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021 on code reviews that teach, aiming to understand the code rather than hunt bugs
Body:
The best code review Victor Rentea ever saw ended with the reviewer throwing away every change he had just typed. At Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021, Victor, a Java Champion, independent technical trainer and founder of the Bucharest Software Craftsmanship Community, argues that a review exists to understand code and teach people, and that finding bugs is a side effect.

It's a short talk about behaviour, not tooling, and it gives you things you can try in your next review.

## What did the perfect review look like?

Victor tells the story of an old friend, a developer with more than 15 years of experience. When he called you for a review, you got the comfortable armchair while he took the bad chair, a cup of tea, maybe some chocolate. He had already read the code. He suggested small improvements and typed them in front of you. When you disagreed after he'd explained his reasoning, he let it go.

After 15 to 30 minutes of small refactorings, the bigger refactoring you had half-seen hours earlier became obvious. And just as you begged him to commit, he reverted everything and told you to do it yourself. You left with the big picture and the energy to rebuild it, missing a few small steps but owning the result.

Victor's reading: when a review is too complex for line comments, the reviewer turns it into an ad hoc pair programming session. Remotely, that means switching your camera on. Reviewing someone's code while they stare at your profile photo of a dog isn't fair. Faces let you soften a point, show hesitation and see how it lands.

## Is the reviewer looking for bugs?

No, Victor says. The reviewer's job is to understand the solution. A review is a readability test: can someone else follow this code? Bugs turn up along the way. The author should also come away having learned something.

When the same topics keep coming up, don't repeat yourself in every review. Take a distilled code sample to a team design meeting, 30 minutes to an hour every two weeks, or a brown-bag session, and debate it there with other teams too.

## The reviewer is already annoyed

The most honest part is about the reviewer's state of mind. You are reverse-engineering someone else's train of thought, which puts you in a passive-aggressive stance before you start. "You are by definition frustrated," as Victor said at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021. So when you find something awful, comparing Strings or boxed Longs with ==, don't explode. Give the author a second chance to find it. With someone new or inexperienced, switch to a more guided, teaching style.

And never confuse opinion with fact. Focus on what really hurts maintainability or causes bugs, not on coding guidelines that don't matter.

## Tips for the author

- Work on it until you'd be proud to put it on your CV.
- Run Sonar before committing so the trivial issues never reach a human.
- For complex work, ask a senior for an in-flight review on your feature branch.
- Make micro-commits, and commit large automated refactorings (an IntelliJ package rename touching thousands of classes) separately from manual edits, so the reviewer looks at the lines where you used your brain.
- Sketch a supporting diagram, on a collaborative whiteboard or as text-based UML.

His closing advice includes tolerating imperfect code. His friend would accept less from a junior than from a senior, because "it's more important to keep a team straight than to have the best coding style." And pair programming still beats any review, because learning goes both ways.

## Who should watch

Team leads and seniors who do a lot of reviewing, and anyone whose reviews have started to feel like a fight. Fifteen minutes with a story you'll want to copy.

Title: Picking a country to see the northern lights, with Java as the data tool
Description: Denys Makogon (Oracle) at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021 on using Java streams, the JDK HTTP client and Project Loom to find where aurora hunting pays off
Body:
A friend asks which country is best for seeing the northern lights. Most people would say Norway or Iceland. Denys Makogon, a principal member of technical staff in Oracle's Java Platform Group and an award-winning photographer, wrote a theory, pulled years of weather and solar data, and built the pipeline in plain JDK Java. His Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021 talk is about that pipeline, and why he chose Java and not Python.

He says up front it isn't packed with technical depth. It's a hobby project used as a guided tour of three JDK features: parallel streams, the HTTP client and Project Loom.

## What does the data look like?

Aurora visibility depends on three things nobody controls: season, latitude and weather. Denys combined historical weather forecasts from the Dark Sky API with solar activity and magnetic field data from the Helmholtz Centre in Potsdam.

Each country is represented by nine or more GPS locations. Each location gets hourly weather forecasts across the autumn, winter and spring nights, about 226 days, which by his count means at least 3,000 measures per location. The work is mostly independent per point, so it splits well, and both data sources come through HTTP REST APIs. That gave him a requirements list: sequences, reusable pipelines, parallelism, and non-blocking HTTP.

## Parallel streams, and when they are a waste

Streams (JDK 8) handle the pipeline: lazy intermediate operations such as mapping three-hour windows of peak magnetic disturbance, then filtering, with a terminal operation that triggers the work. Run in parallel, they use the common fork/join pool, sized by default at one less than the number of CPUs, or a custom pool you configure.

The useful part is his rule for when to parallelise. "We all know that runtime is fast. The only slow thing is your code," Denys Makogon said at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021. Parallel pays off when the cost of processing one item outweighs the overhead of provisioning threads and the data splits efficiently. ArrayList and HashMap split well, because random access makes partitioning cheap. If partitioning takes longer than processing, you've just warmed the CPU. He adds that a stream only holds its own metadata, so memory only grows when a terminal operation collects the results.

## 55,000 HTTP calls and a cheaper way to wait

The weather side needed roughly 55k HTTP requests even after optimisation, each a chance to block a thread doing nothing. The HTTP client incubated in JDK 9 and finalised in JDK 11 supports sync and async calls, HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, reactive-streams bodies and builder-style requests.

Then Project Loom, which at the time was still on the way. Virtual threads make blocking cheap, so you can write simple synchronous code and let the scheduler handle the waiting. His practical advice: do the IO-bound data extraction on virtual threads first, then hand CPU-bound work to the fork/join pool, because the pool has far fewer OS threads than you can have virtual ones.

## Why not Python?

His answer is blunt: Python is slow and single-threaded, and much of its data science stack is C with a thin Python wrapper. Java can do the job with the JDK alone, and he points to Tribuo, Oracle's Java machine learning library, as a sign the ecosystem is growing. The country that won is shown on screen at the end. His real advice for the friend stays the same: pick the one you like and go.

## Who should watch

Java developers who've never reached for parallel streams or wondered what Loom would change for IO-heavy batch jobs, and anyone who likes seeing a hobby problem taken far too seriously. Data engineers fluent in Spark can skip the streams basics.

Title: Split every Java class in two and your system gets easier to read
Description: Yehonathan Sharvit (Cycognito) at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021 on data-oriented programming in Java, separating code from immutable data
Body:
Most object-oriented systems aren't hard to run, they're hard to understand. Yehonathan Sharvit, Clojure Wizard at Cycognito and author of the book Data-Oriented Programming, uses his Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021 talk to show two principles that cut that cost in a plain Java codebase: keep code and data in separate classes, and never mutate the data.

It's a short, focused talk, the core of the book in about twenty minutes, with Java examples rather than Clojure ones.

## Which kind of complexity is he fighting?

Yehonathan separates two meanings of the word. Computational complexity is the CPU and memory a program needs. System complexity is what it costs a human brain. "computational complexity is the time it takes to run a program, and system complexity is the time it takes to understand a program," Yehonathan Sharvit said at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021. Data-oriented programming goes after the second one.

His example is the library management system every OO course draws: a Library with a Catalog and user management, Books with BookItems and Authors, Librarians and Members, BookLendings. The UML looks reasonable until you count. The Library class connects to six others, and the diagram mixes association, composition, inheritance and usage arrows. That is a lot to hold in your head before you've read a line of code.

## Principle one: data classes and code classes

Split each class into a data class (fields, getters, nothing else) and a code class (static methods only, no state). Library becomes LibraryCode and LibraryData, Catalog becomes CatalogCode and CatalogData, and so on.

The tangled graph turns into two disjoint ones, each with tighter rules. On the code side the only relationship left is usage and every method is stateless. On the data side only association and composition remain. Instead of asking an Isaac Asimov object for its full name, you pass the Asimov data object to a static full-name method on the author code class, and the data travels as an explicit argument.

## Principle two: data that cannot change

The second source of complexity is the question every Java developer has asked: did that method just mutate my object? Yehonathan's example is a static method that uppercases an author's last name. From the call site you can't tell whether the original Asimov object still has a lowercase name, so people make defensive copies.

Multithreading makes it worse. A naive borrow method checks whether a member is blocked, then lends the book. A context switch between those two lines and another thread can block the member in the meantime. The usual fix is locks, and locks bring their own risk of deadlocks.

Immutable data removes both problems: no surprise mutations, no defensive copies, thread safety by default. For representing it in Java he offers two routes, with a dig at the ecosystem: "any problem in Java could be solved with Java annotations." Project Lombok's value annotation generates the constructor, private immutable fields, toString, hashCode and equals. Or use records, which he points to as arriving with Java 14, a native JVM implementation with no third-party code generation.

## What the book adds

He closes with what didn't fit in the slot: persistent collections that make new versions without deep copies, representing data as maps and processing it with general-purpose functions (map, filter, reduce, group by), polymorphism without inheritance, managing application state as immutable data with optimistic locking instead of mutexes, and flexible database access.

## Who should watch

Java developers who suspect their class diagrams are working against them, and anyone who's been told to try a functional style but wants it on familiar ground. If you already write Clojure, this is the story you know, retold for the people next door.

Title: A reactive app with a JDBC call at the bottom is a blocking app
Description: Rob Hedgpeth (MariaDB) at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021 on R2DBC, the spec that makes relational database access non-blocking with back pressure
Body:
You can wire up a beautifully reactive service with Project Reactor or RxJava, and the moment it calls a JDBC driver the whole thing waits on a socket like it's 1997. That is the argument Rob Hedgpeth, Director of Developer Relations at MariaDB, makes at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021: reactive only pays off top to bottom, and R2DBC (Reactive Relational Database Connectivity) is the spec that finally takes the database layer along for the ride.

It's a well-paced intro. The first half rebuilds reactive programming from the ground up, the second half walks through the R2DBC service provider interface and a Spring Data R2DBC demo against MariaDB in Docker.

## Why is adding more threads not good enough?

Rob starts with the familiar picture: a server thread sends a query and then sits there. Request two arrives, so you spin up thread two, then thread three, and by request 100 you are paying for all that thread context in memory, and throughput drops with it. The reactive version throws the work over the fence to the database and moves on to the next request, handling the result when it shows up.

He is careful to frame this as efficiency, not raw speed: you are not necessarily chasing performance, you are trying to get more out of the hardware you already have.

## Back pressure is the subscriber holding the hose

The core idea he builds up to is back pressure. A publisher streaming data at a subscriber will eventually bury it, and the backlog grows. With non-blocking back pressure, the subscriber tells the publisher how much it can handle, and the publisher sends that much when it's ready.

Rather than every shop inventing its own version, engineers from Netflix, Pivotal and Lightbend wrote the Reactive Streams specification in 2013: a small set of interfaces (publisher, subscriber, subscription) with request and cancel on one side and next, error and complete on the other. Libraries like RxJava and Project Reactor implement it.

The catch is the bottom of the stack. "if one part of an application or a solution is blocked, then if you think about it, it's all really blocked," Rob Hedgpeth said at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021. JDBC dates from 1997 and is blocking by design, so a reactive app built on it isn't reactive at all.

## What R2DBC actually specifies

R2DBC is, like Reactive Streams, a specification rather than a library, and Rob lists its design goals: open, fully non-blocking, built directly on Reactive Streams, and small. That last one is a lesson learned from JDBC, which he calls opinionated: drivers end up writing their own parameter binding and URL parsing. In R2DBC the SPI parses the connection URL for every driver, and its interfaces come in two levels of compliance, fully and partially supported, so vendors have room for database-specific features.

The interfaces will look familiar: ConnectionFactory, Connection, Statement, Result, Row. The difference is that create, begin transaction, commit, close and execute all return a Publisher you subscribe to instead of a value you wait for. Drivers exist for MariaDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, H2 and Cloud Spanner, among others, and higher-level clients such as Spring Data R2DBC sit on top.

## The demo, including the bit that didn't work

The Spring Data R2DBC demo is a single-file app talking to a MariaDB container: a Lombok-annotated Task class mapped to a task table, a repository built on ReactiveCrudRepository, and save and list methods returning Mono and Flux. "Flux returns zero to many objects, mono returns zero to one," as Rob put it.

The live save fell over on stage, so he switched to a pre-built copy of the app, which is the most honest moment of any demo. That copy shows the part worth seeing: a custom subscriber that requests two tasks at a time and only asks for more once both have arrived. With five rows in the table, it gets two, two, then one, and completes. Back pressure, in about a dozen lines.

He closes by noting R2DBC had joined the Reactive Foundation and was heading for its 1.0 release in 2021, and mentions his book, R2DBC Revealed.

## Who should watch

Java developers already sold on Reactor or RxJava who still have a blocking JDBC call somewhere in the request path. If you know Reactive Streams cold, skip to the SPI walkthrough in the second half.

Title: Groovy and Kotlin compile in the advice from Effective Java
Description: Naresha K at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021 on how Groovy and Kotlin build Effective Java practices into the language, with traps for Java ports
Body:
Joshua Bloch's Effective Java tells Java developers what to do; Groovy and Kotlin were designed after it and simply do some of it for you. At Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021, Naresha K, an independent consultant and founder of the Bangalore Groovy User Group, takes five items from the book, shows the trap you hit when you port the Java solution as-is, and the idiomatic Groovy and Kotlin answer. His takeaway: when the right thing is easy, developers actually do it.

## Equals and hashCode, without the duplication

His first example is a Groovy `Product` with SKU, description and price. Two instances with identical values aren't equal, and using one as a map key and the other to look it up returns null. That's items 10 and 11 of Effective Java: obey the equals contract, and always override hashCode when you override equals, using the same fields.

The Java options both have problems. IDE generation works once, then someone adds a date of manufacture and forgets to regenerate. Apache Commons Lang's EqualsBuilder and HashCodeBuilder make you list the fields twice. Groovy's `@EqualsAndHashCode` AST transformation generates both from one declaration at compile time. Kotlin is more implicit: make it a `data class`. Both support a subset of fields, and here's the trap for entities. Include an auto-generated ID and an object before and after persisting stops being equal to itself. Key on the business key (the SKU) with `includes` in Groovy, or move the ID out of Kotlin's primary constructor into the class body.

## Internal iterators beat for-each

Item 58 says prefer for-each loops to traditional for loops, because fewer moving parts means fewer bugs. Groovy and Kotlin go a level further with higher-order functions on collections: `collect` and `inject` in Groovy, `map` and `fold` in Kotlin. His reading of the advice for these languages: favour internal iterators over external ones. Java can do this too since lambdas, but through the Streams API rather than the collections themselves.

## Null checks: two opposite fixes

Item 54 says return empty collections, not nulls. Groovy rescues you even when a colleague returns null anyway: null there is a NullObject, so calling an iterating method like `collect` or `findAll` on it gives an empty list instead of a NullPointerException (other methods still throw). Kotlin goes the other way: a non-nullable return type means returning null doesn't compile, and you must opt in with a question mark.

"life is too short for null checks," Naresha K said at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021.

## Immutability you don't have to remember

Effective Java's checklist for an immutable class is long, and long checklists get ignored. Groovy's `@Immutable` makes fields final, drops setters and generates a map-based constructor, so you can use named arguments like length and breadth in any order. Kotlin data classes with `val` fields give the same immutability, and with named arguments the compiler reorders them to call the regular constructor, with no map involved.

## Composition without the boilerplate

Inheritance, in his words, is the number one abused feature in Java. Extending `ArrayList` to make a phone numbers type with one extra method fails the Liskov test; composition is right, but in Java it means writing a forwarding method for every list operation. Groovy's `@Delegate` and Kotlin's `by` keyword generate the forwarding for you.

## What to take away

Compiler-generated code beats IDE-generated code, because any practice that assumes code doesn't change is flawed, and the compiler regenerates on every build. Copying Java idioms into Groovy or Kotlin can walk you into traps, so learn the idiomatic way. And knowing other languages improves your Java designs even if you never ship them. He closes by asking whether Effective Java could serve as a litmus test for modern JVM languages.

## Who should watch

Java developers weighing Kotlin, Groovy users wondering what Kotlin does differently, and anyone who has reread Effective Java and wished the language did more of the work.

Title: Dependency injection is not magic, it's reflection with good manners
Description: Mark Hendriks (Ordina JTech) at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021 on building a dependency injection framework from scratch with the Java reflection API
Body:
Spring's `@Autowired` and Jakarta EE's `@Inject` feel like magic until you write one yourself. At Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021, Mark Hendriks, software architect at Ordina, live-codes a small dependency injection framework in plain Java with zero outside dependencies, covering field, constructor and setter injection plus singletons. It's all the reflection API, which has been in Java pretty much since the beginning.

## What is inversion of control, really?

Hendriks keeps the definition short: an outside entity, a container or framework, wires together the dependencies a class needs and passes them in, instead of the class calling `new` itself. Pass a dependency through the constructor and you are already doing dependency injection; a framework just automates it, via constructors, fields or setters.

He built his own framework to understand how the big ones do it, and named it the Injectinator, after the Phineas and Ferb villain who adds -inator to everything.

"I'm just an engineer and I'm terrible at naming things," Mark Hendriks said at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021.

## Step 1: an annotation and a syringe

Rather than depend on `@Inject`, he writes his own `@InjectMe` annotation. Two things matter. Retention must be runtime, because reflection reads it while the program runs. The target must be constructors, fields and methods (there's no setter target; a setter is just a method).

Next, a configuration interface, the Syringe, maps an interface to its implementation class in a `HashMap`. Here the logger interface maps to a concrete logger class. He adds an `asSubclass` check on registration even though generics already enforce it, to fail fast, and throws an `IllegalArgumentException` if no implementation is registered for a type.

## Step 2: field injection

The core is short. Create an instance of the target class, loop over `getDeclaredFields()` (not `getFields()`, which only returns public ones, and you want private fields to work), and for each field carrying `@InjectMe`, call `setAccessible(true)` and set the value. The value comes from a recursive call to inject itself, asking the Syringe for the implementation class first, because the dependency may have dependencies of its own.

The first run fails with a NullPointerException for an honest reason: he forgot to call the Syringe's configure method. Live coding at its most relatable.

## Step 3: constructors and setters

Constructor injection loops over the public constructors, finds the annotated one, reads its parameter types, recursively builds an implementation for each, and calls that constructor with the resulting array.

Setter (method) injection loops over the public methods and invokes the annotated ones with a recursively built argument. To avoid an index-out-of-bounds on the parameter list, he adds the JavaBeans checks: the method name starts with set and takes exactly one parameter.

His warning is worth remembering in any framework: if a setter call fails after construction, you can end up with a half-built object. Constructor injection fails loudly instead, so you never get a half-constructed instance.

## Step 4: singletons

Spring hands out singletons by default; the Injectinator so far creates a new instance every time, which he proves with a call counter in the logger that reads one in both of two separate objects. The fix is an enum, InjectionType, with NEW and SINGLETON values, added as the annotation's `value()` with NEW as the default, plus a map of already-built instances. Mark a setter as singleton and the counter goes to two: both objects now share one logger.

He tested on Java 8, 11 and 15 and says the version doesn't really matter, since it's all reflection. In the spirit of a demo, exceptions are simply rethrown, with a clear request not to do that in production.

## Who should watch

Java developers who use Spring or CDI daily and want to know what happens under the annotation, and anyone who has avoided the reflection API because it looked scary. Not for you if you've already read a DI container's source code.

Title: Your test framework deserves upgrades too, so move to JUnit 5
Description: Jonathan Meek (The Home Depot) at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021 on migrating a Spring Boot app from JUnit 4 to JUnit 5 without JUnit Vintage
Body:
Teams argue for hours about how often to upgrade dependencies and the JVM, then leave the test framework untouched for years. At Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021, Jonathan Meek, software developer at The Home Depot, argues that's backwards for anyone practising TDD, then live-migrates a small Spring Boot app from JUnit 4 to JUnit 5 and adds two features worth the move.

## Why do test frameworks get left behind?

"Test frameworks are usually the last thing to be upgraded," Jonathan Meek said at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021.

His reasoning: we want things to keep working, and nobody wants to touch the ancient code. But the test framework is the tool that tells you the software works as intended, and in TDD it's the first thing you touch. He also points out that conference programmes are full of talks on moving past Java 8 and very few on moving test frameworks.

## Is it just a dependency swap?

No. JUnit 5 is a reorganisation into three projects: the JUnit Platform (including the test engine API), JUnit Jupiter (the implementation you write tests against) and JUnit Vintage (which runs JUnit 3 and 4 tests on the new platform).

Can't you just use Vintage? You could, he says, but it kicks the problem down the road, and in his experience it hasn't worked well: tests fail or behave oddly. Better to make the changes.

The annotation renames are the first thing you'll touch, and he thinks they're clearer:

- `@BeforeClass` becomes `@BeforeAll`, `@Before` becomes `@BeforeEach`, `@After` becomes `@AfterEach`.
- `@Ignore` becomes `@Disabled` (his favourite).
- Imports move to the Jupiter packages, and `Assert` becomes `Assertions`.

## The Spring Boot recipe

Prerequisites: Java 8 or higher and Spring Framework 5 or higher; JUnit 5 became the default in Spring Boot 2.4, which is what he uses. Then:

- `@RunWith(SpringRunner.class)` becomes `@ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class)`.
- `MockitoJUnitRunner` becomes `MockitoExtension`.
- You can now stack several extensions, where JUnit 4 let you pick a single runner. He used exactly that recently to add the Mockito extension to a Spring test.

## Watching it break, then pass

The demo app is a coffee REST API backed by an H2 in-memory database, with endpoints for all coffees, a coffee by ID, and the best-rated coffee, tested with MockMvc. He runs the Maven build first to prove all nine tests pass, bumps Spring Boot to 2.4, and lets the IDE complain.

The controller test needs mostly import and annotation changes. The service test hits the one real semantic change: JUnit 4's `expected` attribute on `@Test` is gone. Instead you call `assertThrows` with the exception class and a lambda that runs the code under test. A bonus he points out: the unused-variable warning on the call goes away, because the call now has a purpose.

## The two features worth the move

`@DisplayName` gives tests a human-readable name. His team used to encode should-do-this-when-that patterns into method names; now a scrum master or a newcomer can read the test report and see what failed. He labels a controller test with the endpoint, HTTP method and expected 200.

`@ParameterizedTest` with `@CsvFileSource` runs one test per row of a CSV file in the test resources folder, with columns matching the method parameters (mismatch them and JUnit tells you). His single-coffee lookup test grows from one case to three, and the suite from nine tests to 11.

## Who should watch

Teams still on JUnit 4 in Spring Boot, especially anyone tempted to leave Vintage in place forever. It's a practical walkthrough, and the code is on his GitHub.

Title: Four ways a JVM misbehaves, and the tool to reach for each
Description: Ranjan Mohan and Silvia Siu Luo at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021 on triaging JVM CPU hogs, GC storms, memory blow-ups and crashes
Body:
A slow Java service shows one of three symptoms: high CPU, high memory, or a crash. At Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021, Ranjan Mohan and Silvia Siu Luo reproduce four common JVM performance problems on purpose, then triage each with jstack, VisualVM, Java Flight Recorder with Mission Control, jmap and crash logs, ending with a decision table you can follow at 3am.

They are upfront about scope: this is triage, getting to the point where you know what to fix, not JVM tuning or the fix itself.

## A quick tour of JVM memory

Silvia opens with the layout: program counter, stacks of frames (local variables, operand stack, frame data with references to the constant pool and exception table), the native method stack, and the heap with young generation (Eden plus survivor spaces), old generation and metaspace. Then the collectors: Serial and Parallel (stop-the-world, single- and multi-threaded), CMS (concurrent mark and sweep, weak at preventing fragmentation) and G1 (equal-size regions, collecting the regions with the most garbage first).

## Scenario 1: one thread hogs the CPU

The test program runs three normal threads that sleep between iterations and one that increments a counter forever. Three jstack samples 30 seconds apart show the hog's CPU time pulling away each time. VisualVM shows the same story visually (one thread always running, the others sleeping), and so does a 60-second JFR recording in Mission Control.

## Scenario 2: the GC is the hog

Here the program creates 500 million small objects of about 16 bytes and keeps a fifth of them in a list. jstack shows a GC thread's CPU usage climbing and settling around 96%. Their charts of collection time make the minor vs major distinction concrete: minor GC time climbs steadily to about 5 seconds, while major GC stays near zero for the first half of the run and then climbs to 43 seconds as the old generation fills.

## Scenario 3: memory runs out

Ranjan generates a random string of 32 million characters and runs it with a 64 MB maximum heap.

"The JVM will just go boom," Ranjan Mohan said at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021.

The tools: jmap to take a heap dump (an hprof file) and Eclipse Memory Analyzer to see which objects take the memory and which threads hold them; VisualVM to correlate live threads with memory spikes; JFR for memory and GC over time. The charts teach something too. Keep one string alive and memory rises, dips once the temporary garbage is collected, then stays flat. Create and drop strings in a loop and you get a sawtooth with peaks of different heights, which shows GC doesn't run the instant an object becomes unreachable.

They repeat one warning: a heap dump pauses every thread while the heap is copied to disk, so taking one in production costs availability.

## Scenario 4: the crash

The crash program reaches into `sun.misc.Unsafe` by reflection and writes to an invalid address. The result is a segmentation fault and a crash summary with four things: the reason (SIGSEGV), the Java version, whether a core dump was written, and where the error report lives. In the report, the crashing thread's stack trace points straight at the `Unsafe` call, and the list of running threads matters because another thread may have caused the bad state.

## The triage table

- **High memory**: check `-Xmx` against the expected load. If the load justifies it, raise it; otherwise take a heap dump, find the biggest objects and the threads referencing them, and go to that code.
- **High CPU**: first ask whether it's GC threads. If so, take the memory route, and consider a different collector (CMS to G1, for example). If not, get the hot thread's stack traces and optimise or deprioritise that path.
- **Crash**: read the crash summary and error report, including all threads at the time.

High GC activity has no row of its own because it always shows up as high memory or high CPU.

They also built an open-source library that collects the same diagnostics from inside the application, including a heap dump in a few lines of code when memory crosses a threshold. Their next step: make it collect only when needed (for example, when a thread passes 70% CPU), since the raw data can reach hundreds of megabytes in minutes.

## Who should watch

Java developers who have stared at an OutOfMemoryError and not known which tool to open first. Experienced JVM tuners will know the tools, but the decision table is worth stealing.

Title: From Runnable to CompletableFuture, Java concurrency stopped being scary
Description: Dmitry Vinnik (Facebook) at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021 on Java concurrency from threads to CompletableFuture, with Fresco, Spectrum and Litho
Body:
Many Java developers met concurrency through `Thread` and `Runnable`, got burned, and went back to single-threaded code. At Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021, Dmitry Vinnik, developer advocate on Facebook's open source team, makes the case that the APIs have moved on, and walks from threads through the JDK 5 concurrency utilities and `Future` to `CompletableFuture`, using Facebook's Android libraries Fresco, Spectrum and Litho as examples.

It's an accessible tour aimed at developers who avoid concurrency, not a Loom-era performance deep end.

## Why bother with concurrency at all?

His motivations are the familiar trio: multi-core machines, microservices everywhere, and cloud providers handing you as many cores as you'll pay for. Idle cores are waste, frozen UIs are bad UX, and safe abstractions make multithreading easier. Vinnik's framing is blunt.

"Concurrency is a new reality. Concurrency is the reality," Dmitry Vinnik said at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021.

He doesn't pretend it's free: thread safety, race conditions, liveness, testing, and the fact that adding threads rarely gives a linear speed-up. He compares concurrency to sharks: frightening mostly because we don't know them well, a feeling he says Brian Goetz's Java Concurrency in Practice cured for him.

## Design for concurrency even if you never use it

The most practical advice comes early. Even a single-threaded app benefits from being designed as if it weren't: design by contract, aim for immutable and atomic objects, and avoid temporal coupling, where an object's state depends on the order you called its methods. His example is an HTTP request object whose response appears only after a particular call.

He also separates three forms of multithreading with coffee. Concurrent: John codes and drinks coffee on one core by switching between them. Parallel: ambidextrous Jenny does both at once on two. Asynchronous: Henry keeps bringing fresh coffee without interrupting anyone, fire and forget.

## What JDK 5 gave us

`Runnable` takes no input, returns nothing and throws nothing, and gives you little control; Fresco's adapter still uses one with Android's run-on-UI-thread call to refresh images. JDK 5 brought `ThreadLocal` (good for confining resources such as date formatters, with memory leak risks), atomics (because `i++` is three operations, not one), and thread-safe collections such as `ConcurrentHashMap`. In the Spectrum demo, a concurrent map stops duplicate image transcodes without wrapping everything in a `synchronized` block.

## Futures and executors, and where they fall short

`Callable` adds a return value and an exception; `Future` holds a result that arrives later; the executor framework manages thread pools so you don't call the many-argument `ThreadPoolExecutor` constructor yourself. Vinnik runs through the factories: single thread for experiments, cached for many small tasks like a crawler, fixed for heavy calculation, scheduled for cron-style work, and work-stealing.

Then the pitfalls: `get()` blocks, so always pass a timeout; you can't chain results; you can't combine futures; and exception handling splits into interrupted, execution and timeout cases.

## CompletableFuture fixes the chain

`CompletableFuture` implements `CompletionStage`, which adds what `Future` lacked. Start work asynchronously and chain a transformation onto the result (brew the coffee, then drink it when ready). Complete a future yourself or take a default if it's not done (give me the espresso if the latte isn't ready). Wait on all or any of several futures (run a WebDriver test in Firefox, Chrome and IE at once). Combine two results before continuing (two teams' API requests both filed before you start). And handle errors with an `exceptionally` stage that reads like try/catch rather than a separate code path. The Litho demo uses a run-async call to change a text component and rebuild the UI on another thread.

## Who should watch

Java and Android developers who still reach for raw threads, or who avoid concurrency entirely. Developers fluent in reactive streams can skip it.
