Title: Event-driven architecture is a trade, and eventual consistency is the price
Description: Bogdan Sucaciu (Deloitte Digital) at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021 on what event-driven architecture solves for microservices and what it costs
Body:
Event-driven architecture is usually sold as the way to build real-time systems. At Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021, Bogdan Sucaciu, tech lead at Deloitte Digital and a Pluralsight author, argues that's the wrong reason. Few use cases truly need events for speed (real-time analytics, fraud detection, sensor readings). The real win is fixing the data-access mess microservices create, and the price is strong consistency.

He uses Apache Kafka to illustrate, and is upfront that seasoned Kafka users won't learn much new about Kafka itself. The value is in the framing.

## What problem do events actually solve?

He starts, provocatively, by praising the monolith: simple, one process, one database. Its weakness is scaling, both of the process and of the team arguing over a button colour. Microservices fix that and introduce a new problem: every domain needs data owned by other domains. A payment needs card details, but also the user's name and address from another service, and one incoming REST call can fan out into 20 or 30 more. Distributed transactions, timeouts, coupling and data ownership follow.

Event streams cut that knot. Producers write to a stream; consumers subscribe. Control is inverted: the consumer fetches what it needs instead of the producer pushing to known clients. Subscribing to a stream or two beats making 30 API calls.

## The rules of the stream

A few design rules stand out:

- **One producer type per event stream.** Many instances of the same producer are fine; mixing producer types into one stream complicates consumption a lot.
- **Consumers are flexible.** Many consumers can read one stream, and one consumer can read many.
- **Producers don't know consumers, and vice versa.** Only the architecture diagram does.
- **Anything you can subscribe to asynchronously is a stream**: queues, topics, logs, websockets, reactive APIs. The difference that matters is that queues and websockets let you react once and the event is gone, while topics and logs persist events so you can replay them. Kafka uses topics backed by logs, which is a big part of why it suits this style.

## What does it cost?

"the key to building successful event driven architecture is understanding and accepting eventual consistency," Bogdan Sucaciu said at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021.

You can't take a synchronous REST flow and transliterate it into events and expect it to work. Not every flow should be event-driven, and real systems end up a mix of synchronous APIs and events.

## Commands, queries and two kinds of events

He separates commands (directed, effect in the future, maybe a response), queries (directed, present state, always a response) and events (undirected, something that already happened, never a response). Events come in two flavours.

**Event notification**: tell the world something happened and don't care who listens. His example is a large e-commerce site that sends an event every time your cursor hovers over a product, then uses those hovers to build the suggestions at the bottom of the page. In the Kafka demo, one producer emits a record every second and three consumers each receive every event almost simultaneously, with the consumer side being a poll inside a `while (true)` loop.

**Event-carried state transfer**: send the changed state. The trap is sending too little. An address-change event with only the new address breaks the tax service that needs the old one, which then calls back to the source system, and you've rebuilt the coupling you were escaping. Design events so consumers never need to query back.

## Event sourcing, and why Git is one

The most demanding pattern is event sourcing: append every change to a log and replay it to get current state. His bank account opens at zero, takes deposits of 500 and 200, pays 300 for a new TV, and replaying the log gives 400. Git works the same way: your working tree is a replay of commits.

In Kafka terms, each consumer builds its own materialised view from the log. If one consumer's data store is wiped, the others don't notice; you bring up an empty store, rewind to the beginning of the log and rebuild.

## Who should watch

Engineers whose microservices talk mostly over REST and who keep adding calls to assemble one response. It's a concepts talk with a small Kafka demo, not a Kafka operations guide.

Title: Adding Kafka doesn't make your system reactive
Description: Grace Jansen (IBM) at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021 on why Kafka alone isn't reactive, and the acks, offset and partition settings that make it so
Body:
Put Apache Kafka in the middle of your microservices and you have an event backbone, not a reactive system. At Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021, Grace Jansen, developer advocate at IBM, uses a coffee shop to show where a Kafka-based app still blocks, then walks through the Kafka settings and reactive frameworks that make it non-blocking end to end.

## Why isn't Kafka enough?

The demo starts with coffee lovers ordering over HTTP from a coffee shop that calls a barista over HTTP. Every customer waits at the till until their drink is made. Put an event backbone between shop and barista, add a board that announces finished orders, and customers can sit down after ordering. Better, but the usual next thought is that using Kafka makes you non-blocking and highly responsive by default, and that's where she pushes back.

"Kafka is a great tool, but it isn't enough just to have a good tool shove it in," Grace Jansen said at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021.

An influx of customers leaves one barista with a growing backlog. A full serving table (her stand-in for a slow downstream service) leaves the barista stuck holding coffees. Neither failure is fixed by the backbone itself.

## The Reactive Manifesto, one coffee at a time

She maps each failure to a trait from the 2013 Reactive Manifesto. Message-driven communication decouples components (version 1.0 said event-driven; Kafka itself talks about records, which covers both). Elasticity means scaling baristas up and back down, which is why "scalable" was renamed. Resilience means circuit breakers or back-pressure when the serving table is full. Responsiveness is what you get when the other three are in place.

Then she covers the layers you have to make reactive. Between services: patterns like CQRS, circuit breakers, sagas and back-pressure. Inside services: reactive programming with futures, libraries like RxJava and SmallRye Mutiny, and the Reactive Streams specification. And the Kafka configuration itself.

## Which Kafka settings decide resilience?

Kafka brings resilience out of the box. Consumers don't delete records, so a consumer can re-read after a crash. Partitions are replicated across brokers (a cluster usually has at least three), and if the leader dies a follower is elected automatically. The settings are where you can still lose data:

- **Producer delivery**: at most once gives throughput and may lose messages; at least once guarantees delivery but may duplicate.
- **acks**: 0 means no acknowledgement; 1 means the leader has it but followers may not; all waits for every replica. Only all is fully resilient.
- **Retries**: needed when acks time out, but think about what retries do to ordering.
- **Offset commits**: this is the best barista story. With auto-commit on a timer, the barista commits the coffee order, trips, spills it, restarts at the cappuccino, and the customer's coffee is gone for good. With a manual commit after serving, the restarted barista starts again at the coffee and no order is lost.

## Partitions decide how far consumers scale

Producers scale because a topic's partitions spread across brokers. Consumers scale through consumer groups, and the rule is one partition to one consumer within a group, which is how Kafka keeps per-partition ordering and avoids double reads. Three partitions and four consumers in one group leaves one consumer idle: handy as a spare, wasteful otherwise. You can add partitions later, but ordering is only guaranteed while the partition count stays the same, and more partitions make leader elections heavier. Plan the count up front.

## Reactive frameworks for Kafka

The plain Java producer and consumer clients aren't built for reactive systems, so she compares three alternatives: the Alpakka Kafka connector (Akka Streams and the actor model, a mindset shift if you think in microservices), MicroProfile Reactive Messaging (`@Incoming` and `@Outgoing` annotations joined by channels, with connectors that depend on the implementation), and Eclipse Vert.x (a polyglot event-loop toolkit). Her team converted an open-source Kafka test app to Vert.x, and start/stop from a websocket went from what she called a threading nightmare to simple pause and resume. A live lab closes the talk: two MicroProfile microservices exchanging system load over Kafka.

## Who should watch

Java developers who already have Kafka in the architecture diagram and want to know if they are actually non-blocking end to end. The acks and offset section alone is worth it before your next incident review.

Title: There is no perfect garbage collector, only the right trade-off
Description: Igor Braga (IBM) at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021 on OpenJ9's five GC policies, their barriers, and the double-mapping trick for big arrays
Body:
Every garbage collector is a bet between throughput and pause times, and the barriers that make concurrent collection safe are where the bill arrives. At Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021, Igor Braga, software developer at IBM working on Eclipse OpenJ9, walks through OpenJ9's five GC policies from the simplest stop-the-world collector to region-based ones, and ends with a virtual memory trick that made some array operations 30 times faster.

It starts gently and gets properly deep by the halfway mark. If you've only ever tuned `-Xmx`, this is a good evening's upgrade.

## What does a GC actually do?

Braga's definition has three jobs: allocate memory, work out what's live, and reclaim everything else. The upside is no manual `malloc`/`free` and no dangling pointers or double frees. The downside is extra CPU and memory, stop-the-world pauses, and little control over when memory comes back. A fun fact on the way: OpenJ9 started life as an embedded JVM for Java Micro Edition, which is why it's frugal with memory. It was open-sourced in 2017.

## Five policies, from stop-the-world to pauseless

- **optthruput**: parallel mark, sweep and optional compaction, all stop-the-world. The heap splits into a small object area and a large object area. Compaction fixes the swiss-cheese heap where there's free memory but no contiguous block big enough.
- **gencon**: generational copying, close to HotSpot's CMS. Nursery (allocate and survivor) is scavenged stop-the-world; tenured space is marked concurrently. That concurrency needs write barriers, and he walks through the object graph where a mutator moves a reference mid-mark and the collector would wrongly free a live object without one.
- **gencon concurrent scavenge**: the scavenge itself runs concurrently with two short pauses at the ends. The hard bit is a GC thread and a mutator racing to move the same object. The fix: both copy it unconditionally, then race to install the forwarding pointer, so the loser always finds a complete copy. He notes Shenandoah version 2 uses the same read barrier.
- **metronome**: incremental soft real-time. In each time window only 30% of the time goes to the GC. It uses a snapshot-at-the-beginning barrier, which keeps references alive before a store and so leaves more floating garbage.
- **balanced**: region-based and generational, close to G1, aiming for 1,000 to 2,000 regions. Partial GCs copy out the regions with the best return on investment, and a global mark phase refreshes their knowledge so fragmentation doesn't creep back.

## Do you put the cost on the mutator or the GC?

The recurring theme is that every barrier is a decision about who pays. In balanced, OpenJ9 uses an unconditional card-dirtying write barrier and makes the GC scan the cards, keeping application threads cheap. His summary of the whole field follows from that.

"no perfect GC that fits everything, all workloads," Igor Braga said at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021.

If you don't care about pauses, a pure stop-the-world collector will always win on throughput because it carries no barrier overhead. If you only care about pauses, go pauseless. Balanced, G1 or gencon sit in between. And whatever the table says, try three or four policies on your actual workload.

## Arraylets and double mapping

The finale is the most fun. Region-based collectors split very large arrays into arraylets: a spine pointing at leaves, each filling a region. That's fine for Java code, but JNI critical APIs need a contiguous array, which used to mean copying the whole array out and back again. Expensive at hundreds of megabytes.

Double mapping uses the fact that physical memory is limited but 64-bit virtual address space is not. OpenJ9 maps the scattered leaves a second time into a contiguous virtual range backed by the same physical pages, and hands that address to JNI. Writes through either mapping show up in both, with no copying. That boosted array operations by 30 times. The catch: Linux and 64-bit only, which is why the team was working on an off-heap approach for large objects next.

## Who should watch

Java developers and SREs who want a mental model of what their GC flags trade off, and anyone comparing OpenJ9 with HotSpot (his mapping of gencon to CMS and balanced to G1 is a handy translation table). He also recommends `-verbose:gc` logs with the GCMV tool for visualising heap behaviour on OpenJ9.

Title: OpenJ9 warms up fastest, then HotSpot and GraalVM overtake it
Description: Frank Kriegl at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021 on benchmarking JVM warm-up with JMH, and why OpenJ9 leads for the first few hundred runs only
Body:
Which JVM gets your code fast soonest? At Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021, Java developer Frank Kriegl benchmarked the warm-up of HotSpot, GraalVM and OpenJ9 on JDK 11 by solving the same sudoku millions of times. His answer: OpenJ9 reaches speed fastest, but only wins the race for the first few hundred iterations. After that HotSpot and GraalVM are faster.

He calls it a learner's journey, and it was his first public talk. It grew out of a research paper for his master's degree, and it is honest about what went wrong along the way, which is the most useful part.

## What does warm-up actually mean?

Kriegl defines warm-up as the number of iterations the JVM needs to speed up a method between its first and nth invocation by applying JIT optimisations. The baseline section is a compact refresher: Eden, survivor and tenured spaces; the tiered JIT in HotSpot (level 0 interpreting, C1 for levels 1 to 3, and C2 at level 4 once code turns hot after roughly 10,000 invocations); and the difference between JIT, which profiles and compiles selectively, and ahead-of-time compilation, which compiles everything up front.

## Writing a benchmark is the hard part

His first attempt was to reuse existing suites. SPECjvm2008 and DaCapo felt dated, not every benchmark ran on Java 11, and the output didn't suit further analysis. So he wrote his own, and promptly hit the classic trap.

"writing a good benchmark is not easy," Frank Kriegl said at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021.

His example of a conceptual flaw: a loop that sums an array but never returns the result. The JIT notices, eliminates the work, and your timer starts reporting almost zero milliseconds. JMH (the Java Microbenchmark Harness) fixes most of this with Blackholes that consume results so dead-code elimination can't kick in. Since he wanted to measure warm-up rather than avoid it, he set JMH's warm-up iterations to zero.

## The setup

The workload became a sudoku backtracking solver, published on GitHub. Each run was 21,000 iterations in 20 forks (20 fresh JVMs, so no JIT state leaks between them), repeated in 12 runs on different days and times to smooth out noise from the virtual machine he ran on. That multiplies out to just over five million sudoku solves per JVM.

He left JVM flags mostly at defaults, to mimic a developer who just runs their code, with two exceptions. Garbage collection was switched off where possible with Epsilon, the no-op collector from JEP 318, and memory was pre-touched so the JVM claimed physical memory up front. GraalVM had no no-op collector in his version, so he set an oversized young generation that leaves no room for an old one. OpenJ9 on Linux has no pre-touch option at all.

## What did the numbers show?

On average, HotSpot and GraalVM settled around 0.4 ms per solve, GraalVM a touch faster, with OpenJ9 just behind at almost 0.5 ms. OpenJ9 in AOT mode beat OpenJ9 in JIT mode but was still slower on average than the other two.

The warm-up curves tell the more interesting story. OpenJ9 took about 150 iterations to go from 5 ms down to 0.5 ms; HotSpot needed around 700. During that early phase HotSpot was 4.6 times slower than OpenJ9. By about 600 iterations OpenJ9's curve sits above the other two and stays there. OpenJ9's AOT mode starts at full speed and stays flat, while JIT catches up after a few hundred runs.

He also left some mysteries open, which is refreshing. HotSpot and GraalVM both show a sudden drop around iteration 100; GraalVM has an unexplained bump between iterations 6,000 and 6,800; OpenJ9 shows recurring spikes. He tested whether the missing pre-touch explained the spikes by disabling it on the other two JVMs, and it didn't.

## JITWatch didn't show the cause

To see why warm-up happens, he loaded HotSpot's compilation log into JITWatch. It showed C1 and C2 compilations only after about 20 seconds, long after the curve had flattened. The terminal output from the print-compilation and print-inlining flags told a different story: early inlining decisions by C1, which the XML log omits. Those are the likely driver of the steep early decline.

## Who should watch

Developers new to JVM internals who want a worked example of JMH, and anyone choosing a JVM for short-lived processes where the first thousand calls matter more than steady state. The results are JDK 11 and late 2020, so treat the numbers as a method to copy rather than a verdict.

Title: Cucumber turns your JUnit 5 nested tests into plain English, and shorter
Description: Catalin Tudose (Luxoft) at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021 on moving JUnit 5 tests to Cucumber and Gherkin so the business can read them
Body:
TDD tells you the code works. It doesn't tell you the code does what the business asked for. At Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021, Catalin Tudose, Java and web technologies expert at Luxoft and author of JUnit in Action (third edition), takes one small flight management app, tests it with plain JUnit 5, then rewrites the same tests in Cucumber. The Cucumber version reads like a spec and ends up shorter.

It's a hands-on demo, not a theory lecture, and a good first look at BDD for a Java developer who already lives in JUnit.

## What is wrong with plain TDD?

Nothing, Tudose argues, except where it points your attention. TDD tests are tightly coupled to the implementation: to write them you need to know what the method or class does inside, and the business goals drift out of view. His one-line summary is the one to keep.

"if TDD is making sure that you are doing the things right, BDD is making sure that you are doing the right thing," Catalin Tudose said at Conf42 Enterprise Software 2021.

BDD also gives business analysts and developers one shared artefact to argue over, instead of a requirements doc on one side and test code on the other.

## The demo app has just enough business logic

The vehicle is an airline with economy and business flights and regular and VIP passengers. The rules are small but fiddly: anyone can join an economy flight, only VIPs can join a business flight, a VIP on an economy flight can never be removed, and nobody can be added to the same flight twice. Later a bonus policy joins in: VIP passengers earn mileage divided by 10 in points, regular ones mileage divided by 20.

## JUnit 5 already gets you halfway

Before any Cucumber appears, Tudose shows how far JUnit 5 alone goes. Nested test classes (an airport test containing economy and business flight tests, each containing regular and VIP passenger tests) plus `@DisplayName` produce a test report you can read as given/when/then sentences. He also makes the case for `assertAll`: with a run of plain `assertEquals` calls, the first failure hides every assertion after it, while `assertAll` runs them all and reports every failure.

## Cucumber flattens the tree

Then the same policy moves into a Gherkin feature file: a feature, scenarios, and `Given`/`When`/`Then` steps in plain English. Each step maps to a Java method annotated with the matching Cucumber annotation, a small runner class points Cucumber at the features folder on the classpath, and the nesting disappears. All step methods sit at the same level, and a step repeated across scenarios is implemented once.

The payoff he measures is concrete: the Cucumber test class is about 157 lines against 207 for the nested JUnit 5 version, for the same behaviour.

Tudose is also clear that the three annotations carry no semantic difference for Cucumber. They exist so a reader knows which line is a precondition, which is an action and which is a consequence.

## The IntelliJ plugin writes your step skeletons

With the Cucumber for Java and Gherkin plugins installed in IntelliJ IDEA, you can run a feature file directly (six scenarios and 22 steps in the passenger policy) and get instant feedback. Delete a step implementation and the plugin highlights the orphaned line; run the feature and Cucumber prints a ready-to-paste method snippet for the missing step. That is the BDD loop in practice: write the sentence, let the tool hand you the stub, fill in the Java.

## Scenario outlines cover the parameterised case

For the bonus policy he uses scenario outlines: parameterised steps with an examples table underneath. Four columns map one-to-one to the method parameters (through regular expressions in the step annotations), and five rows mean each outline runs five times. Two outlines, regular and VIP, give ten scenarios and 30 steps from a few lines of Gherkin.

## Who should watch

Java developers who write good JUnit tests but find the business never reads them, and teams curious whether Cucumber is worth the extra moving part. If you already run Cucumber in CI, this is a refresher; if you're on JUnit 4, watch the migration talk below first.

Title: A bad system beats a good engineer, so debrief the system
Description: Amir Shaked (PerimeterX) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 on building a learning culture with blameless debriefs, checkpoints and process fixes
Body:
An engineer merges failing code to main late at night, sure it won't reach production until morning. Then an autoscaling event deploys it anyway. Amir Shaked, Senior VP R&D at PerimeterX and, by his own description, an experienced breaker of production environments, used that incident at [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Amir_Shaked_learning_culture) to show how his team built a learning culture around debriefs. The core idea: fix the process, because fixing people doesn't work.

PerimeterX sells web app protection as a service, running on about 15,000 cores and 300 microservices. In a business where the threat changes constantly, being able to ship quickly is part of the product. The goal Shaked set was rapid deployments, zero downtime, and every mistake made once so the team learns, but never twice.

## Where the team started

The starting point was not great. Code and configuration changes kept causing the same kinds of production failures, and the system was too sensitive to incidents in the underlying cloud. Worse was fear of judgment: every attempt to dig into an issue met pushback along the lines of why so many questions, don't we trust our people? Shaked's view is that people who feel judged underperform, and a team like that cannot learn. "A bad system will beat a good person every time," Shaked said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021.

## The late-night merge that deployed itself

Back to the merge. Earlier that week a DevOps engineer had added a process that deployed that service from main whenever it needed to autoscale. That night traffic rose, new instances came up and they ran the buggy code. You could spend the debrief asking why the engineer merged failing code, or why the autoscaling hook was added. Shaked's point is that both miss the real flaw: an engineer could merge into what was effectively production without knowing it. The fix was a rule everyone understands, main branch equals production for every service, and that changes how people merge.

## How a debrief runs

The process has four steps: the incident, the immediate fix, a debrief 24 to 72 hours later (depending on how much sleep people lost), and a checkpoint two weeks after that to review the action items. As the culture matures, teams start opening incidents for minor things just to learn from them, which he calls a healthy stage to reach.

The meeting starts with a detailed timeline from the moment the problem really began, when the code was merged or the third-party provider started failing, not from the first customer complaint. Then the impact, in cost, customers affected and complaints, so everyone understands why the team is spending time on it. Then two leading questions with fixed targets. Did we identify the issue in under 5 minutes? Did we fix it in under an hour, or under 10 minutes, or did it resolve itself? Any no means working out what to change or build so the answer becomes yes. Shaked says this simple framing drove a big culture change over time, because it is about the system, not whoever caused today's incident.

## What made it stick

Two problems kept coming back: lack of trust in a new manager's process, and action items that were never done. For the second, Shaked labels every Jira ticket from a debrief and reviews all of them monthly, on top of the checkpoints. For the first, the team publishes debriefs widely across the company, with what happened and what will change. Being that open also brings in people who spot gaps the debrief missed.

His four rules for the meeting: avoid blame altogether and stop it politely when it starts; go easy on the why questions, which can sound like judgment; be consistent; stay calm.

## The engineering lessons

The learnings list is worth the video on its own. Gradual rollout is a great tool but not a silver bullet. A crisis-mode process matters. Feature flags let the team disable a feature instead of rolling back many services, sometimes thousands of containers, which also shows quickly whether the code is to blame at all. Avoid in-place changes in tightly coupled microservices: add the new behaviour, verify it, then remove the old one. Look 10x ahead for breaking points. Treat config as code.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers trying to bring in postmortems against pushback, and anyone whose retros end with a name rather than a ticket. It is a short talk, heavy on process and light on tooling.

Title: Write the postmortem about what went wrong, never who did
Description: Pranjal Deo (Google) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 on blameless postmortems - what goes in one, when to write it, and how leaders keep the culture alive
Body:
A postmortem that names a culprit teaches the company one thing: next time, keep quiet. Pranjal Deo, Engineering Program Manager in Google's SRE organisation and co-author of the blameless postmortem chapter in *The Site Reliability Workbook*, made that case at [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Pranjal_Deo_postmortem_culture_blameless). The takeaway: psychological safety and learning from failure only look like they pull against each other. A well-written postmortem gives you both.

Deo is clear about scope at the start. This is not a lecture on SRE or on fixing outages, and not a step-by-step template tutorial. It is about why postmortems matter, why good ones are hard to write and what to do once you have a pile of them. The talk also sets out to dispel the idea that the practice is only for big companies or deep technical problems. Deo has even used the same framework for personal situations where things didn't go to plan.

## What goes into a postmortem?

The definition: a written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, the root cause and the follow-up actions that stop it recurring. The template in the talk starts with an executive summary (dates, who has access, duration, user impact, how it was detected and resolved). Next comes background for readers from elsewhere in the company, since the best practice is that anyone can read any postmortem. Then impact, root cause, trigger and recovery. Then lessons learned, split into what went well, what didn't, and the speaker's favourite section: where did we get lucky? Finally action items, each measurable, with an owner, a priority and a tracking ID, plus a glossary.

You don't write one for every failure. Teams agree the criteria before an incident happens, and those differ a lot: an e-commerce reliability team measures failure in a different way from a product team. The examples cover business triggers (users affected, revenue lost), product ones (a canary showing a regression, a risky push during a freeze) and people ones (a disruptive reorg, a project that overloaded people for months). Small, similar incidents can share one postmortem.

## Why blame breaks the whole thing

A blameless postmortem assumes everyone acted with good intentions on the information they had. "It focuses on what went wrong instead of who did wrong," Deo said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021. The reason is plain human nature. Postmortems are permanent artefacts, so the person who caused an outage worries about being fired, not getting promoted, or being laughed at by future colleagues, and people with those worries hide facts. Blame is bad for the business too. The action item fire the human leaves the system that allowed the mistake in place, ready for a newer, less experienced hire to repeat it.

The worked example is a root cause line that names one engineer for not setting up alerting on a storage cluster and calls the result a disaster. It is blameful and dramatic, and those words add nothing. The rewrite sticks to facts: "the hard drives in one of the trading storage clusters run out of space, and this was not noticed due to a lack of alerting." Add the knock-on effect (trades redirected to other clusters that were nearly full too) and an action item with an owner and a tracking ID.

## What leaders can do

Write a few postmortems yourself and share them widely. That sets the tone and lets you try out the format. Once there is a collection, use it as training material, for example the Wheel of Misfortune, a role-play where a cast of employees re-enacts a past postmortem. Reward the right behaviour: highlight good postmortems in meetings, reward closing action items, and count reliability work in performance reviews. With senior management's support, you can even publicly celebrate the person who was the proximate cause of a big outage, if they escalated sensibly and honestly documented the system failures that let it happen.

## The part after the document

Action items that are never closed mean the incident comes back, probably bigger. Review postmortems and their action items on a regular schedule, look for recurring themes, and as a stretch goal build tools that aggregate postmortems across product boundaries. The talk also lists the signs a culture is fading: no time to write, the same incidents repeating, blameful language from someone senior, people avoiding the process altogether. The closing line is the one to remember: the cost of failure is education.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers starting a postmortem process, and SREs whose postmortems are written but never read. It is a culture talk with a usable template inside it, and it pairs well with the SRE Workbook chapter Deo co-authored.

Title: Three outages no new monitoring tool would have caught
Description: Piyush Verma (last9.io) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 on three outages whose real root cause was a missing first principle, not missing tooling
Body:
A deleted port 443, a disk mount that didn't survive a reboot and a clock running behind: none of these needed a smarter alerting stack. Piyush Verma, CTO and co-founder of last9.io, has held a pager for about a decade, and at [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Piyush_Verma_breaking_software) he dissected three outages to show that the real root cause is usually a first principle the team skipped.

The title is the premise. A popping balloon or a failing RAM stick used to make a noise. Modern software fails quietly. He sorts failures into software, human, network, process and culture. Software failures are the easiest to catch: a 500 in a log line, a rule, a page. Culture failures surface last, and they are the ones he cares about.

## Three questions after every fire

His routine has three steps: put the fire out, ask where else the same thing is breaking, then ask how to stop it happening again. Most teams stop at the first. "Unlike product, reliability cannot be improved as one feature at a time," Verma said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021. Customers do not give you enough chances to fix one failure at a time.

## Outage one: the security group edited by hand

Customer service reported that login was down. Datadog, Papertrail and CloudWatch all looked fine, which makes sense: requests that never reach you never trip your monitoring. Twitter knew before the alerts did. A DevOps engineer had been whitelisting home IP addresses during the lockdown and deleted the 443 inbound rule on a load balancer's security group by accident. So it was not just login: everything was down, and the real impact could not even be measured.

The fix he argues for is not an audit-trail policy that someone then has to read. "The answer to solve a human problem cannot be another human reviewing it every time," he said. The root cause was a culture that allowed manual changes, because a Terraform apply took around ten minutes. His answer: if Terraform is too slow, make it faster, but never allow the manual shortcut.

## Outage two: the shard that forgot its mount

About 25 hours before a country launch, in a data centre, PagerDuty went off for 500s, auto-resolved, then fired again as the public API became unreachable. The team checked Rundeck for changes, the firewall, Grafana, Stackdriver, Docker restarts and APM, and found nothing. Ten engineers worked on it for 20 hours. In the end it was a mount command that had not run on one database shard. A fix for mounts that did not persist across reboots had been applied to ten machines with Ansible, but not to the machine that was out for repair at the time. It was added back before the launch, rebooted, lost a slice of data, failed health on those requests, got cut off by the load balancer and came back, over and over.

He doubts this one could have been prevented the first time. The class of error could be: a startup script using osquery to check the machine for configuration drift would have caught it.

## Outage three: blaming etcd for a clock problem

A hosted Terraform service used an etcd lock with compare-and-swap and a TTL, so a dead process would not hold the lock forever. Yet both competing jobs got key-not-found errors. A GitHub issue about etcd TTLs expiring too early during leader elections looked like the answer. The team spent a week-long sprint replacing etcd with Consul. Then someone asked the question Verma rates above all others: how was it working before? The real cause was clock drift between cluster machines, larger than the short TTL. A basic check that NTP is installed and running, a few lines of bash, would have saved the team all those hours.

## Outage four is tomorrow's

His last outage hasn't happened yet: the one where you learned nothing from the previous three. He then shows what last9.io was building, a knowledge graph that maps how infrastructure components relate, so you can ask questions like how instances are spread across availability zones today versus a few days ago, or what else a bucket permission change will hit. It was not open source at the time. That closing part is a product pitch, and the talk says so openly.

## Who should watch

SREs who write RCAs whose only action item is another alert, and anyone who has replaced a component because of a GitHub issue. The three stories are the value here. Each one is a few lines of checklist away from never happening again.

Title: Production support is mostly talking, and the fix comes second
Description: Quintin Balsdon (Zuhlke Group) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 on surviving production support - questions, runbooks, code review at 3am and a buddy rota
Body:
Your phone rings at 03:00 and the first decision is not which log to open but which hat to put on. Quintin Balsdon, Expert Software Engineer at Zuhlke Group and an Android developer by day, turned seven years of production support into a talk at [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Quintin_Balsdon_production_support_experiences). His main point: support is a communication job first. The way you ask questions, share roles and refuse shortcuts matters as much as the fix.

The talk started as a write-up his company asked for after an intense three-year project where support was a big part of the work. His credentials include supporting an Excel macro he wrote, for seven years. He also wrote a joke app that took off after someone made a Reddit page for it, and suddenly had 30,000 people using it at once with no way to support them.

## Why should everyone do some support?

Balsdon thinks everybody should be involved, which does not mean everybody gets woken at 03:00. People who have done support understand how the infrastructure really fits together and spot trouble earlier. The more you do it, the less you have to, because you learn which component keeps failing and go and fix it. There is an upside too: a team that has walked off the battlefield together, tired and broken, gets very close.

He also learns from other people's outages in the news: TSB's month-long migration failure in 2018 that locked 1.9 million customers out of their accounts, an expired third-party certificate that cut 30 million mobile customers off for most of a working day, and Google's single sign-on going down for an hour in December 2020. His lesson from that last one: when YouTube, Gmail and Docs all fail together, stop blaming each service and look at the shared authentication layer.

## Drop your agenda and ask questions

His first rule is to leave your agenda at the door. If you go in sure that the component you have always wanted to rewrite is the culprit, you will push that theory, and when you are wrong you become the person nobody trusts in a crisis. "Blaming will only get you so far. Understanding will get you so much further," Balsdon said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021.

Questions do the steering instead. Ask "could it be this component?" rather than announcing it. Make testers spell out their repro steps: did you press back before or after the next screen finished loading? Agree on what words mean, because one person's crash is another's freeze. Then the operational ones: where did the report come from, how many unique users are affected, how will we know it is fixed? Did the user try iPhone, or the web? That one question often tells you whether the backend or the Android app is at fault.

## Split the roles before the pings arrive

His best war story is a failed hardware security module. All traffic ran through a single server while a new part was driven to the data centre. Two people were on call, and they agreed early that one would monitor and diagnose and the other would only handle communication. Requests came in over WhatsApp, email, Slack, Teams and an internal tool, and none of it reached the person doing the diagnosis. He recommends agreeing on one communication tool with management for the same reason.

The rest of the toolkit is plain, and that is why it works. Runbooks per feature, each with the core team to ask (not to blame), emergency contacts, a link to a status report, an architecture diagram and the repository. Access reviewed ahead of time, so the one person with the production password does not get woken for every incident. Reports read with suspicion: a crash count is not a count of unique users, because one frustrated customer may retry ten times.

## Trust the process when people are standing over you

At one of his first jobs, with people standing over him demanding a release, Balsdon woke another developer for a code review anyway. The review caught an error that would have caused a massive crash. Skipping review and testing in the name of a quick fix is a risk you take on behalf of the whole organisation. Sometimes the right call is to leave a problem alone: "If it's not worth waking up 20 developers, six qas, and five managers at that particular point in time, you might have to leave it."

He closes on people. Take time off after a call-out and agree the terms in writing before an incident, because being on call costs sleep even on nights nobody pages you. That is where the talk's title comes from. Run a wash-up the next day so others learn from the incident, keep release notes, and run a primary-and-secondary buddy rota so nobody is on call three weeks in a row.

## Who should watch

Anyone about to join their first on-call rota, and team leads writing one. It is all stories and habits rather than tools, and none of it is specific to Android.

Title: Your QA team is already half an SRE team
Description: Reuben Rajan George (Accenture) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 on why quality engineers make natural SREs, from test observability to chaos tests
Body:
The people who spend all day asking what happens when this breaks already exist in most companies, and they sit in the QA team. Reuben Rajan George, Cloud Reliability Architect at Accenture with more than ten years in performance engineering, used a short lightning talk at [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Reuben_Rajan_George_sre_quality_engineers) to argue that quality engineers are a ready-made SRE talent pool, and to map out the four areas where their work is heading.

He aims it at three audiences: quality engineers who want to move into SRE, quality engineers who have just been told they are doing SRE now, and product managers who want to point their existing QE people at operations work.

## Why do testers make good SREs?

His starting point is that the job title of tester undersells what the role became. "Modern day sdets, or in other words, software development engineers in testing, or in other words, quality engineers, are actually highly skilled automation engineers," George said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021. They cover functional, performance, security, usability and accessibility validation, they write code, and they understand the system end to end from the user's side.

He sums up the mindset in three words: curiosity, adaptability and exploratory. Curiosity is the one that maps straight onto SRE. Someone who keeps asking why a task is done by hand every sprint is, in SRE vocabulary, hunting toil. The what-if scenarios testers are trained to write are, he points out, the basis of any hypothesis-based testing technique, which is a polite way of saying chaos experiments.

## Four places the work is going

The core of the talk is a list of four areas where testers "today and tomorrow" will spend their time.

**Autonomous functional validation.** Test frameworks that notice a new deployment, pick up changed environment variables and update their own test code. Testing the deployment templates themselves: spin up the CloudFormation or Terraform stack through the SDK, check the stack outputs, and fail the deployment if the integration test fails. Then tear the environment down after the run, so the whole thing stays automated.

**Test session observability.** Wire APM into lower environments so functional test runs also report performance regressions between builds: the number of database calls, calls between services, how long reads take. He admits the cost and licensing trade-off and notes that open source tools cover a lot of it. The payoff is that testers can trace latent failure chains through logs before they turn into outages.

**Test optimisation with analytics.** Statistics, NLP and machine learning to prune redundant scenarios, merge duplicate defects, prioritise and sequence test cases and improve coverage. The stated goal is to cut as much toil as possible.

**Continuous performance optimisation.** This is his own field, and where the talk gets most specific. Instead of a big performance test before release, frameworks keep tuning the configuration of applications, runtimes, databases and cloud environments, and study how those parameters interact. The skill set grows accordingly: JMeter and NeoLoad, monitoring with Prometheus and Splunk, plus Ansible, bash, APIs and dashboards as code.

## Where chaos engineering comes in

The last area, reliability evaluation, is the one closest to the conference theme. Quality engineers write scripts that verify resilience patterns actually work: circuit breaking, rate limiting, bulkheading, timeout handling and result caching, using libraries such as Hystrix or Resilience4j. They use FMEA to find single points of failure, test failover for multi-region deployments, check recovery playbooks end to end and run dry runs of failure scenarios.

Chaos testing itself gets two jobs: automating how failure scenarios are picked, created and injected in pre-production and production, and checking that the results match the expected behaviour. The failures he lists include network brownouts and instance failures, across every component and external dependency.

## Who should watch

It is a short talk, closer to a career map than a tutorial: no demo and no code. Watch it if you lead a QA team and wonder how to pitch them for SRE work, or if you are a performance engineer wondering which skills to learn next. Experienced chaos engineers will recognise most of the list, but it is a handy checklist to give a manager who still thinks testing ends at the UI.

Title: Deutsche Bahn's first game day hit a 100% error rate
Description: Maik Figura (codecentric AG) and Oliver Kracht (Deutsche Bahn) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 on a year of game days at DB Vertrieb
Body:
The first experiment was a rolling update under load, and every veteran in the room bet nothing would break. Maik Figura, IT consultant at codecentric AG, and Oliver Kracht, Implementation Lead at Deutsche Bahn, told that story at [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Maik_Figura_Oliver_Kracht_clear_the_ring_deutsche_bahn): a year of chaos engineering at DB Vertrieb, the part of Deutsche Bahn that sells train tickets, told as a circus show, with the detours, the failures and the five excuses they heard most.

## Why did DB Vertrieb need chaos engineering?

DB Vertrieb sells a couple of million tickets a day through vending machines, apps, the web and, outside a pandemic, in person. The old platform was a stable WebSphere monolith surrounded by even older systems, some in COBOL, and changing anything took three months or more. Operations loved it. Business wanted changes in hours.

So they changed everything at once: a cloud-ready stack, many more teams split along domain boundaries, continuous delivery and deployment, automated testing instead of manual QA, new incident processes. The abstract puts the result at 300+ microservices and 100+ developers. As Kracht puts it, a CI/CD cannon shoots features straight into a running show.

## What went wrong first?

The first feature on the new platform was Komfort-Check-in, which lets you check in to your seat so the conductor doesn't ask for your ticket. It was also the first feature connecting the new platform to the old monolith. On a Friday at 5pm it went down silently, the restart caused a cascading failure, and customers couldn't download tickets they had already bought, right when everyone was taking the train home. The post-mortem efficiently found who was responsible; the lesson they took was that they had asked the wrong question, and post-mortems became blameless.

## Can you just deploy the monkeys?

Their next fix was technical acceptance tests: developers ran performance tests, then threw the artefact to a separate Ops department, which tested a rolling update. That didn't work either. Then they asked what Netflix would do and deployed Chaos Monkey for Kubernetes, which killed pods and containers as advertised. The microservices weren't ready, they started far too big, and worst of all nobody noticed, because they lacked the observability to see the errors.

"A fool with a tool is still a fool," Figura said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021.

## What happened at the first real game day?

They started over with the basics: pick an aspect of the system, plan the experiment, prepare the environment, measure the steady state, run it, write down what you found. No budgets, cages or consultants required. The first game day put Ops, architecture, business operations and developers in one room, and combined the two tests that had always run separately: a rolling update while the service was under load.

The error rate sat at about 100% for 15 minutes. Dev had only ever load-tested and Ops had only ever done rolling updates without load, so nobody had tried both at once. It was depressing, Figura admits, and also the end of their buy-in problem: after showing management that result, they never had trouble getting support.

## Which excuses did they hear most?

Their top five, with answers:

- **Go-live is in a few days.** Make QA a friend and fold experiments into the test plan, or shift them left into daily development.
- **We don't have the access rights.** Often a knowledge gap; ask whether they've tried, and talk to Ops.
- **We can't think of a useful experiment.** A coaching problem: offer standard experiments, use-case-driven ones and other formats such as red teaming.
- **We're only doing features right now.** Functional and non-functional requirements are connected, and technical debt you ignore finds you in production.
- **The product owner won't prioritise it.** Show the value with one small-scope game day, and recruit security as a lever.

## What did a year of game days produce?

More than 80 game days and more than 120 weaknesses that won't hit production, enough trust to run their first game day in production, and teams hosting their own. They added formats such as red teaming, wheel of misfortune and incident-process drills, and keep all experiment write-ups in one shared place. Tooling: an APM solution (they use Instana), Pumba and Chaos Monkey for Spring Boot to start, with Steadybit under evaluation and the awesome-chaos-engineering list on GitHub for the rest. They only automated experiments after about half a year and 50 game days.

The final warning: don't let the process eat you. Once chaos engineering succeeded, QA wanted mandatory experiments on a checklist; they pushed back, because teams know best what to test.

## Who should watch

Anyone bringing chaos engineering into a large organisation with a Dev/Ops split and a monolith that still matters. It's culture-first and full of honest failures.

Title: Five tech trends of 2021, read as a career map
Description: Derris Boomer (BoomerTechGroup) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 on AI, IoT, machine learning, SaaS and big data, and the jobs each one creates
Body:
At a conference about breaking systems on purpose, Derris Boomer, founder of BoomerTechGroup, gave the talk for people still deciding which systems to work on. His [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 session](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Derris_Boomer_technology_trends_startups_fortune_500_companies) walks through five technology trends (AI, IoT, machine learning, SaaS and big data), the jobs growing around each, and one piece of career advice for people early in their career.

Honest scope: there is no chaos engineering here. It's a high-level career primer aimed at newcomers and career changers, not at practitioners.

## Where are the job openings?

Boomer opens with a chart from a survey published by Forbes at the end of 2020 on job openings by skill area over the previous twelve months. Software development comes first, cloud second and security third, with automation growing. At the bottom sit fintech, parallel computing and quantum computing: small, but growing.

"So if you're looking to jump on something new from scratch, definitely look into quantum computing and parallel computing as well," Boomer said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021.

## What do the five trends look like up close?

He explains each through everyday examples first, then the business side, then the jobs:

- **AI.** Voice assistants, recommendations on streaming services, call centres that understand you say "hardware issue", website chatbots. Hot areas include gamification for training staff, manufacturing, education and customer service; hot jobs include data analytics, NLP engineering, UX development and data science.
- **IoT.** Washers and dryers that call the manufacturer, and assembly lines where a manager can see that one line in one plant is down for the next six hours. Smart buildings, cars, wearables and smart cities, down to sensors on manhole covers. Jobs: IoT security (he calls them IoT hackers), support technicians, UI/UX designers, solution architects.
- **Machine learning.** His example is a phone that notices you buy coffee on the same route every day and fuel on Wednesdays, and reminds you when you skip the gym on Saturday. In business: virtual agents, biometrics, learning platforms, speech recognition. Jobs: ML engineers, computer scientists, AI programmers.
- **SaaS.** Microsoft Office on every device, Salesforce for sales teams, Xbox Live subscriptions, Smartsheet, and companies such as Shopify, Zoom, Slack, HubSpot and Atlassian. Jobs: lead developers, SaaS specialists, software and support engineers.
- **Big data.** A company with records going back to 1924, a fast-growing product tracking every customer in detail, a cable provider that knows what you watch and when. The skill is pulling the KPIs out of it; the jobs are data scientists, developers and DBAs.

## What's the career advice?

His closing point is for juniors and mid-level people who lack the skills yet: consider the large consultancies, and he names Deloitte, PwC, Ernst & Young, KPMG and Accenture. Whether as an employee or a contractor, he says you get three things there: a regular paycheque, on-the-job training where you apply what you've learned, and exposure to many clients across sectors and cities. Roles he sees in constant demand include data scientists, report writers, trainers, project managers, QA analysts and solution architects.

## Who should watch

Students, career changers and early-career engineers looking for a broad overview of where hiring was heading in 2021. Experienced engineers, and anyone who came for chaos engineering, can skip this one and pick from the related talks below.

Title: More observability data can mean fewer answers
Description: Mahesh Venkataraman (Accenture) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 on treating failure prognosis and diagnosis as a spatio-temporal-causal problem
Body:
Every observability tool promises more data, and more data is exactly the problem. Mahesh Venkataraman, Managing Director at Accenture, argued at [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Mahesh_Venkataraman_spatio_temporal_causal_uncertainty_observability) that the job of observability is two decisions, predicting failures and explaining them, and that both are best modelled as uncertainty spread across time, across architecture layers and along causal chains.

"The more data you have, the less insights you can discover due to noise and nondeterminism," Venkataraman said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021.

Honest scope: this is a short, conceptual talk. It proposes an approach and names the techniques; it doesn't show an implementation or results.

## What is observability actually for?

The textbook definition is how well you can infer a system's internal state from its outputs. Venkataraman makes it practical with two objectives. Diagnosis infers the cause from the effects after a failure. Prognosis gives early warning of a failure that is coming, from current behaviour and likely failure pathways. Combined with chaos engineering, the experiments inject the conditions and observability is meant to make the results interpretable and actionable.

In practice, he says, dashboards and logs produce a data deluge and a decision dilemma. The signal-to-noise ratio is low because many systems interact, reconciling and correlating their data is hard, and third-party components make it worse.

## Why is the timing of an alert a trade-off?

After a fault or anomaly, events can go three ways: it leads to a failure, it's transient and fades, or it was never a fault at all. Deciding which, and when, is the uncertainty. Decide early, long before the expected failure, and you get more false alarms and alert fatigue. Decide late, close to the failure, and the warning is probably too late to act on. The longer the causal chain between the original cause and the later effect, the more uncertain the call.

There's space as well as time. If CPU and memory spike alongside other events, will a service fail at the end of a long chain, and where: which layer, which component, when?

## Can't data analysis just find the cause?

Not on its own, he argues. Cause, correlation, consequence, confounder and coincidence are easy to mix up, and a failure is rarely one chain of events; it is a network of conditions. He calls the assumption that analysis alone will settle causality a common underestimate.

His inspiration comes from fields that already model problems in space and time: city traffic, weather, epidemiology, social networks, and cancer prognosis, where doctors reason about where a tumour started and how it spread.

## What does the proposed approach look like?

Data from the system under normal conditions and under fault injection goes into a spatio-temporal-causal database. On top sits a mix of techniques: statistics, time-series analysis, association rules, Bayesian networks, Markov models, pattern recognition and cluster analysis, all applied in both time and space. A knowledge graph adds qualitative reasoning from text outputs such as logs, which matter for causal chain analysis.

The output is recommendations, not verdicts: likely fault pathways, anomaly alerts, imminent failures and time to failure, event correlation and recovery suggestions. He's explicit that the engine should complement human experts, not replace them, and that aiming for 100% automation is the wrong goal.

## Who should watch

SREs and observability leads drowning in dashboards who want a vocabulary for why their alerts are either early and noisy or late and useless. It's a short framework talk, so pair it with something hands-on.

Title: Fail over all the time, and get paged at 2pm instead of 2am
Description: Ryan Guest (Salesforce) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 on an architecture that fails over on every request, so the error path is the normal path
Body:
Failover code is the code you run least and trust most, which is a bad combination. Ryan Guest, Software Architect at Salesforce, used his [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Ryan_Guest_cloud_architecture_embracing_failover) to describe a reference architecture his team runs in production that removes the distinction: every request may go to any server in the pool, so failover happens all day long, and failures show up when the whole team is awake.

It's a short talk built around one idea and its trade-offs.

## Why optimise for 2pm pages?

Every seasoned engineer, Guest says, has a 2am page story, and the industry treats it as a rite of passage. He admits the firefighting feels good. But it burns people out, crowds out innovation, and organisations tend to reward the person who saves the day over the one whose system never needed saving. His premise: design so that when something breaks, you deal with it in the afternoon with full cognitive ability and the team on hand.

Some context: Guest has spent 13 years at Salesforce, mostly on the core platform in data privacy and security, and the talk comes as Salesforce finished re-architecting its infrastructure as Hyperforce, with goals such as local data storage, B2B and B2C scale, backwards compatibility and running on more than one cloud substrate.

## Where do the worst bugs hide?

The classic pattern is try server A, and if that fails, try server B. It works for simple systems, but the fallback only runs after something has already gone wrong.

Guest's favourite distributed systems paper, an analysis of production failures in distributed data-intensive systems from the University of Toronto, studied the worst bugs in open-source systems such as Cassandra and Hadoop. Most catastrophic failures could have been prevented by simple testing of error-handling code, and grepping error handlers for TODO and FIXME comments was a good way to find the trouble spots. If the error path is where the bugs are, run the error path constantly.

## What does failing over all the time look like?

"What if all the time we were just in failover mode and just operate like that?" Guest said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021.

Version one is a coin flip: heads goes to server one, tails to server two. If one dies, traffic keeps flowing to the other, users notice nothing, and the logs and alerts wait for business hours. Split the two servers across cloud providers and you gain more reliability. The mindset changes too: there is no primary and no secondary, just a pool, and neither client nor server cares which path a request took. One practical addition: they sign requests, so a server that is out of date or on the wrong version can be detected.

## Isn't 50/50 naive?

Yes, so the choice of server becomes a function with probabilities that add up to one. His illustrative split sends 90% of requests to the nearest server (the speed of light still wins), 2% to a service on another cloud provider, 2% to another region and 3% to an on-premises service. The small slices are the point: every failover route gets real traffic every day, so you know it works before you need it.

## When should you not do this?

Guest is clear about the trade-offs:

- **Data that changes often.** Write-heavy workloads bring replication and consistency trouble when requests bounce around the world.
- **Chatty protocols.** Keep those close together.
- **Performance over reliability.** If a fast failure beats a slow answer, this is the wrong design.

It fits best where data is mostly stable or versioned, and where a request taking ten times as long is fine as long as it gets an answer.

## Who should watch

Architects and on-call engineers designing multi-region or multi-cloud services, especially read-heavy ones. A short talk, one idea, worth it.

Title: Inject the syscall errors your app already sees, just more often
Description: Long Zhang (KTH Royal Institute of Technology) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 on Phoebe, which amplifies real system call errors into chaos experiments
Body:
Linux has more than 300 system calls and more than 100 error codes, and most of the combinations never happen in production. Long Zhang, PhD student at KTH Royal Institute of Technology, presented Phoebe at [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Long_Zhang_error_injection_system_calls): a fault injection framework that watches which syscall errors your application already hits, then turns up their rate in experiments. Realistic failures, observed in less time.

## Why not inject errors at random?

Zhang lists three open problems in chaos engineering: evaluating resilience at different levels, automating experiments, and efficiency. He tackles the third. Experiment time in production is limited and risky, so spending it on failures that can never occur is waste. If the failure model comes from errors that really happen, every experiment teaches you something about a scenario you will meet.

## Do healthy apps really fail system calls?

His demo is the best part. He attaches a syscall monitor to OBS, the program recording his talk, which is plainly working. Within seconds the per-second report shows failing calls: futex returning EAGAIN, and execve failing four times in one second with ENOENT.

"Every application indeed does lots of system calls, and some of them failed naturally," Zhang said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021. A dashboard from an email server they ran in production, subscribed to real mailing lists for natural traffic, shows the same thing at scale: about ten kinds of syscall errors, some frequent, some rare, all while the server worked fine. The question is what happens when the rare ones become common.

## How does Phoebe amplify errors?

Phoebe has two monitors, one for natural errors at the kernel boundary and one for application behaviour (response codes, CPU, heap), so a steady state exists to compare against. An error model synthesiser turns the observations into injection models, an orchestrator runs the experiments through a syscall injector that rewrites return codes, and the output is a resilience report.

The error rate is the share of calls of one type that return a given code within a monitoring interval. Phoebe sorts each syscall/error pair into three categories and amplifies each differently:

- **Sporadic** (low maximum rate): inject at a fixed, predefined rate high enough to see the effect.
- **Fluctuating** (high maximum, high variance): inject at the observed maximum, which is known to occur in production.
- **Steady** (high maximum, low variance): multiply the maximum by a factor, to look for the threshold where the app stops coping.

## What did it find?

They evaluated it on two Java applications. Hedwig, the email server, crashed or ended up in a corrupted state under some injected errors, so it misbehaved even after injection stopped, while it shrugged off others at rates well above the natural ones. TTorrent, a Java BitTorrent client, was resilient to some syscall errors and broke on others that were critical to downloading. Thanks to eBPF, the overhead on response time, CPU load and memory was slight, even in production.

The idea came from Conf42 itself: Zhang learned eBPF and BCC at a Linux observability and chaos engineering workshop at the 2020 edition, went back to Sweden and turned it into a paper.

## What are the limits?

Phoebe targets Java because it wants observability at three layers: the OS, the JVM and the application. The concept should carry over to any Linux executable, and the monitor, visualiser and injector can be reused with small changes. The JVM itself can create or absorb syscall errors, and that interplay is future work. Phoebe is open source in KTH's royal-chaos repository on GitHub, and the paper is on arXiv (2006.04444).

## Who should watch

Chaos engineers looking beyond pod-killing toward kernel-level, evidence-based fault models, and anyone who enjoys eBPF. It's a research talk, but the demo makes it concrete.

Title: Let a solver pick your cloud, then let it change its mind
Description: Paweł Skrzypek and Alicja Reniewicz (7bulls.com) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 on Melodic, open-source multi-cloud deployment that re-optimises itself
Body:
Minimise cost and the optimal deployment is no deployment at all; maximise performance and you rent the biggest machines going. Paweł Skrzypek, CTO of 7bulls.com, and Alicja Reniewicz, full stack engineer there, showed at [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Pawe_Skrzypek_Alicja_Reniewicz_proactive_optimization_cloud_resources) how Melodic turns that trade-off into a utility function and a solver, then keeps re-solving it as metrics come in.

Melodic is an open-source platform, built in the EU Horizon 2020 Melodic project and developed further by 7bulls.com, released under the Mozilla Public License 2.0. It deploys virtual machines, containers, serverless functions and big data frameworks across cloud providers, and chooses the resources for you.

Honest scope: the abstract leads with forecasting-based proactive optimisation. In the talk, Melodic reacts to current metrics, and forecasting is presented as the next step in its successor project, Morphemic.

## How does Melodic decide what to deploy?

You model the application once in CAMEL, a cloud-agnostic modelling language Skrzypek compares to TOSCA with extras: components, connections, security, infrastructure, plus requirements, constraints and a utility function. Melodic turns that model into a constraint programming problem, fetches offers from the providers with prices and hardware specs, and solves for the deployment with the highest utility.

The utility function can mix technical metrics (CPU, memory) with business ones such as average response time or time to process a job. When a metric crosses its threshold, which Melodic calls an SLO violation, it starts a new optimisation with the fresh values and reconfigures the running application. The solvers include constraint programming, genetic algorithms and Monte Carlo tree search with a neural network, in the spirit of AlphaGo.

Under the hood: one microservice per module, Mule ESB community edition as the control plane, Camunda for the BPM flow, ActiveMQ for metrics.

## What did it save in practice?

The first case is AI Investments, a Polish fintech that trains a separate forecasting model for each of more than 200 markets and retrains them regularly. Training starts on premises; if Melodic estimates it will take too long, it adds cloud workers, re-estimates, adds more if needed, and removes every cloud resource when the job finishes.

The headline figure is $175,000 over three years, measured as the gap between optimal and non-optimal deployments. "Probably the real savings are lower but are still very significant," Skrzypek said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021, which is the kind of footnote vendor talks usually leave out. The methodology is published on the Melodic site.

The second case is a Spark application that finds mutations in genomes against a reference genome, used by researchers at a Polish university who want each job done within an hour.

## What does the demo show?

Reniewicz deploys that genome application on AWS from a Melodic instance. She uploads the CAMEL model, keeps the AWS credentials in a secure store behind placeholders rather than in the model, and walks through the process view: fetching offers, generating the constraint problem (one to ten Spark workers, core counts, provider), reasoning, deploying. There is also a simulation mode that shows the chosen solution without starting real machines.

A Grafana dashboard shows a traffic light for whether the job will finish in its 60 minutes. With one worker the light goes red, the estimate says at least four to seven cores are needed, and Melodic triggers a reconfiguration that adds a second worker, which appears in the Spark master UI moments later. Near the end of a run it removes workers it no longer needs.

## What comes next?

Morphemic adds two ideas. Polymorphic adaptation changes the architecture itself, for example swapping VMs for serverless or moving work to GPUs and FPGAs. Proactive adaptation forecasts the workload and reconfigures ahead of the spike, closing the window in which a reactive system is still catching up.

## Who should watch

Teams with batch or ML training jobs that have deadlines and budgets, and anyone curious about treating deployment as an optimisation problem. It's a project presentation with a live demo, light on chaos engineering despite the event.

Title: An Android pentest lab, from APK to hard-coded password
Description: Romansh Yadav (Aptiva Corp) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 on attacking Android apps with apktool, dex2jar, JD-GUI, Frida and Burp Suite
Body:
The fastest way to find a mobile app's secrets is often to decompile it and search for the word password. Romansh Yadav, Senior Security Consultant at Aptiva Corp, spent his [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 session](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Romansh_Yadav_mobile_apps_attack_defend) building an Android penetration testing lab live and walking a deliberately vulnerable app from APK to credentials.

Honest scope: the title promises Android and iOS, but the session covers Android only, and the defensive tooling on the agenda gets little time. What you get is a hands-on beginner's tour of the attacker's side.

## What do you need to know about Android first?

Yadav starts with the stack: the Linux kernel (process and memory management, the permission model, process isolation), native libraries such as WebKit and SQLite, the Android runtime, the application framework and the apps on top. ART replaced Dalvik with ahead-of-time compilation, so bytecode is compiled when the app is installed rather than when it runs.

The security model rests on the kernel: every app gets its own Linux user ID, and that UID is the sandbox that keeps app one out of app two's data. The components you will be poking at are activities (screens), services (background work), broadcast receivers, content providers (sharing data between apps) and intents, which wire them together at runtime.

## How do you set up the lab?

Two routes. Download a ready-made mobile pentesting VM with the tools preinstalled, or assemble your own: Genymotion (it needs VirtualBox, and the ARM translation package if an app won't install), a custom Android image, and ADB for push, pull and a root shell on the emulator.

He splits the work into static testing, on an APK at rest, and dynamic testing, with the app running and its traffic going through Burp Suite.

## What does static analysis find?

The target is PIVAA, a purposefully insecure Android app that makes a good training ground. apktool decompiles it into smali and resources, and the first stop is the manifest.

"Our first job should be like understanding the Android manifest file," Yadav said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021. The manifest lists every activity, service, receiver and provider, which ones are exported, and the permissions the app asks for. In PIVAA it also shows backups allowed, so anyone can pull the app's data.

dex2jar turns the DEX into a JAR that JD-GUI can read, and a string search for username, password, API key or token turns up hard-coded test credentials in the authentication class. He then flips a flag in the manifest, rebuilds with apktool, re-signs with jarsigner and reinstalls: the whole tampering loop.

## And at runtime?

Frida handles runtime manipulation: hooking the app by package name with a script, for example to bypass SSL pinning or root detection. Two practical notes from the demo: the Frida server on the device and the client on your machine must be the same version, and Frida Gadget lets you work on a device that isn't rooted. His emulator hook crashed the app on camera, which he notes tends not to happen on a real device.

Back in an ADB shell, the app's shared preferences hold the same test credentials in plain text on the device. With Burp's CA certificate pushed to the emulator he intercepts traffic, points at IDOR, access control and JWT issues, and shows why a WebView with JavaScript enabled that loads remote URLs without validation is an open door to cross-site scripting. PIVAA's own list goes further: weak hashing such as MD5 and SHA-1, predictable random numbers, world-readable files, path traversal and accepted untrusted CAs.

## Who should watch

Developers and testers new to mobile security who want to see the toolchain in action. If you already live in Frida, you can skip it.
