Title: Attackers see one target where your tools see four layers
Description: Kennedy Torkura (Mattermost) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 on risk-driven fault injection, a feedback loop for security chaos experiments in the cloud
Body:
Cloud-native security tools split the world into code, container, cluster and cloud, and each layer gets its own product. Kennedy Torkura, cloud security engineer at Mattermost, argued at [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Kennedy_Torkura_fault_injection) that security chaos engineering is the layer that stitches them together, and that framing experiments in terms of risk is how you get security teams and management to say yes.

The talk draws on his PhD research at the Hasso Plattner Institute, so expect a framework and a research tool, CloudStrike, rather than a vendor pitch.

## How is security chaos engineering different?

Torkura starts from Aaron Rinehart's definition: identifying security control failures through proactive experimentation, to build confidence that the system can defend against malicious conditions in production. Classic chaos engineering targets availability with resiliency patterns such as timeouts, bulkheads and circuit breakers. The security version covers the whole CIA triad (confidentiality, integrity, availability) and tests the controls security already owns: preventive ones like firewalls, detective ones like intrusion detection, corrective ones like incident response. The goal is to find the blind spots those controls can't see.

He leans on Bruce Schneier's essay *A Plea for Simplicity* (complexity is the worst enemy of security) and on Gartner for the claim that 99% of attacks against cloud infrastructure will come down to user faults, mostly misconfiguration. His diagnosis is a knowledge gap plus thin tooling: people still hand-edit huge AWS IAM policies.

## Why do layered tools miss layered attacks?

Defence in depth for cloud native means security at the code, container, cluster and cloud layers. The tools follow that split (CSPM for the control plane, workload protection for containers, CASBs for on-premises-to-cloud traffic) and mostly don't talk to each other, so a human ends up correlating the outputs.

"Unfortunately, attackers still look at this as one single target," Torkura said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021. An attacker can enter at any layer and move across the rest.

## What does the feedback loop look like?

His security chaos engineering feedback loop adapts the MAPE-K loop from autonomic computing:

- **Execute.** Define the aim and a hypothesis, set scope and intensity, coordinate with the responsible teams, and make sure you can roll back, for example from infrastructure as code in Git.
- **Monitor.** Watch logs, observability or traces in real time so you can stop an experiment that goes too far.
- **Analyse.** Rate the findings with the OWASP risk rating methodology: threat agents, attack vectors, the vulnerability, the failed control, technical and business impact.
- **Plan.** Feed vulnerability backlogs, threat modelling and awareness training, and write the hypothesis for the next round.
- **Knowledge.** Store every experiment report so it can drive CloudWatch alarms, CSPM rules or IAM Access Analyzer checks, ideally in a security data lake next to threat intelligence feeds.

## What does an experiment look like?

CloudStrike, the tool his team built, runs at chosen intensities such as 30%, 60% or 90%, and chains single actions into attack scenarios, because real attackers string steps together. One example: create a user called bob, list the buckets, pick a random one, create a malicious policy and attach it so bob gets access. Then ask the questions that matter: did your CSPM, or even plain CloudTrail, flag the new user? The malicious policy? How long did the notification take to reach a human?

The abstract adds that CloudStrike was evaluated against AWS and Google Cloud infrastructure; the talk itself stays on the method and the AWS example, and points to the team's papers for results.

## Who should watch

Cloud security engineers who own a CSPM and want to know whether it works, and chaos practitioners curious about the security side. It's a research talk: diagrams and a loop, no live demo.

Title: The firewall caught the bad port only 60% of the time
Description: Aaron Rinehart (Verica) and David Lavezzo (Capital One) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 on testing that security controls work before an attacker does
Body:
Security teams find out a control has failed when the incident is already running. Aaron Rinehart, CTO and co-founder of Verica, and David Lavezzo, Director of Cyber Chaos Engineering at Capital One, used their [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Aaron_Rinehart_David_Lavezzo_cyber_chaos_engineering) to argue for the opposite order: inject the misconfiguration yourself, on a quiet afternoon, and watch what your firewalls, logs, alerts and SOC actually do with it.

## Why do security controls fail quietly?

Rinehart's starting point is that systems have outgrown our ability to model them in our heads. Continuous delivery, cloud, service meshes and immutable infrastructure let teams ship faster, and every layer adds complexity. Over weeks and months a system drifts away from the clean diagram it started as, and we learn how it really works through surprises: an outage on the payments API, a hard-coded token, a DNS error fixed in a war room.

Security tooling, he says, is still mostly monolithic, expert-driven and tied to commercial products, so it struggles to keep up. Incidents are also a bad place to learn. Within 15 minutes an executive is on the call asking for the thing to be back up, and nobody is asking why it broke.

"I've never seen a chaos engineering experiment succeed the first time we run it," Rinehart said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021. His reading: our model of the system is almost always wrong.

## What did ChaoSlingr find at UnitedHealth Group?

As chief security architect at UnitedHealth Group, Rinehart wrote ChaoSlingr, the first open-source tool to apply Netflix-style chaos engineering to security. It has three parts: a generator that picks a target, a slinger that makes the change and a tracker that reports it to Slack. The published example, PortSlinger, opens an unauthorised port on an AWS EC2 security group.

The team expected the firewall to block it every time, since misconfigured ports are a 30-year-old problem. It did so about 60% of the time, because the commercial and non-commercial environments had drifted apart. The cloud-native configuration management tool, which they were barely paying for, caught it almost every time. Both tools sent good logs and an alert fired. Then the SOC got the alert and couldn't tell which account or instance it came from. Mapping the IP back by hand could take anywhere up to 30 minutes, or two hours with SNAT in play. They added metadata to the alert and fixed it, with no incident and no customer pain.

## How do you start without making enemies?

Lavezzo's half is the practical one. Start with something you can test yourself, without borrowing other teams' time: he took critical endpoint alerts that hadn't fired in a while, wrote down the attack path he expected, the defences and the alerts, and had his first results in about 15 minutes. He used non-destructive techniques such as living-off-the-land binaries and PowerShell, because leaving a machine worse than you found it is a very bad day. Then he automated it and ran it daily.

"Always be running the attacks," Lavezzo said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021. Run them at a consistent time, say 08:00 every day, and an alert that shows up at 08:15 tells you something changed in your logging pipeline. Over time you get a history of alert uptime, find rules tuned so tightly that a small variation slips past, measure time-to-alert, and train new analysts on real signals instead of slide decks.

He also covers gap hunting (does switching from PowerShell to Python produce a false negative?), counting how many layers of defence can fail before you're in trouble, and turning a one-off audit snapshot into continuous evidence. And bring the data to teams as a question, not an accusation: here's what I see, here's what I think it means, what am I missing?

## Who should watch

Security engineers and SOC leads who suspect some of their alerts are decorative, and SREs who want to bring chaos experiments into the security team. Expect war stories and a method rather than tool demos, plus jokes about metal albums and Kevin Bacon.

Title: Chaos engineering wins the day it gets boring
Description: Mikolaj Pawlikowski (Bloomberg) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021 on why chaos engineering should become boring, and the myths still blocking buy-in
Body:
The best thing that could happen to chaos engineering is that nobody finds it exciting any more. That is the argument Mikolaj Pawlikowski, Engineering Lead at Bloomberg and author of Manning's *Chaos Engineering: Site reliability through controlled disruption*, made in the opening keynote of [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Mikolaj_Pawlikowski_chaos_engineering_2021). His takeaway: the tools are there, and what still holds teams back is buy-in, which you win by debunking a handful of myths and putting numbers on the risk.

"I'm going to argue that it should be boring and that boring is a good thing," Pawlikowski said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021.

## Why does chaos engineering matter more now?

He names three trends that make the practice necessary: scale, the cloud and the cloud-native stack. Each adds a layer you have to understand when things break. Kubernetes gives you scheduling and self-healing for free, until a misconfiguration quietly turns the self-healing off. Even if every brick is coded correctly, you can still break the system with a wrong dependency version, an expired certificate, timeouts that don't line up between components, retries that turn into a thundering herd, or CPU limits nobody quite understands.

His definition, borrowed from principlesofchaos.org, comes with the fluff removed: experimenting to build confidence that the system withstands turbulent conditions. It sits on top of unit, integration and end-to-end tests rather than replacing them, and it is a game of "what if": what if latency rises, traffic spikes, the database slows down. The recipe is four steps: ensure observability, define the steady state, form a hypothesis, run the experiment. Either outcome is a win, because a break is a bug you found before a client did.

## What is actually blocking adoption?

He ran a LinkedIn poll near the end of 2020 asking what stops people doing chaos engineering. Difficulty generating buy-in took 50% of the votes and inadequate training 27%. Missing or hard-to-use tools got only 11%. In 2015 your choice was Chaos Monkey or write your own; by 2021 there were dozens of open-source and commercial tools. The bottleneck had moved from software to persuasion.

## Which myths need debunking?

Pawlikowski lists the ones he keeps hearing, so you can answer them before they come up in the meeting:

- **It's Chaos Monkey.** Random breakage is one end of a spectrum; the other is experiments designed from an analysis of your system's weak points.
- **It's testing in production.** Production is the holy grail, not the entry requirement. Some systems should never go there, and that's fine.
- **It's only for Kubernetes, microservices or giant distributed systems.** His book opens with a single legacy process on a single machine, verifying its retry logic by manipulating system calls.
- **We're not mature enough.** Start with a small part of the system.
- **We already have chaos.** The point is to reduce chaos by injecting failure you understand and control.

## How do you sell it to the people who sign off?

Two conversations, he says. For whoever carries the pager the pitch is simple: experiments run during working hours, so you get called less at night. For the manager it is risk versus reward, and that's where the sharks come in. By his count the US saw three fatal shark attacks in 2020, while heart disease kills about 650,000 Americans every year. People fear the shark and order the hamburger. A carefully scoped experiment with a small blast radius is the shark; the outage you never rehearsed is the hamburger.

## Who should watch

Anyone who has to make the case for chaos engineering to a sceptical manager, and newcomers who want a clear map of the field in 2021. Practitioners will know the definitions, but the myth list and the shark-versus-hamburger argument are worth stealing for your next planning meeting.

Title: A useful map is a static site with good tiles, and Leaflet does the rest
Description: Colby Fayock (Element 84) at Conf42 JavaScript 2020 on building impactful maps with Leaflet, React and the JAMstack, from road trips to wildfire response
Body:
A mapping app is a JAMstack app that happens to have a very large background image. That's the core of Colby Fayock's talk at Conf42 JavaScript 2020: the Front End Developer at Element 84 shows that the same few lines of Leaflet behind a summer road trip demo also power a disaster-response tool for wildfire crews, and that none of it is as scary as GIS jargon makes it sound.

## Why should a front-end developer care about maps?

Fayock opens with everyday Google Maps (coffee, transit, a four-hour drive that never takes four hours), then asks where the data comes from. Scientists and analysts, Street View cars, and satellites: ESA's CryoSat measuring ice thickness, NASA's MODIS Terra covering every point on Earth every one to two days. Then OpenStreetMap, where millions of volunteers map features, Apple fills gaps where commercial data isn't available, Lyft contributes back, and humanitarian mappers mark refugee camps on the border of South Sudan and Ethiopia.

The examples that follow are the ones that justify the talk title: NASA Worldview tracking Cyclone Idai, which affected close to 2.2 million people in eastern Africa, NASA FIRMS showing active fires in California, and the Johns Hopkins COVID-19 case map. "Maps are literally giving people tools to save the world," Colby Fayock said at Conf42 JavaScript 2020.

## How does a web map actually work?

His framing: JavaScript is the mapping library, the APIs are the imagery and data you layer on, and the markup is the static HTML you compile down to. Leaflet is the library of choice. A map instance mounts on a div by id, you set a view with latitude, longitude and a zoom level, add a tile layer from an endpoint URL with an attribution, and drop a marker with a bound popup. React Leaflet wraps the same pieces as components (map, tile layer, marker, popup), and Angular and Vue have their own flavours.

For the data, he has a memorable model. "When dealing with maps, I like to think of a poorly drawn cake," he said at Conf42 JavaScript 2020. The base map is the cake, overlays such as high-resolution patches or a population heat map are the icing, and your data is the sprinkles: points for active fires, polygons for fire boundaries or evacuation zones.

The base map is cut into tiles because the whole globe could run past a gigabyte, and a user only ever looks at a fraction of it. The endpoint scheme of zoom, x and y is common enough that you can swap NASA imagery for OpenStreetMap by changing a URL. Some data is free (NASA publishes plenty of tile endpoints), some isn't: DigitalGlobe's open data program covers disaster areas, the rest is a paid product.

Compiling is the short part. Create React App or Gatsby outputs HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and from there it's object storage: an S3 bucket or Azure's equivalent.

## What does this look like when lives are on the line?

The serious demo is FilmDrop, Element 84's interface for first responders, shown on the Australian bushfires and California's 2018 Camp Fire. After talking to people in the field, the team set a usability target with no wiggle room. "We determined that we need to get this thing to a point where an operator can understand it in less than 15 minutes," Fayock said at Conf42 JavaScript 2020. Granular controls lose to a single toggle between active fire points and burn boundaries over satellite or street imagery.

Two details stand out for anyone who builds web apps. Reports, such as a missing person, are stored locally in the browser and synced to the cloud once connectivity returns. And drone imagery captured on site can be uploaded to an AWS Snowball Edge, which he calls a cloud in a box, processed in the field and shown as a fresh layer. No cell service, a drone and a grey box, and the crew can see which areas are no longer safe.

## And the fun version?

The lighter demo maps a 2015 road trip along the US east coast (ignore the stray lines to Las Vegas; they flew that part). Locations go into structured data, get mapped into GeoJSON twice (once as points, once as two-point lines), and are added to the map with a Leaflet GeoJSON layer. The map fits itself to the data's bounds, and a point-to-layer function turns each point into a marker with a custom HTML popup and a photo.

Both the road trip app and a plain Leaflet setup ship as Gatsby starters, spun up with the Gatsby CLI and deployable straight to Netlify, plus tutorials for a travel bucket list and a COVID-19 stats dashboard.

## Who should watch

React and JavaScript developers who have never touched a map and assume they need a GIS degree to start. It's an introduction, code-light and example-heavy, and the FilmDrop section is a good case study in designing for users with no time to learn your UI. Leaflet veterans can skip to FilmDrop.

Title: A smart litter box is a lesson in event-driven JavaScript
Description: Joe Karlsson (MongoDB) at Conf42 JavaScript 2020 on building an IoT kitty litter box with Node.js, Johnny-Five, a Raspberry Pi and load cells
Body:
Hardware is just callbacks with a soldering iron. At Conf42 JavaScript 2020, [Joe Karlsson](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2020_Joe_Karlsson_internet_of_toilets_iot_kitty_litter_box), Developer Advocate at MongoDB, introduced the Internet of Things to JavaScript developers by way of the Internet of Toilets: a Raspberry Pi-powered litter box that weighs his cat on every visit and logs the time, built with Node.js and Johnny-Five. The argument underneath the jokes: IoT is event-driven, and so is Node.

## Why JavaScript for hardware?

His case has four parts. Plenty of people already do it: he cites a figure that 58% of IoT developers self-identify as Node.js developers. It's beginner-friendly: embedded work traditionally means C, C++ or now Rust and manual memory management, while JavaScript has a garbage collector. Updates are easy: instead of physically reflashing a device, a connected Raspberry Pi can `git pull` and `npm install`. And the model matches: a sensor detects an event and something happens, which is exactly how Node handles callbacks, promises and async/await.

"JavaScript and Nodejs core structure directly translates how we develop applications with hardware and sensors," Joe Karlsson said at Conf42 JavaScript 2020. He's upfront that memory management and other concerns may push some projects to other languages, but for a first project, use what you know. The two big libraries he names are Cylon.js and Johnny-Five; he uses Johnny-Five.

He also likes IoT for its silliest projects, the line between ridiculous and smart, and thinks developers are well placed to explore it as a kind of art. Then he checked the market and found well-reviewed smart litter boxes selling for up to $500, so maybe not so silly.

## How does the box work?

A mid-century-style cabinet hides a Raspberry Pi, a magnetic switch on the lid and load cells under a plywood pad, essentially an internet-connected bathroom scale.

- Lift the lid and the box enters maintenance mode, since cleaning or adding litter changes the weight.
- Close it and the box records a new base weight.
- When a cat-sized object (he can't rule out a raccoon) adds weight, it logs the cat's weight and a timestamp.
- When the cat leaves, the base weight resets and it waits for the next event.

The point is passive health tracking: weight over time and how often he goes, to spot drastic changes.

## What does the code look like?

The IoT hello world is blinking an LED. In Johnny-Five you create a board with the Raspberry Pi IO plugin, wait for its ready event, create an LED on a GPIO pin and call `blink`. The lid switch works the same way: open and close events flip the app's maintenance state.

The load cells were the hard part. He couldn't find a Node package for the ones he bought, but found a Python one. So Node's `child_process.spawn` runs a Python script that reads the weight every tenth of a second and prints it; Node receives each reading as data, parses the float and updates the current weight. He calls it a bit of a hack, and his favourite thing he learned on the project.

Data goes to MongoDB, which, he notes, is his employer, as time series: one document per day with an array of events (timestamp, weight, type: maintenance or bathroom), designed around how the dashboard reads it. When he added the door sensor later, he changed the schema going forward and ignored the old data, which took seconds.

## Where does he think IoT is heading?

Four predictions, offered so you can replay them in five years and laugh: more processing at the edge as devices get more powerful (his box already does some), JavaScript runtimes optimised for small hardware, more hardware support in the Node ecosystem (he hit that gap with the load cells), and power as the hard limit. "The batteries are and will continue to be the bottleneck," he said.

His advice for getting started: buy a Raspberry Pi for about $35, pick a dumb project, make an LED blink or build a plant moisture sensor, and search your way out of every wall you hit.

## Who should watch

JavaScript developers who have never touched hardware and want a friendly first look at Johnny-Five and a Raspberry Pi. It's light on depth and heavy on fun; if you already build with GPIO, the child-process trick for unsupported sensors is the bit to take away.

Title: Move work off the main thread for reliability, not speed
Description: Majid Hajian at Conf42 JavaScript 2020 on freeing the main thread with web workers and Comlink, AssemblyScript and CSS Paint worklets
Body:
At 60 frames per second the browser gives you about 16.6 milliseconds per frame, at 90 about 11, at 120 about 8, and that budget is the same on an iPhone and a Nokia 2.1. At Conf42 JavaScript 2020, [Majid Hajian](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2020_Majid_Hajian_main_thread), a software engineer based in Oslo, PWA book author and conference organiser, walked through three ways to keep heavy work off the main thread: web workers made pleasant with Comlink, WebAssembly written in AssemblyScript, and worklets. His central point is that moving work to another thread may not make it faster. It makes the app predictable.

## Why the main thread is out of breath

He starts with who's on the web: by his numbers, connected users went from around 50% of the world's population in 2018-19 to around 60% in 2020, many of them on phones that look smart but have weak hardware. Meanwhile the main thread handles events, JavaScript execution, style, layout, paint and compositing, and we keep adding APIs and work to it while expecting smooth scrolling and no janky frames. The same task can fit the frame budget on one phone and blow through it on another. That unpredictability is the enemy.

## Web workers, without the postMessage pain

Workers have been stable across browsers since around 2012. Each is like a headless tab: its own event loop, isolated memory, no DOM, and on a multi-core device they can genuinely run in parallel. What stops people using them is `postMessage`. Comlink, from Google's developer team, wraps the worker in a proxy so you call exposed worker functions from the main thread and `await` the result like any promise. His React example moves a slow synchronous sort into a worker and sets state when it returns (and terminates the worker when done).

How do you decide what moves? Ask whether the task needs the UI. If not, treat the main thread as the UI thread and run business logic elsewhere. His bigger example: keep the view and action dispatch in the main thread and move the Redux store and reducers into a worker, since reducers are synchronous and can block.

Then the honest bit about speed. Spinning up a worker and passing data has overhead, so a single task may not be faster. "The question is that how more reliable is your application?" Majid Hajian said at Conf42 JavaScript 2020. Parallelism across cores can make it faster, but that is hard to measure and outside a web developer's control. His demo makes the case visually: sorting on the main thread freezes an animation; the same sort in a worker leaves it smooth.

## WebAssembly, if you'd rather not write C++ or Rust

AssemblyScript compiles a strict subset of TypeScript to Wasm. You install it from npm, scaffold a project, and write ordinary TypeScript using WebAssembly's numeric types. The AssemblyScript loader's `instantiateStreaming` takes care of the usually fiddly part of loading the module and getting at its exports. His larger example encodes camera video to MP4 entirely in the browser without blocking the UI.

He warns against assuming Wasm is simply fast: measure. Its real advantage is that it starts on a predictable performance path and stays there, while JavaScript may start slow and speed up only as the engine optimises it.

## Worklets: off-thread access to rendering

Worklets give low-level access to the rendering pipeline from a separate thread, in paint, animation, layout and audio flavours. Most are still new and patchily supported, so he focuses on the CSS Paint API from Houdini, which had the widest support. You register a paint class in a JavaScript module, feature-detect support (important for progressive web apps), add the module to `CSS.paintWorklet`, and use `paint()` in CSS. His demos draw a checkerboard background and generate barcodes on the fly while an animation keeps running.

## Who should watch

Front-end developers whose apps stutter on mid-range Android phones, and React developers wondering whether workers are worth the hassle. The talk is a broad tour with short demos rather than a benchmark study, and his own conclusion is that each tool needs measuring in your app.

Title: MongoDB schema design is one question, embed or reference
Description: Joe Karlsson (MongoDB) at Conf42 JavaScript 2020 on designing MongoDB schemas around queries, from one-to-one up to one-to-squillions
Body:
The most common reason a MongoDB database is slow, according to the person people email when theirs is slow: it was designed like a SQL database. At Conf42 JavaScript 2020, [Joe Karlsson](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2020_Joe_Karlsson_mongodb_schema_design), Developer Advocate at MongoDB, gave an introductory talk on schema design that boils the whole discipline down to one decision made again and again, embed the data or reference it, plus a handful of personal rules for making it.

It's the follow-up to his SQL-to-NoSQL introduction at the same event, and like that one it's an intro from a MongoDB advocate, with his own opinions flagged as his.

## How is this different from relational design?

In a relational database you design the schema independently of the queries. The question is what data you have, and the answer is a prescribed process: normalise, usually to third normal form, split into tables, link with foreign keys.

MongoDB has no equivalent. "There's no process and there's no pre prescribed algorithm for how to split up that data," Joe Karlsson said at Conf42 JavaScript 2020. The question becomes how the application will use the data. You design for query performance, for how the data is stored, and for not burning money on hardware.

## Embedding versus referencing

**Embedding** puts related data inside the document: arrays, nested objects, whatever shape fits. One query gets everything, no joins (which he describes as expensive, blocking, in-memory work), and updates to a single document are atomic. The costs: big documents mean shipping data you may not need over the wire every time, and a hard limit of 16 MB per document. If you're getting close to that, he calls it a code smell.

**Referencing** stores an object ID pointing to another document, like a foreign key, and joins at query time with lookups. Documents stay small and you avoid duplication, and you don't fetch rarely used data on every read. The cost is the lookups themselves.

He adds a note for SQL veterans: duplicated data is not an anti-pattern in either world. Relational teams denormalise for speed all the time.

## Five relationship shapes

- **One-to-one**: key-value pairs in the document.
- **One-to-few**: an embedded array, such as a user's handful of addresses. Nobody has 16 MB of addresses.
- **One-to-many**: a product with thousands of parts (a bicycle, a car, a tractor, an Xbox). The product holds an array of part IDs; the parts live in their own documents, since an e-commerce page reads the product far more often than its parts list.
- **One-to-squillions**: logs from a server farm. Even an array of IDs on the host would grow without limit, so flip it: each log document stores its host's ID. He admits squillions is a made-up word.
- **Many-to-many**: a kanban-style to-do app where users have many tasks and tasks have many owners. Each side keeps an array of references to the other.

## His rules of thumb

He's just said there are no rules, and he acknowledges the irony, but he has some:

1. Favour embedding unless you can articulate a reason not to.
2. Needing to access an object on its own is a compelling reason not to embed it.
3. Avoid joins and lookups where you can, but they're not an anti-pattern. If a reference gives a better schema, use it.
4. Arrays must not grow without bound. "Note your array should not grow without bound," he said in the recap, calling unbounded arrays a huge code smell.
5. Above all, the model depends on your application's needs. What works for someone else's project may not work for yours.

## Who should watch

Developers moving from relational databases to MongoDB, and anyone who has inherited a MongoDB schema with a normalised table hiding inside it. It covers the basics clearly; for depth he points to MongoDB University's M320 data modelling course. Expect a pitch for MongoDB along the way, since that's who he works for.

- Joe Karlsson on [an IoT kitty litter box](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2020_Joe_Karlsson_internet_of_toilets_iot_kitty_litter_box), which stores its time-series data as one document per day.

Title: Write form validation like unit tests, and keep it out of your components
Description: Alush Evyatar (Facebook) at Conf42 JavaScript 2020 on Vest, which borrows Mocha and Jest syntax to keep form validation in its own testable suite
Body:
Form validation usually starts as three `if` statements in a change handler and ends as the part of the feature nobody dares refactor. At Conf42 JavaScript 2020, [Alush Evyatar](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2020_Alush_Evyatar_form_validations_vest), Front End Developer at Facebook in Tel Aviv, presented Vest, his open-source library that writes validation the way you write unit tests: a suite of `test` calls with `enforce` assertions, living in its own file, with a narrow point of contact with your UI code.

First, the disclaimer he leads with: "Vest is not a Facebook project and it is not affiliate with Facebook," Alush Evyatar said at Conf42 JavaScript 2020.

## Why another validation library?

He asks the question himself, and answers it with the usual failure mode. Validation code ends up inside change handlers, components and feature logic, so as the form grows it becomes part of the spaghetti. It's hard to read, hard to test, hard to maintain, and a refactor of the feature usually means scrapping the validation and starting over. Vest's pitch is structure: borrow the syntax of Mocha or Jest, describe each field's rules as tests, and keep them separate from the feature.

## What does a Vest suite look like?

The demo is a React sign-up form, though he stresses it could be Angular, Vue or no framework. A new `validate.js` file exports `vest.create('user_form', ...)`, a suite that receives the form data. Inside, each `test` takes the field name and the message to show on failure, and the body uses `enforce` (Vest's version of `expect`), for example enforcing that the username is not empty, or longer than or equal to three characters.

Wiring it up takes very little. The change handler calls the suite with the next state; the component reads `res.getErrors('username')` and passes the messages to the input. A `classNames` helper maps valid, invalid and warning states to CSS classes, so fields go green or red without extra logic. From there he adds rules for password length, a password confirmation that has to match (and only runs once there is a password), and a terms-of-service checkbox enforced as truthy.

## The features that make it pleasant

- **Validate only what the user touched.** Without it, typing a username lights up every field in red. `vest.only(currentField)` runs just the tests for the field being edited.
- **Warnings that don't fail the form.** A test marked with `vest.warn()` lands in a separate basket: his example nudges users to add a number to a weak password, shown in orange, without blocking submission.
- **Async tests.** A test can return a promise; a rejection fails it. His mock server call rejects if the username is taken. The result's `done` callback fires once all async tests finish, which he uses to hide a loading spinner.
- **Skip the server when you already know.** `vest.draft()` exposes the intermediate result, so the async check runs only when the username has no other errors yet.
- **Memoise.** `test.memo` with a dependency array (the username) reuses an earlier result, so retyping a name you already checked doesn't hit the server again.

## How much code did it take?

"It took us about, I think, five lines of logic to add vest to our features," he said, plus a few lines to display the results. The rest is the suite itself, which you could change, test or move without touching the UI. That separation is the point: change the feature, or even the UI framework, and the validation code stays where it is.

He says he has used Vest in multiple production apps and was looking for contributors and feature ideas from the community.

## Who should watch

Front-end developers with a form that has outgrown inline validation, and anyone who likes the idea of validation rules readable as a spec. It's a live-coding talk, so it shows exactly how much glue the library needs. If your forms are a login box and nothing else, a few `if` statements are still fine.

Title: The candidate who skipped React got the job
Description: Colby Fayock (Element 84) at Conf42 JavaScript 2020 on why HTML and CSS fundamentals beat framework-first habits for SEO, accessibility and simplicity
Body:
Two junior developers get the same 45-minute coding challenge: turn a mockup into a web page. One reaches for React and spends the interview fighting script tags, Babel and `createElement`. The other writes semantic HTML, adds Flexbox, and spends the last 15 minutes explaining his choices. At Conf42 JavaScript 2020, [Colby Fayock](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2020_Colby_Fayock_building_fundamentals), Front End Developer at Element 84, uses that story to argue that understanding HTML and CSS properly is what levels you up, and that it pays off three ways: SEO, accessibility and simpler code.

"Everyone stop what you're doing and put down the Javascript," Colby Fayock said at Conf42 JavaScript 2020, opening the talk. He isn't anti-framework. He is against reaching for one before you understand what it compiles to.

## Is the interview story real?

Only slightly exaggerated, he says. He has sat through interviews watching candidates struggle with exactly this, and it isn't unique to React; any framework does it when the candidate wants to impress with the newest tools under time pressure. A more experienced React developer might not have hit the same walls, but the person who knew the platform got further with less.

## Your framework is still writing HTML and CSS

JSX compiles down to HTML, and CSS-in-JS or Sass compile down to CSS. The only difference is how it's served. That makes the platform's quirks your problem too. Two he shows: the browser silently fixes invalid HTML, so a `div` inside a `p` gets pulled out and the paragraph's styles stop cascading to it; and vertical padding in CSS is relative to the element's width, which gives you the old height-zero, padding-percentage trick for background images that keep their aspect ratio.

## SEO is mostly tags you already have

His own site gets most of its traffic from organic search, and his advice is the low-effort kind: a logical heading outline from h1 to h6 instead of h1 everywhere, `alt` text on images, descriptive link text instead of a dozen read-more links, and a `title` tag that changes per page, since that's what shows in Google results.

## Accessibility uses the same habits

The same semantic HTML helps screen readers jump through a page by its headings and describe images through their `alt` text. He cites the World Health Organization's estimate that 15% of the world's population has some form of disability. Applied to the 2,400 visitors his own site had that year, that would be over 360 people.

"Each of us as developers, are responsible for how our creations are being used," he said. The practical list: use real list elements for navigation (set `list-style` to none and you're back where the div was), and use real buttons. A `button` gives you a pointer cursor, keyboard focus and Enter for free, and inside a form it submits the form without a custom handler. A `div` gives you none of that.

## Can CSS replace that JavaScript?

Often. His examples:

- `datalist` for a basic autocomplete on an input.
- A loading shimmer from a CSS gradient and animation, as a reusable class.
- The `:checked` state of an input for UI that only needs state to change styling.
- Responsive headings with a font size of 10vw, plus media queries if it gets too small.

He isn't against complex tools for learning; rebuilding your blog with a pile of them is a fine low-risk way to learn them (he lost count of his own rebuilds). For client or company work, ask what the extra JavaScript costs the browser and how much time it really saves.

The fun part is pure-CSS CodePen work: a pen that turns any uploaded image into a cake you can cut, a CSS-only collector's cabinet, a coronavirus-clicking game with no JavaScript, and his own six-year-old recreation of the Alien title sequence, which he built instead of watching the film. He still hasn't seen it. He also points at CSS Houdini as the next step.

## Who should watch

Juniors and bootcamp graduates heading into front-end interviews, and framework-first developers who have never had to think about what the browser does with their markup. Senior front-end folks will know most of it, but the interview story is worth passing along to your next hire.

Title: From SQL to MongoDB, 73 lines of code become 30
Description: Joe Karlsson (MongoDB) at Conf42 JavaScript 2020 on mapping SQL concepts to MongoDB documents and four reasons to pick a document database
Body:
You can't make light go faster, but you can make your database stop doing joins. At Conf42 JavaScript 2020, [Joe Karlsson](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2020_Joe_Karlsson_sql_nosql), Developer Advocate at MongoDB, gave a short, friendly introduction to document databases for developers who grew up on SQL: how the vocabulary maps, which myths to drop, and four reasons to consider MongoDB. The headline number: a fetch-and-update of a user profile took 30 lines of code with MongoDB and 73 with SQL.

It's a vendor talk and he says so, with the usual disclaimer that controversial opinions are his, not his employer's. It's also a genuine 101, pitched at new developers.

## Why care about the database at all?

His framing: the two main bottlenecks of a web app are network speed and database execution speed. The first is capped by the speed of light (you can only move servers closer). The second you can actually work on.

## What is a document, in SQL terms?

A MongoDB document is a JSON-like structure stored as BSON, the binary form. It looks like the object, dictionary or hash map you already use, and unlike JSON it keeps real types: strings, integers, arrays, nested objects, and GeoJSON for latitude and longitude.

He models the same user in a normalised SQL schema next to it: a users table, a professions table linked by a foreign key, a cars table with more columns. Then the translation table:

- A document maps to a row, or to several rows joined by foreign keys.
- A field maps to a column.
- A collection maps to a table.
- A database is a database.
- Embedding related data in a document is MongoDB's answer to a join.

And the obligatory joke: "a DBA walks into a NoSQL bar, but immediately leaves because he couldn't find a table," Joe Karlsson said at Conf42 JavaScript 2020.

## Three things people get wrong about MongoDB

It isn't schemaless. It has a flexible schema, and you can enforce schema validation at the database level as strictly or loosely as you want. It supports indexes, with the same B-tree structure relational databases use. And it supports multi-document ACID transactions: a chain of updates, deletes and queries can roll back together if one fails.

## The four reasons

**Program faster.** Documents map directly to objects in most languages. In SQL, results come back as rows and columns that have to be mapped into objects (the object-relational impedance mismatch), the professions need a second query, and updates have to be translated back into each table. His count for the same profile-page CRUD: 30 lines with MongoDB, 73 with SQL.

**Pivot easier.** Flexible schemas make change cheap. His example: he added a new sensor to a home IoT device and started writing its readings into his time-series data straight away, without migrating the old records, because his charts only showed a week of history anyway.

**Query faster.** Joins pull data from several tables into memory and query it there, which he calls blocking and slow at scale. If everything you need lives in one document, it's one read.

**Scale cheaper.** A SQL server that runs out of space usually means a bigger machine, a migration and possible downtime, with costs that climb steeply as hardware gets bigger. MongoDB scales horizontally by sharding: add a server and data starts flowing to it, with strategies such as placing data close to users by geography. His caveat for anyone shopping around: "A lot of document databases do not horizontally scale."

## Where to go next

He points at MongoDB University, its free courses (he recommends starting with the introductory one), and the MongoDB community forums, and tells people to swap the database in a side project and learn by breaking it. He'd hoped to cover the four biggest mistakes SQL developers make with NoSQL, but ran out of time.

## Who should watch

Developers with SQL experience evaluating MongoDB, and juniors who've only heard NoSQL as a buzzword. If you already run MongoDB in production, the companion talk on schema design is the one for you. Bear in mind the comparison is presented by a MongoDB advocate; the 30-versus-73 figure is his example, not a benchmark.

Title: Rolling your own canvas charts for sensor data, outliers included
Description: Renaldi Gondosubroto (Gres Studio) at Conf42 JavaScript 2020 on building a custom canvas graphics library that rescales itself for live sensor data
Body:
Your temperature chart is scaled for 20 to 30 degrees, and a sensor reports 100. Do you squash the real data into a flat line, or clip the spike? At Conf42 JavaScript 2020, [Renaldi Gondosubroto](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2020_Renaldi_Gondosubroto_custom_graphics_library), founder of Gres Studio, walked through the small canvas graphics library he wrote to plot his own sensor readings, and the answer he built in: an axis that widens for the outlier and quietly shrinks back once the spike scrolls off the chart.

It's a code walkthrough of one real project rather than a framework pitch, and a useful look at what a chart library actually has to do underneath Chart.js.

## Custom doesn't mean dependency-free

He opens with what to aim for: visuals people can read at a glance, and a reason to exist. If the standard canvas API or an existing library already does the job, why write a new one? Then a caveat that saves a lot of yak shaving. Building your own library does not mean refusing other libraries, because "reusability is a very important part of software development," Renaldi Gondosubroto said at Conf42 JavaScript 2020. He names Chart.js, CanvasJS and Two.js as fair game. His own project uses jQuery and the canvas API.

## A four-point checklist before writing code

His personal guideline has four parts:

- **Aim**: why the library exists and which problem it solves.
- **Information**: what you're plotting. Temperature, particulate matter and HTTP error counts all have different ranges, thresholds and units.
- **Resilience**: how the chart copes when the data stretches past the thresholds you planned for.
- **Structure**: bar, line or something else, chosen so people can interpret the data.

## How the library is put together

The use case: devices send readings to ThingSpeak, a cloud IoT platform, and his website pulls them back down to draw eight graphs, one per sensor field. The code follows four steps.

1. **Initialise variables**: a state flag for whether the charts have been drawn, step sizes, and per-graph y-min, y-max and y-step values (eight of each), plus the averaging period, the device's sending period, a time zone and the ThingSpeak channel URL.
2. **Web functions**: a classic XMLHttpRequest getter with an ActiveXObject fallback for older Internet Explorer, and functions that fetch the latest data or poll on a period.
3. **Core drawing functions**: canvas setup, background grid lines, axes and y-scale labels; a function that averages readings into time buckets and plots each average as a small red circle; time-axis labels every two hours, adjusted for the time zone.
4. **Execute**: an Ajax ready-state handler that stores the historical feed in localStorage on first load, then polls every 120,000 milliseconds (two minutes), appending only entries newer than the latest stored ID.

Averaging readings per period does double duty: it smooths noise and keeps a single wild sample from dominating the plot.

## Resilience is the interesting part

The y-axis labels are computed from the gap between the current maximum and minimum, not hard-coded. When a new value lands above y-max or below y-min, a loop widens the range a step at a time and the labels redraw. Because the chart is a window over a fixed period, data keeps moving left. The outlier stays visible for a while, and once it falls off the edge the range shrinks back to 20 to 30. Nothing gets dropped silently, which matters if that spike is the reading someone needs to analyse later.

There's also a table view of the same data, rebuilt from localStorage with one column per field, which uses the same min and max checks.

## What he wants you to take away

"It's not hard to make your own libraries," he said in his wrap-up, with the condition that you know what you're making and why. Use dependencies, experiment a lot, and if you plan to share the library in open source, write it so others can read it. He admits he is still working on making his own more efficient.

## Who should watch

Developers who have only ever used chart libraries and want to see the moving parts: axes, scaling, polling and time labels drawn by hand on a canvas. IoT hobbyists plotting their own sensors will get the most out of it. If you just need a line chart by Friday, use Chart.js; this talk explains what it's doing for you.

Title: Ship the small image, upscale it in the browser
Description: Kevin Scott (Upscaler.js) at Conf42 JavaScript 2020 on running ESRGAN super-resolution client-side with TensorFlow.js, warm-ups and padded patches
Body:
The CSI enhance button is real now, and it runs in a browser tab. At Conf42 JavaScript 2020, [Kevin Scott](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2020_Kevin_Scott_image_super_resolution), creator of Upscaler.js, showed how he took an ESRGAN super-resolution model, converted it for TensorFlow.js, and made it upscale images 2x, 3x or 4x on the user's machine. His strongest argument isn't image quality. It's bandwidth: at 4x, the image you send can be up to 16 times smaller.

## Why not just upscale on the server?

The talk starts from a problem he hit at work: an e-commerce-style site designed around beautiful photos, launched into a world of user-uploaded, pixelated ones. Asking users for better images works sometimes, but often the screenshot from a PDF is all they have.

Server-side super-resolution is the obvious route. Most implementations are Python, beefy hardware runs the most accurate models, and upload-once, display-often workloads can afford slow processing. He lists two drawbacks: the round trip delays feedback, and deployment is painful when research-fresh implementations come with unstable dependencies and GPUs that are expensive and hard to scale.

In the browser, those go away. There's nothing to provision, the result appears as soon as inference finishes, and the bandwidth saving is the clincher. He is fair about the trade-offs: a team with real ML expertise and desktop-heavy users may do better on the back end, and on-device performance depends heavily on hardware, so older devices can be awful.

"JavaScript is absolutely a first class citizen when it comes to applications of machine learning and neural networks," Kevin Scott said at Conf42 JavaScript 2020.

## How does a JavaScript developer find the right model?

Papers with Code, which organises research by topic with metrics and links to implementations. He spends a minute on why metrics like PSNR and SSIM mislead here: humans prefer a sharper but less saturated result that a pixel-difference metric scores worse, and models tuned for those metrics drift toward a blurry, washed-out look. For browser use he wanted good accuracy, speed and JavaScript compatibility, not the top of the leaderboard. That led him to an ESRGAN implementation.

## From Python notebook to a tensor in the page

The conversion happens in Google Colab. The key step is saving the full model, not just the weights, so the JavaScript side knows how to interpret it. He also had to hand-edit a bit of the JSON configuration before TensorFlow.js would load it, and says so plainly: he isn't sure whether that is a bug or his own mistake.

In CodeSandbox, the model loads from its JSON entry point (the sharded `.bin` weight files exist to help browser caching). The image becomes a tensor, goes through `model.predict`, and the output tensor is turned back into a base64 source for an `img` tag. It works on a baboon photo. The first run takes north of 900 milliseconds; later runs take around 100.

## The 900 ms problem, and the patch trick

That first-run penalty is the TensorFlow.js warm-up: the first invocation of a model is much slower than the next. The standard fix is to push dummy data through on page load, but it only helps for inputs of the same size, and real uploads aren't. Inference also blocks the UI. Web workers help somewhat, he says, but are not a silver bullet.

His solution: cut the image into patches and upscale them one at a time, releasing the UI thread between each. That introduces artifacts at the patch edges, a known habit of upscaling models that is invisible on a full image and glaring on a grid. Padding each patch fixes it. The neat side effect is that if the patch size is smaller than any image you expect, every call gets a consistently sized input, so you dodge the warm-up as well.

For production he points to quantising the model (smaller over the wire), pruning poorly performing weights (faster) and training on domain-specific data (more accurate). He closes by speculating on face- or illustration-specific models and on video, if 8x or 16x upscaling becomes practical in the browser.

## Who should watch

Front-end developers handling user-uploaded images, and anyone who assumed neural networks need a Python back end. It is also a good, honest example of the gap between a working demo and something you can put in a consumer app.

Title: Your Vue pages don't belong in components, and other UI habits
Description: Ahmed Bankole (Ambiantic AI) at Conf42 JavaScript 2020 on Vue UI libraries, a views and shared folder layout, and lazy loading routes and images
Body:
Every Vue codebase that has lived past its first birthday has a `components` folder holding a login page, a navbar and forty buttons in no particular order. At Conf42 JavaScript 2020, [Ahmed Bankole](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2020_Ahmed_Bankole_ui_applications_vue), Software Engineer at Ambiantic AI in Lagos, gave a beginner-friendly tour of building UIs with Vue.js: why he picks it, which UI libraries save you from writing CSS, how to lay out the folders so the app stays navigable, and how lazy loading keeps a good UI from being ruined by a slow one.

He says up front that it is a talk session, not a hands-on workshop, pitched at people new to Vue or still finding their way with it.

## Why Vue, according to Ahmed

He is careful not to turn it into a framework war. His case for Vue is practical: reactive data binding that moves data to the DOM without hand-written glue, composable components you reuse across the app, an API that's easy to learn, and a small footprint. He cites the standalone Vue file as under 16 KB, so you can drop it in from a CDN or a local file without hauling in megabytes of framework. The Vue CLI gives you a minimal project structure, and single-file `.vue` components let you write plain HTML plus a script block instead of JSX.

He also shows a runtime-speed chart with Vue ahead of Angular and React, and is honest about where it came from: his own observation and testing, not a published benchmark. Treat it as one engineer's experience rather than a number to quote in your next architecture review.

## Which UI libraries does he reach for?

A long list, all of which plug into a Vue project without changing its structure. Vuetify for Material-style components with layout and flex handled for you. Vuesax for components designed by UI specialists. Quasar, which is a component library and a whole framework built on Vue. Element UI, Vue Material, Buefy, iView, Mint UI, and BootstrapVue for people who want Bootstrap 3 or 4 without a CDN include. The point is that you rarely need to hand-roll buttons and grids.

## Where do pages go?

This is the most useful part of the talk. The Vue CLI scaffold gives you `components` and `assets`, and developers pile their pages into `components`.

"The mistake most people make is actually putting your pages into the components," Ahmed Bankole said at Conf42 JavaScript 2020. His fix: add a `views` folder for pages (home, contact, login) and keep `components` for pieces. Inside `components`, add a `shared` folder for everything used across the app: navbar, footer, sidebar, icons, captcha, common buttons. Dashboard-only or client-area-only components live elsewhere. Two or three years later, when you come back to the app, you know where to look instead of scrolling a flat list.

## Lazy loading is UX, not just performance

He frames lazy loading as part of UI work because nobody admires a design that hasn't loaded. He also admits the term scares people: "I found out that lazy loading is one of the things that caused imposter syndrome among frontend developers," he said.

Two techniques. First, native HTML lazy loading with `loading=lazy` on images and iframes: his example shows an eager page pulling down 3 MB up front against 0 MB for the lazy version until the content scrolls into view. Second, lazy-loaded routes in Vue Router: a small `lazyLoad(view)` helper that returns a dynamic `import()` of the page, so visiting the home route loads only the home component instead of bundling home, contact and everything else into one file. For apps heavy on images or views, that's the difference between loading bit by bit and loading everything at once.

## Who should watch

Developers starting with Vue who want sensible defaults for structure and a map of the UI library options. If you already split routes with dynamic imports and keep a `views` folder, you can skip it; if your `components` folder scrolls, watch the middle section.

Title: A VR game that moves the loot when you're losing, in plain JavaScript
Description: Milecia McGregor (Conducto) at Conf42 JavaScript 2020 on building a VR game with A-Frame and training a Brain.js network to keep players playing
Body:
Most VR tutorials stop at a spinning cube. At Conf42 JavaScript 2020, [Milecia McGregor](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2020_Milecia_McGregor_vr_brainjs), Senior Software Engineer at Conducto, builds a search-and-find VR world with A-Frame and then bolts on a Brain.js neural network that predicts whether a player will finish the game, and quietly moves the hidden objects closer if they won't. The takeaway: both halves of that sentence fit in an HTML file and a small Express server.

It is an intro talk with live-ish coding, aimed at JavaScript developers who have never touched VR or machine learning.

## How much code is a VR world in A-Frame?

Less than you'd think, and most of it is HTML. Every A-Frame app lives inside an `a-scene`. Assets (textures for wood, metal and brick, even a background music track via an audio tag) load first so they're ready when entities use them. Then come the primitives: an `a-box` with a height of three, a rotation of 60 degrees around y and 45 around z, a wooden texture and a position 37 meters along x. Every unit in A-Frame is meters, which saves you from wondering what a height of 3 means.

Behaviour is attributes all the way down. An animation attribute makes that box float between 1 and 2.2 meters over a two-second loop, forever. An `a-plane` holds the text listing what the player has to find. For anything custom there is the bare `a-entity`, with no presets and full control. She pulls a community environment package in so you're not standing in a white void, and adds a small black ring to the camera so players know where they're looking. Her advice on that background animation: only move things if it helps the user, not because it's cool.

Interaction is a custom attribute too. A found-item script registers event listeners; click an object and it flies back to home base.

## Why Brain.js and not TensorFlow.js?

She explains a neural network in two minutes: inputs (features), weights that decide how much each input sways the output, layers of nodes, a prediction. Then she picks Brain.js over TensorFlow.js on ergonomics. TensorFlow.js handles complex problems somewhat better, she grants, but makes you learn what a tensor is before you get anywhere.

"If you understand how to work with objects, arrays and arrays of objects, you're fine," Milecia McGregor said at Conf42 JavaScript 2020. She also notes she has zero affiliation with the library; she just likes it.

## What does the model actually predict?

Whether the player will finish the game. The training input is an array of objects: the player's x, y and z location, a discrete value for whether they've found an item, and a count of steps taken. The output is another array of objects with a single finish-or-not value. A `map` zips them into one training set, the network is one line (`new brain.NeuralNetwork` with three hidden layers), and training is one call to `train`, which reports iterations and error as it converges.

An Express endpoint takes the player's data from the front end and returns a new position for an item. When the favourite box gets triggered, a POST to that endpoint comes back with coordinates, and the object moves. Struggling players get objects pulled closer; players doing well get them pushed away. As she says, that's the simple version: the same pattern could drive bots or reshape the whole world.

The hardest part, she points out, is not the model. It's getting the data and getting it into that shape.

## The parts most tutorials skip

Before training anything, ask whether users will care. Her scenario is a fancy model shipped to production that nobody notices. Feature choice drives everything, so decide what you're predicting and where the data comes from first.

Ethics gets more than a slide. Location and how someone moves around a room is delicate data, and she asks developers to treat it that way. "Choosing the best algorithm doesn't exist," she said; pick what fits your data, your hardware (CPU-only machines limit you) and an acceptable error rate. For heavy work such as SLAM on autonomous cars or person detection from camera data, which she has done before, she would reach for Python.

She also mentions React 360 as an alternative to A-Frame for React developers.

## Who should watch

JavaScript developers curious about WebVR or browser-side ML who want a first project with a working end-to-end loop. If you already ship TensorFlow.js models, the ML half will be familiar; the A-Frame walkthrough is still a quick way to see how a scene is put together.

Title: Tinkerbell provisions bare metal with Docker containers and a YAML template
Description: Aman Parauliya (InfraCloud) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020 on how Tinkerbell turns bare metal provisioning into templated workflows
Body:
Provisioning a rack of servers can look a lot like running a CI pipeline: a template of steps, each step a Docker container. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020, [Aman Parauliya](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2020_Aman_Parauliya_tinkerbell_provisionning_engine), Senior Software Engineer at InfraCloud and a core contributor to Tinkerbell, the open-source bare metal provisioning engine started by the Packet team, explained how it works and ran a workflow live.

The first third is a primer on bare metal; the rest is Tinkerbell's architecture and a CLI demo, rough edges included.

## Why bare metal at all?

Parauliya's two pictures of bare metal are a data center rack and a Raspberry Pi, and Tinkerbell aims to cover both. A server needs network interfaces with IPMI support, storage (with RAID if you want to survive disk loss) and a boot environment that supports iPXE for network boot. Network booting means PXE or iPXE, DHCP for addresses, TFTP for the initial file system, and NFS when the hardware has no storage of its own, like a Pi whose microSD card just died.

The reasons to stay on metal: existing data centers companies want to use, data security for things like bank account balances, lower latency, and consistent, predictable performance, because on your own hardware you know exactly what adding RAM will do.

The price is complexity. "Increase of control comes with the increase of complexity," Aman Parauliya said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020. Hundreds of servers, Intel x86 and Arm64 CPUs, half the fleet on CentOS and half on Ubuntu.

## What are Tinkerbell's moving parts?

A provisioner machine runs the control plane, every service in Docker containers:

- **Tink**: the workflow engine, as tink-server, tink-cli for operators, and tink-worker on the machine being provisioned.
- **Boots**: DHCP and TFTP.
- **Hegel**: serves each machine's metadata.
- **OSIE**: not a service but the set of files for the network-booted install environment, a minimal Alpine.
- **PBnJ**: power and boot control, such as switching a machine to boot from iPXE.
- **Postgres** for hardware, template and workflow data and events, a **private Docker registry** holding the tink-worker image and every action image, and Nginx serving the boot files.

## How does a workflow come together?

Three objects. Hardware data is JSON per machine: a unique ID, at least one DHCP interface with a MAC address, hostname, architecture, the IP it should get, and netboot flags allowing PXE and workflows. UEFI was no longer required at the time of the talk.

A template is YAML with a version, a name, a global timeout, and tasks made of actions. Each action names an image from the private registry and can have its own timeout; a disk wipe that doesn't finish in 90 seconds fails the workflow. A typical OS install runs disk wipe, disk partition, install the root file system, then install GRUB, so the CentOS and Ubuntu templates differ only in the last image. Volumes and environment variables, like a mirror host, can be set per task or per action.

A workflow binds a template to a machine: `tink workflow create` takes the template ID and maps the template's device key to a MAC address. The worker only receives the workflow when a request arrives from that MAC.

## Does the demo work?

Eventually, which is the honest version of a live demo. The provisioner runs in a Vagrant VirtualBox VM. Parauliya pushes a third hardware record and shows that pushing the same ID again overwrites it. He creates a second template, a hello world action named server partitioning with a 600-second global timeout, and a workflow at 0% and pending.

The first worker boots over iPXE, gets an IP and the OSIE files, then errors because of the tink-worker image. He tags and pushes the latest tink-worker into the local registry, destroys the worker and boots it again. The workflow goes to 100%, state success, and the worker's log shows the action image pulled from the private registry rather than Docker Hub, each action in its own container, printing hello from Docker.

## Who should watch

Infrastructure engineers who own physical fleets or edge devices and want provisioning in version control. If you only know cloud VMs, the bare metal primer is a useful refresher on what PXE and TFTP do. Docs and setup guides are on tinkerbell.org and the GitHub organisation, plus community projects such as Alex Ellis's tinkerbot.

Title: Most of your app's resilience lives in code you don't own
Description: Uma Mukkara (Chaos Native) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020 on raising Kubernetes resilience with declarative chaos experiments run through GitOps
Body:
Your application's uptime depends mostly on things your team didn't write: nodes, kubelets, DNS, Prometheus, Envoy, databases. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020, [Uma Mukkara](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2020_Uma_Mukkara_kubernetes_resilience_sre), CEO of Chaos Native, argued that SREs on Kubernetes should check resilience continuously with chaos experiments, written as YAML and shipped through GitOps, and demoed it with LitmusChaos.

Mukkara is closely involved with Litmus, and the second half of the talk is a Litmus walkthrough. The first half stands on its own.

## Why does Kubernetes make resilience harder?

His definition: resilience is a system's ability to absorb a fault and recover automatically without hurting user-facing services. Pods get evicted, nodes go NotReady (more common on large cloud setups), containers leak memory. Faults will happen however careful you are.

Two things make it worse on Kubernetes. Everything changes faster: with microservices and strong CI/CD, a database that used to upgrade every six months or a year now upgrades every quarter. And your app sits on a stack of dependencies, from platform services through Kubernetes itself to the cloud-native services around it.

"So to summarize, 90% of resilience of your application really depends on the components that you are not developing or you don't own," Uma Mukkara said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020.

So you can't check once. Know your steady state, inject the fault yourself instead of waiting for it, and verify the steady state holds. If not, you found a weakness.

## What does cloud-native chaos look like?

Do it the way you already run Kubernetes: declaratively, through Git. Mukkara's four principles are open-source infrastructure with a community you can rely on, chaos APIs as CRDs, bring your own chaos model so you aren't locked into one style of experiment, and community-contributed experiments, because no single team can write them all.

Litmus maps onto that. At the time it was a CNCF sandbox project with more than 10,000 installations and maintainers and contributors from Intuit, Amazon, RingCentral and Container Solutions, among others. It had 30-plus experiments on its ChaosHub: infrastructure faults such as node CPU, memory and disk, Kubernetes faults such as network loss, packet duplication and a kubelet service kill (a community contribution, for the day Kubernetes itself goes down), and application-specific ones such as making a database unavailable or taking down a Kafka broker. There is an SDK in Go, Python and Ansible for writing your own.

## How do you automate and scale it?

Three YAML pieces: the experiment custom resource, a ChaosEngine that ties it to the target application, and a schedule. Commit them to Git, let Flux or Argo CD apply them on merge, and Litmus emits results, Prometheus metrics for alerting, and events for correlation when you go to debug.

To scale, embed experiments in Argo Workflows: two faults in parallel in different namespaces, wait, two more, then drain a node. Mukkara says the same pattern stretches to hundreds of experiments on clusters with thousands of nodes.

His rollout advice is to start small: small experiments in short-lived CI pipelines, deeper ones on long-running test beds, more in staging, and production last, once management and developers are on board. Developers resist; letting them test their own services first is how SREs win them over.

## What does the demo show?

A two-node Amazon EKS cluster running the Sock Shop microservices demo, with Litmus in admin mode. Two Argo workflows fire every five and ten minutes: a CPU hog on the catalog pod and a memory hog on the orders pod, tuned through Git. A Grafana dashboard marks each injection, and you can watch catalog and orders performance dip with it. The Litmus Portal for managing workflows end to end was an early version at the time, expected around the end of 2020.

## Who should watch

SREs running Kubernetes who want chaos experiments that live in the same Git repo as everything else. Teams already happy with another chaos tool can skim the Litmus parts and keep the GitOps pattern.

Title: Your model works in winter. It still recommends coats in summer
Description: Ryan Dawson (Seldon) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020 on why running ML in production differs from DevOps, from training to drift detection
Body:
A model can be bug-free and still go wrong because the world changed. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020, [Ryan Dawson](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2020_Ryan_Dawson_machine_learning_in_production), an engineer on the Seldon open-source team, gave SREs an introduction to MLOps: how the build, deploy and monitor loop for machine learning differs from the DevOps one, and which tools sit at each stage.

It's a 101 aimed at ops people, and a clear one. Dawson works on Seldon Core, so expect its examples in the serving section.

## Why isn't MLOps just DevOps with bigger files?

"Fundamentally, MLops is different from DevOps because machine learning is different from programming," Ryan Dawson said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020.

Programs codify rules. Models capture patterns from data and reapply them to new data, so the training data becomes part of the artifact. He cites surveys suggesting 80% to 90% of models never make it to live, and points to the Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems paper, where the ML code is a tiny box surrounded by data collection, processing, infrastructure and monitoring.

His worked example: a salary benchmark model built with scikit-learn. One prediction is easy. Then the business wants it every year, then another department wants it, and suddenly you need a predict function behind a REST API, in a Docker image that shouldn't contain the training data. Hence the common pattern of pickling the model to a file and loading it into a separate serving app.

## How is the workflow different?

In DevOps the trigger is a code change in Git, Jenkins builds, an executable in a Docker image gets promoted. In ML the trigger might be new data, which won't live in Git once it reaches gigabytes, and the work is exploratory: a slice of data on a laptop, longer experiments in a hosted environment, Jupyter notebooks, a serialised model at the end. Dawson focuses on offline training, the more common case, where training is separate from prediction.

Organisational silos make it harder. A data scientist hands notebooks to a DevOps team, and the DevOps team's reaction is, roughly, what is this? Mature setups have data engineers, data scientists and ML engineers with clear handoffs.

## Where do the tools fit?

He splits the lifecycle into data prep, training, serving, and rollout plus monitoring, and the tool sprawl gets easier to read:

- **Training**: Kubeflow Pipelines, MLflow, Polyaxon. Pipelines look like CI, but they are also parameterised experiments: run the same pipeline with different step sizes and pick the best model, which means you need an automated definition of best.
- **Serving**: TensorFlow Serving, TorchServe, cloud offerings, and framework-agnostic Seldon Core and KFServing, both in the Kubeflow ecosystem. In Seldon, a Kubernetes custom resource points at a storage bucket URI and names the toolkit.
- **Rollout**: A/B tests over a statistically significant sample, shorter canaries as a sanity check, and shadowing, where the new model gets all the traffic but only the live model's answers go back. In Seldon you set a traffic percentage per model in the manifest.
- **Monitoring**: Prometheus metrics and Grafana dashboards out of the box, plus asynchronous request logging to Elasticsearch for audits and for comparing a shadow with the live model.

## What can go wrong after deploy?

The interesting part. Outliers: models can be overconfident on data far from the training distribution, giving high probabilities to answers that are completely wrong. Drift: the whole input distribution moves, like a fashion recommender trained on winter purchases that keeps pushing coats into the summer. Detectors fed asynchronously from live traffic can flag both, and can also watch for adversarial inputs.

Then governance: explaining why a loan was denied, spotting bias, and reproducing exactly what was trained when. That last one is harder than in DevOps, because you need the data, every transformation, the parameters, and luck with randomness.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers about to inherit their first model in production. Data scientists curious what their ops colleagues worry about will get the other half of the picture. If you already run Seldon or KFServing, skip to the drift section.
