Title: The paid firewall caught 60% of bad port changes. Config management caught all
Description: Aaron Rinehart (Verica) and Jamie Dicken (Cardinal Health) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020 on security chaos engineering in practice
Body:
Inject a misconfigured port change on purpose, and you learn how good your security tooling really is. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020, [Aaron Rinehart](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2020_Aaron_Rinehart_Jamie_Dicken_applied_security_resilient_distributed), CTO and founder of Verica, and Jamie Dicken, Manager of Security Engineering at Cardinal Health, presented security chaos engineering: the same experiments SREs run for availability, aimed at security controls, before an attacker runs them for you.

Rinehart brings the origin story (he pioneered the practice at UnitedHealth Group). Dicken brings what a new team did with it inside a Fortune 20 healthcare company.

## Why can't you just threat model the diagram?

Because the diagram is wrong. Dicken walks through how documentation is written before the system exists, or afterwards from someone's memory, and is rarely updated. Integration points, downstream effects and people quietly scripting against your APIs never make it in. Threat modelling a stale picture means missing the problems you didn't anticipate.

Rinehart frames the alternative as continuous learning rather than continuous fixing. Legacy systems become stable through a series of painful surprises; chaos experiments let you learn the same lessons on purpose, when nobody is panicking. That matters, he says, because people think badly during an active incident, worried about blame and their jobs.

"I've always said, in general, that engineers don't believe in two things. They don't believe in hope or luck," Aaron Rinehart said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020.

## What did the port experiment find?

ChaoSlingr, the open-source tool Rinehart's team wrote at UnitedHealth Group about four years before the talk (now deprecated on GitHub, its experiment framework still there), shipped an example called PortSlingr. The hypothesis: an unauthorised, misconfigured port change on AWS gets detected and blocked by the firewall immediately, and the security operations centre gets a useful event.

Three things came back. The firewall caught it only about 60% of the time. The cloud-native configuration management tool, which they weren't paying extra for, caught and blocked it every time. And the SOC got the event but couldn't tell which AWS account it came from, commercial or non-commercial. Mapping an IP back to an account might take 30 minutes or 3 hours, which is a long time mid-incident. The fix was adding metadata to the event, and they found a drift problem between environments along the way, all without an outage.

The use cases they list: incident response, security control validation, observability (are the logs any good?) and compliance, since every experiment leaves evidence.

## How did Cardinal Health start?

Dicken's team, named Applied Security, formed in the summer of 2019 with five people covering software development, architecture, privacy, risk and networking. Their mission was to find unknown technical security gaps and drive them to remediation first. They chose security control validation as the first use case and built a five-step process called continuous verification and validation (CVV):

1. Pick the security control to validate.
2. Set benchmarks the company already agreed to, from the security architecture team's standards approved by the CISO.
3. Implement continuous checks, usually custom scripts against tool APIs and configurations, after looking for open-source or commercial options.
4. Build a dashboard of real-time compliance with those benchmarks.
5. When adherence drops, log it in the risk register so the risk team drives remediation.

Dicken calls CVV the systems-level equivalent of a scheduled automated test suite, and wants to go further: write the security chaos tests while the standards are being defined, test-driven style.

"Like Aaron said, the problem with incident response is that it's always a response," Jamie Dicken said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020.

## Where do you begin?

Small. Break PortSlingr into separate tests: config management access, whether the alert fires, or simply turning off a log source to see if the detection notices. Her advice is to be the right kind of lazy and automate the checks you already do by hand on weekends.

## Who should watch

Security engineers who want something more empirical than threat models, and SREs who already run chaos experiments and wonder what their security team could borrow. Expect stories and process, no live demo.

Title: 100 ms of database delay, 500 ms for the user
Description: Mikolaj Pawlikowski (Bloomberg LP) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020 on using chaos engineering to verify SRE assumptions and SLOs
Body:
Add 100 milliseconds of latency between a blog engine and its database, and users wait about 500 more. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020, [Mikolaj Pawlikowski](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2020_Mikolaj_Pawlikowski_sre_chaos_engineering), Software Engineer Project Lead at Bloomberg LP, argued that chaos engineering is how SREs check the assumptions behind their SLOs, and showed it in two short demos.

It's an introduction: definitions first, then a plug for his book, then the demos. The demos are the reason to watch.

## Is chaos engineering just breaking things in production?

No, and he spends some time on why the Chaos Monkey reputation hurts. Randomly killing VMs makes a good headline, and it also makes people say they would never do that here. His definition is more modest and more useful.

"What we're after is experimenting to verify hypothesis about our system's behavior in the presence of failure," Mikolaj Pawlikowski said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020.

You inject failure you reasonably expect, in controlled amounts, and either confirm the system behaves as you think or learn what needs fixing. Production is the holy grail because no staging environment is a perfect copy, but it isn't the entry fee. His book, Chaos Engineering: Crash Test Your Applications (in Manning early access at the time), starts from a single process on a single machine, blocking system calls to see whether the error handling and retries you assumed are actually there. It then climbs through network failures, JVM bytecode injection, Docker, Kubernetes and front-end JavaScript.

On the SRE side he walks through SLIs, SLOs and SLAs with a meme API whose 99th percentile response time should stay between 100 and 200 milliseconds, and defines SRE as operations with software engineering used to automate the toil away.

## What does the Docker demo show?

Ghost, the blogging engine, runs on Docker Swarm next to MySQL 5.7. Apache Bench with concurrency 1 for 10 seconds gives the steady state: after a cache warm-up, about 50 milliseconds per request.

Then Pumba, an open-source tool that wraps the Linux tc traffic control utility, adds 100 milliseconds of delay to the database container's network for 120 seconds. It runs tc from a separate container attached to the target, so the database image needs no changes. Per-request time jumps to roughly 500 milliseconds, from about 200 requests in 10 seconds down to 18.

The lesson is the multiplier. Ghost talks to the database several times per page, so the delay compounds. By the same reasoning, a one-second database delay would probably cost users closer to five seconds. That's the kind of fact you want before the incident, not during it.

## What does the Kubernetes demo show?

On a single-node minikube cluster, Pawlikowski uses PowerfulSeal, a Kubernetes chaos tool he wrote. Policies are YAML scenarios of steps and checks. The first one, about twenty lines, matches pods in every namespace, filters out the running ones and asserts the count is zero: 11 pods matched, none failing. Flip the filter and it fails as expected. PowerfulSeal can fail fast or run continuously and expose metrics for scraping.

The second policy encodes a real deployment SLO: a new deployment and service must answer within 30 seconds. It applies a Goldpinger deployment (his other tool, which builds a connectivity graph between nodes), waits 30 seconds, hits the service with an HTTP probe and cleans up after itself. Run continuously, it tells you whether that 30-second promise still holds. PowerfulSeal also has drivers for AWS, Azure, OpenStack and Google Cloud for node-level actions such as stopping a master.

## Who should watch

SREs who have heard of chaos engineering but filed it under Netflix-only. Anyone with an SLO they have never tested will get an afternoon project out of it. If you already run chaos experiments, the demos will feel familiar.

Title: When SRE stopped owning binaries and started owning Google Ads
Description: Nikolaus Rath (Google) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020 on moving an SRE team from supporting services to supporting whole products
Body:
Your SRE team can keep every supported service inside its SLO while the product is down. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020, [Nikolaus Rath](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2020_Nikolaus_Rath_application_product_ownership), Tech Lead of an SRE team at Google in London, explained how his team stopped supporting individual binaries and started supporting products, with SLOs rewritten around what users actually do.

It's a story about an engagement model, not a tool. Rath says so himself: this was first a cultural and philosophical change, and only then a technical one.

## Who is this team?

Forty people split between London and the US west coast, with two on-call rotations so at least two people hold the pager at any time. The team is more than a decade old. It started with AdWords and now covers most of Google's advertiser and publisher front ends: the interfaces where publishers sell ad inventory and advertisers buy it. By the end of 2019 that meant roughly 200 executables and microservices.

Their time splits about 30% interrupt work, 20% routine service maintenance and 50% project work. Rath is upfront that this was "complaining at a high level": the products were reliable, and the change was an efficiency play. He also argues they could only afford it because nothing was on fire.

## Why does per-service support stop working?

Automation got very good. Moving a service to another data center used to take days; it became a small commit and a state machine that works out how to reach the desired state. Every binary exports metrics out of the box, and alerting infers basic alerts from each service's SLO. But the cost per service never reaches zero, so SRE support went only to the most important services, and importance needs a human judgment call that keeps going stale.

Onboarding a service meant a long production readiness review. Offboarding was technically easier and socially worse: it means telling a developer team their service no longer matters much.

Worse, nobody knew what a failing service meant for users. Rath's example page says a service's error ratio is above 0.5 for 15 minutes, and he admits he can mitigate it and root-cause it without ever learning what users saw. The real reliability bottleneck ends up in the services SRE doesn't support, and the team is badly placed to even find them.

"Typically when we have an incident, we spend at least as much time to figure out the user impact than we spend time fixing the issue," Nikolaus Rath said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020.

## What did they change?

Three steps. First, critical user interactions (CUIs): a user action that succeeds or fails, measured as close to the user as possible, usually in browser JavaScript, then logged on the server. SLOs were rewritten against CUIs, so SRE answers for product features rather than services.

Second, developers own and run all services. SRE becomes the second line of defence, gets involved when CUIs are at risk, and takes on time-limited engagements to fix a specific reliability issue or teach a skill. Rath's analogy is a production doctor: SRE can diagnose and treat, but the patient has to follow the advice.

Third, tooling. Hand-drawn architecture diagrams were useless because everything talks to everything, so the team generates them from RPC traces per CUI. Select two failing CUIs and the diagram shows only the services in their intersection. They also built a CI for production that continuously checks what runs against their best practices, plus a written production curriculum of the skills developers need.

"SRE support means that the product is operated efficiently and works well for its users," Nikolaus Rath said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2020, replacing the old feeling that SRE support meant developers never had to worry about ops.

## Did it work?

The pages read differently now: some publishers can't preview video ads, error budget exhausted in 78 minutes. Per-service metrics still matter, but only once SRE is engaged. The change was welcomed, with some worry further down the dev org about extra work. Still open at the time of the talk: CUI coverage for every product, retiring the legacy supported-service status, and alerting granular enough to tell a fully broken feature from a few affected users.

## Who should watch

SRE leads whose team has scaled by automation and now supports more services than anyone understands. Product-facing SLO people will find the CUI section the most useful. Expect no code: it's a well-told organisational case study.

Title: Policy as code with OPA comes before infrastructure as code, not after
Description: Josh Stella (Fugue) at Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020 on Open Policy Agent and Rego for cloud security checks from Terraform plan to running infra
Body:
Plenty of teams say they're not ready for policy as code because they haven't finished moving to infrastructure as code. At Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020, [Josh Stella](https://www.conf42.com/Open_Source_Showcase_2020_Josh_Stella_cloud_security__open_policy_agent_opa), co-founder and CTO of Fugue, argued the order is backwards, and made the case for Open Policy Agent (OPA) and its Rego language as the standard way to check cloud configuration, from the Terraform plan to the running account.

Fugue builds a commercial product on OPA, and he says so. The talk is mostly about OPA itself and the open-source tools around it.

## Why can't humans review cloud config anymore?

Stella's starting point is that misconfiguration is the main security risk in the cloud. Fugue's survey of more than 300 organisations running at scale found 93% concerned about a major breach due to misconfiguration. Identity and access management topped the list of worries at 66%, ahead of security group rules (59%), object storage access policies (51%) and encryption in transit being disabled (42%). His view is that IAM is effectively a network, which is why getting it right is so hard.

Two things make manual review hopeless. Compliance frameworks such as NIST, SOC 2 and the CIS benchmarks lag behind real attacks, so dangerous settings pass audits. And attackers use automation: he cites a friend's estimate that a new internet-facing resource gets scanned within about seven minutes. In the data centre, change control boards could debate firewall ports for weeks. In the cloud, developers build infrastructure through APIs as they go; he built a global network in about five minutes that morning.

## What does policy as code give developers?

His analogy is the compiler. Nobody keeps a whole program in their head; the tooling tells you when you're multiplying a string by a float. Policy as code is the same feedback loop for security: if your tooling tells you a security group exposes a port to the whole internet, you fix it without waiting for an audit. And because it's code, it's repeatable, testable, shareable and peer reviewed.

He is wary of the alternatives. Proprietary policy languages lock you to one vendor and don't make a career skill. Policy libraries bolted onto general-purpose languages, in his experience, aren't very good, because this is a domain that wants its own language. And the code lasts. "I view all lines of code as financial liabilities to the company," Josh Stella said at Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020, so pick a policy engine that will still be around.

## What is OPA, briefly?

OPA is a CNCF project created and maintained by Styra, written in Go. Rego is declarative, closer to a query language than a program, and it validates any JSON document, which these days describes almost everything. You can run OPA as a daemon, as a microservice in your architecture, or embed it as a library; Fugue embeds it because it runs more than a billion policy evaluations a day and can't afford the network hop. The adopters list he shows includes Atlassian, Capital One, Cloudflare, Goldman Sachs, Intuit, Netflix, Pinterest and SAP.

His example rule is the KMS key rotation check: a package name, the resource type, a mapping to a CIS control, then a default of not allowed, overridden only when key rotation is enabled. A few lines, readable by anyone. A fancier VPC flow log rule imports helper libraries and still comes to about ten lines of logic in 35.

## Why policy before infrastructure as code?

Most organisations mix Terraform, CloudFormation, Ansible and console clicks. Tie your policies to one IaC tool and you need a policy set per tool. Instead, use the same Rego files at every stage: check the Terraform plan at design time, gate the CI/CD pipeline before promoting to stage or production, and keep scanning the running infrastructure, because someone in a maintenance window can still change it by hand. If you can only do one, he'd do enforcement first, then deployment, then design.

Fugue's open-source tools cover the first stages. Regula checks Terraform plans against Rego rules for AWS, GCP and Azure (for example, that ports 22 and 3389 aren't open and KMS keys rotate), and runs locally or as a GitHub Action. Fregot adds breakpoints and a faster evaluator for large data sets, about a hundred times faster than stock OPA in that case. It's written in Haskell, if that tempts you.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers deciding how to bring policy checks to cloud accounts, especially those stuck waiting on an IaC migration. It's a slide-led introduction with a short code walkthrough, not a hands-on workshop.

Title: chezmoi keeps one dotfiles repo for every machine, minus the wrong secrets
Description: Tom Payne (chezmoi.io) at Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020 on chezmoi, a dotfiles manager with per-machine templates and password-manager secrets
Body:
Your `.gitconfig` wants a different email at work, your `.netrc` holds a password that must never land in a public repo, and you have four machines. At Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020, [Tom Payne](https://www.conf42.com/Open_Source_Showcase_2020_Tom_Payne_chezmoi_dotfiles_manager), the creator of chezmoi, spent ten minutes showing how his dotfiles manager handles all of that from a single git repo.

It is a short, demo-led talk, and it moves quickly. You come away knowing what chezmoi is for, how its source format works, and why it stores secrets the way it does.

## Why manage dotfiles at all?

Payne's definition: dotfiles are the personal configuration files where you tune Git, your editor, your shell and the rest. If you've put time into them, you want them on every machine, from the home laptop to the work server. A manager gives you a backup when a disk dies, a fast start on a new machine, version control with history and rollbacks, and careful handling of secrets.

## What does the workflow look like?

The demo starts on a freshly installed Mac mini with nothing on it but Homebrew. chezmoi installs from Homebrew (there are also deb and rpm packages, prebuilt binaries and a one-line install script), checks out an example dotfiles repo, previews what it would change, then writes the files.

Then a Linux box using the same repo. He adds a tmux config there and pushes it to GitHub; back on the Mac, one update pulls and applies the change. chezmoi can commit and push automatically, but he does it by hand to show each step.

## Where does the per-machine logic live?

There is no separate config file. The repo maps one-to-one onto your home directory, and a file's attributes are encoded in its name. A `.tmpl` suffix marks a template, so the source of `.gitconfig` can switch on variables: the email chezmoi asked for on first run, your own variables, or built-ins such as operating system and architecture.

Secrets get the same treatment. The `.netrc` source carries a `private_` prefix, so chezmoi writes it with user-only permissions, and it's a template that calls a secret function instead of storing the password. That function talks to password managers: Payne uses LastPass, and 1Password, Keychain and gopass work too. The repo stays readable by anyone; the password only exists on disk where chezmoi put it.

The selling point is separation by machine. As Tom Payne said at Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020, it means that "your home secrets don't get checked out on your work machine and your work secrets don't get checked out on your home machine."

## Why this one and not another dotfiles manager?

His closing list is concrete. More than 2,600 GitHub stars at the time. It runs on Linux, macOS, Windows, Windows Subsystem for Linux and Termux. It writes real files into your home directory instead of symlinks into a central folder the way GNU Stow does, so leaving chezmoi later is easy. It ships as a single statically linked Go binary, so there's no Python or Ruby runtime to install before you can bootstrap a new machine. It uses Git for the repo, GPG for encrypted files and the password managers' own CLIs. And updates are atomic: it never writes a partial file, so an interrupted update can't leave you with half a `.bashrc`.

It's MIT-licensed, and he describes it as something he wrote to scratch his own itch.

## Who should watch

Anyone who has ever copied dotfiles between machines by hand, or who keeps a dotfiles repo with secrets awkwardly carved out. Ten minutes, well spent, though it's an overview: the docs on chezmoi.io carry the rest.

Title: Webiny wants to be the missing application layer of serverless
Description: Sven Al Hamad (Webiny) at Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020 on Webiny, an open-source framework and app set that fills the serverless application layer
Body:
Serverless saves you from running infrastructure, and then many teams spend the savings building their own tooling. At Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020, [Sven Al Hamad](https://www.conf42.com/Open_Source_Showcase_2020_Sven_Al_Hamad_fastapi_webframework), founder of Webiny, pitched the open-source project as the layer that was missing: not another deployment or monitoring tool, but a framework and set of ready-made apps for building the application itself.

It is a founder's overview of his own project, so read it as a product tour. It is also a useful snapshot of what made serverless hard to adopt in 2020.

## What actually stops teams from going serverless?

Al Hamad leans on an O'Reilly survey of organisations to frame the problem. Those that hadn't adopted serverless listed security concerns first, and he traces that to the fear of the unknown and a lack of experience: you can't secure something you don't understand. Those that had adopted it struggled with educating the rest of their staff, vendor lock-in, and testing and debugging requests that hop across many services.

The one that sets up his pitch: most organisations built serverless apps with custom tooling. "But what you've saved there you're going to usually removes here," Sven Al Hamad said at Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020, meaning the time serverless saves on infrastructure gets spent again on home-made tooling.

He does give the upside its due. No servers to manage, paying only for what you use, and enterprises reporting bills cut by half and in some cases by up to 80%.

## Where does Webiny sit in the stack?

His diagram has three layers. Clouds at the bottom (AWS, GCP, Azure). Then deployment and monitoring tools such as the Serverless Framework, AWS CloudFormation or Lumigo, which orchestrate and observe but don't help you write the app. Webiny sits on top, in the application layer.

The 2020 stack is JavaScript throughout: Node on the backend, React on the frontend, a GraphQL API layer, and MongoDB Atlas as the database behind an abstraction layer, with DynamoDB next on the list. It ran on AWS, with GCP and Azure planned. It is MIT-licensed.

## What comes in the box?

The framework is the core: a CLI that deploys to serverless infrastructure with multiple environments, and a GraphQL layer built on Apollo Federation, where each microservice exposes its own schema and they merge into a single endpoint. Routing, server-side rendering, access control and CI/CD support come with it. His argument is that these behave differently on serverless than on a VM or a container, which is why teams underestimate them.

The admin UI is made of reusable React components, and every piece of it, down to the menu and the logo, is a plugin you can swap or turn off. He notes, deadpan, that the most important feature is dark mode.

Then the apps: a page builder where you drag and drop React components (so business logic and dashboards, not static HTML), a form builder with triggers, webhooks and exports, a file manager with thumbnails and an in-browser image editor, and a GraphQL headless CMS with content modelling, multiple languages and environment aliases. All of it scales on serverless, and if it sits idle, "you won't pay a dime for it."

## Who should watch

Teams weighing serverless for a full-stack JavaScript app who would rather start from a framework than wire up their own tooling. It's a short overview with screenshots, not a build-along, so expect breadth rather than depth.

Title: XWiki borrows ActivityPub from the fediverse to federate wikis
Description: Clément Aubin (XWiki SAS) at Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020 on an XWiki extension that uses ActivityPub to share documents across wiki instances
Body:
ActivityPub is the protocol behind Mastodon and PeerTube, built for people talking to people. At Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020, [Clément Aubin](https://www.conf42.com/Open_Source_Showcase_2020_Clment_Aubin_webiny_serverless_full_stack), a developer at XWiki SAS, showed what happens when you point it at knowledge management instead: an XWiki extension that lets users and whole wikis follow each other, exchange messages and share documents across separate instances.

It is a short talk about an early research project, and it says so. Expect a working demo and an honest list of what's next, not a production rollout.

## Why use a social protocol for a wiki?

Aubin's framing is that knowledge sits in separate silos, and the useful connections are often between sources of knowledge, not just between users. ActivityPub already solves the hard part of federation: actors on different servers, running different software, sending and receiving messages. It first appeared around 2016 and became a W3C Recommendation in early 2018, so there is a stable standard to build against.

He points to the projects already using it: Mastodon for messaging, PeerTube from Framasoft as a decentralised YouTube alternative, and Nextcloud for federated file sharing, one of the first document-centric adopters. The implementation report on activitypub.rocks lists the rest.

## What does XWiki bring to the pairing?

XWiki is a wiki engine with two traits that matter here. It holds structured data, so a meeting-notes page can have typed fields for title, author, date and participants. And it is extensible, with more than 700 extensions from the community. The ActivityPub integration is one of those extensions: you find it in the wiki's administration, install it, and a new ActivityPub section appears.

The work was funded by the NLnet foundation and built mainly by Simon Urli and Manuel Leduc. The goals were cross-instance communication, following a user's activity, following the activity of a whole wiki, and eventually integrating with other platforms.

## What did the demo show?

Two wikis side by side, one user on each. Alice follows Bob by pasting his identifier; Bob gets the follow request as a notification. Bob messages Alice, and the message can go to one user, to all followers or to the public, which is ActivityPub's collections concept at work. Each user decides in their profile which events (announcements, document creation, follow requests, messages, updates) arrive in the web UI or by email.

The more interesting part is the knowledge side. Alice shares a page with Bob, and Bob can open an HTML preview of it without leaving his own wiki, useful when he has no access to the other instance. When Alice edits a page, Bob, who follows her, is notified. And an administrator on the second wiki follows the first wiki as a whole, so any edit there shows up as a notification on the other side.

"what we are trying to do is really to help the collaboration and the sharing of information between two sources of information that might be very distinct," Clément Aubin said at Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020.

## What's next?

The roadmap has three items. Integrate with Nextcloud and Matomo, which he calls a good example of an ActivityPub integration, while Nextcloud fits the knowledge-sharing goal. Improve reliability, since this is still research code and events must reliably reach their destination. And define new actors, so you could follow a set of pages or a type of event rather than a user or an entire wiki.

## Who should watch

Wiki admins and knowledge-management folks curious about federation, and developers wondering whether ActivityPub works outside social media. It is short, so it also suits a quick look at the protocol in practice.

Title: CryptPad edits documents in real time while the server sees only ciphertext
Description: Ludovic Dubost (XWiki SAS) at Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020 on CryptPad, a collaboration suite where the server stores only encrypted patches
Body:
Most collaboration suites can read every document you put in them. CryptPad is built so that its own hosts can't. At Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020, [Ludovic Dubost](https://www.conf42.com/Open_Source_Showcase_2020_Ludovic_Dubost_cloud_security_hacker), founder and CEO of XWiki SAS, explained how the suite does real-time co-editing entirely in the browser, with the server reduced to a store of encrypted patches, and how a small open-source team pays for it.

It is part product tour, part architecture walkthrough, part honest funding report. The last part is rarer than the first two.

## Why build it at all?

Dubost frames the problem in two halves. Privacy: the "we value your privacy" banner usually means your data is used and sold. Security: work moved from laptops and company networks to the cloud, where most data sits unencrypted and you have little visibility into how it is handled. Self-hosting is the obvious escape, but securing your own server takes real experience. CryptPad started as a question XWiki SAS, a 40-person open-source company from France and Romania, asked itself: can encryption enforce privacy inside a collaboration tool, with no business model based on users' data?

## How does real-time editing work without the server?

The origin story is the key. The team was working on real-time collaboration for XWiki and realised the server didn't need to understand the edits at all. Every change in your browser becomes a patch, encrypted with the document's key and sent to the server. The ChainPad algorithm merges concurrent patches on the clients, without the server being involved.

The trade-off is spelled out plainly. "So there is not 100% guarantee that your change is going to make it through if you're in a collaboration session. But what is 100% guaranteed is that everybody will be at the same result in the end," Ludovic Dubost said at Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020. If one person edits a paragraph while another deletes it, every client picks the same order.

Documents are stored as a history of patches, with a full checkpoint every 50 patches so a reload doesn't replay a document from its birth. Every editor is written in JavaScript with no server component, which is the constraint that makes the whole design possible.

## Where do the keys live?

Key management is the second hard problem. Your username and password never leave your machine: CryptPad derives a key from them with scrypt, and that key points at your personal drive, itself an encrypted CryptPad document holding the keys of all your other pads. Shared and team drives share keys along with documents. To send a pad to a contact, CryptPad uses personal mailboxes and public-key cryptography.

The consequence: lose your password, or even your username, and the hosts can't recover your account. "So it's really your job to secure this properly and make sure you're not losing them."

He is just as precise about what the operator can see. IPs and the public keys tied to them are visible but not collected. Encrypted files, the identity of paying users (required by law) and opt-in telemetry are stored. Passwords, usernames and content (text, titles, structured data, the names of collaborators) are not knowable.

## What can you actually do in it?

The demo covers a rich text editor with comments and mentions, a Markdown code pad with author colours and Mermaid diagrams, Markdown slides, a Kanban board, a whiteboard, polls, and spreadsheets built on OnlyOffice. The spreadsheet export to Excel runs OnlyOffice's C conversion code compiled to WebAssembly, in the browser, so even the file conversion stays client-side.

The roadmap items are candid about the cost of encryption: every editor competes with mature unencrypted tools, and mobile, offline, search and decentralisation between instances all need significant work.

## Who pays for it?

The usage numbers are from the COVID spring of 2020: more than 50,000 users and 350,000 pads opened per week on cryptpad.fr, four times the earlier level, with Germany ahead of France. Pads went from 150,000 a month to 1.3 million in a year, and more than 400 independent instances run elsewhere. The team behind it: three full-time developers.

Funding came from BPI France at the start, then NLnet's NGI Zero PET fund (150,000 euros), NGI Trust (70,000 euros) and a 10,000 dollar Mozilla Open Source Fund grant. Long-term, cryptpad.fr was a paid service from day one: about 170 subscribers bringing 1,000 euros a month, plus around 500 euros a month from 150 Open Collective donors. That is not yet enough to run the team without grants, and he says so.

## Who should watch

Anyone building collaborative software who wants to see what end-to-end encryption costs in architecture, and open-source maintainers who want real numbers on funding.

Title: FastAPI turns plain Python type hints into docs, parsing and validation
Description: Sebastián Ramírez (FastAPI) at Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020 on how standard Python type hints give you API docs, conversion and validation for free
Body:
You write `item_id: int` once, and FastAPI uses it to document the endpoint, convert the incoming string and reject anything that isn't an integer. At Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020, [Sebastián Ramírez](https://www.conf42.com/Open_Source_Showcase_2020_Sebastin_Ramrez_cryptpad_collaboration_suite), the creator of FastAPI, gave a code-first introduction to the framework, and the whole talk hangs on that one idea: standard Python type annotations are the API definition.

It is a 101, and a good one. If you already ship FastAPI services you will know most of it; if you are still hand-writing request parsing in Flask, this is the half hour that explains why people moved.

## What did FastAPI look like in 2020?

Ramírez opens with the numbers of the moment: about 15,000 GitHub stars, growing by roughly 1,000 a month, with Microsoft, Uber and Netflix among the users. The framework sits on open standards (OpenAPI, JSON Schema, OAuth2), which is why the interactive documentation page appears without anyone writing it.

The smallest app is a few lines: create a `FastAPI` object, decorate a function with the path and HTTP method, return a dictionary. FastAPI turns the dict into JSON. Plain `def` works as well as `async def`, so you don't have to learn async before you can write your first endpoint.

## One annotation, three jobs

The talk builds up a food-ordering API, tacos included. A path parameter declared as `int`, a query parameter `q` that defaults to `None`, then a request body modelled with Pydantic: a `Food` class with a `name` string and an `ingredients` list of strings. Each declaration does three jobs at once. It shows up in the generated docs, it converts input (a `delivery=true` query string arrives in your function as a real boolean, not as a string), and it validates.

The validation demo is the best part. He sends a list of orders with a sneaky object hidden inside an ingredients list and an item that spells its key `food_name` instead of `name`. FastAPI rejects the request with two errors, each pointing at the exact location: the index in the list, the field, and what was expected.

"This is saving us like, I don't know, 50 lines of code in here, something like that," Sebastián Ramírez said at Conf42 Open Source Showcase 2020. By the time your function runs, the data is already valid, so the function body is business logic only.

Because it is all standard typing, the editor keeps up too. Two `for` loops deep into a list of Pydantic models, autocompletion still knows that `ingredient` is a string, and the type checker flags adding it to an integer before you run anything.

## Required query parameters and the ellipsis trick

Extra metadata goes through `Query`: a description for the docs, or numeric bounds such as greater than zero and at most ten. The catch is that `Query(...)` sits where the default value would be, so to keep a parameter required you pass Python's ellipsis, `...`, as the first argument. Small, odd-looking, and exactly the kind of thing you'd otherwise lose an afternoon to.

He also has an opinion on required query parameters in general: clients rarely expect them, so keep them few. "One does not simply make all query parameters required."

## Docs that can't drift

His pitch for the generated documentation is organisational, not technical. No wiki page to forget to update, no frontend team discovering a changed endpoint in production, because the description lives next to the parameter. In his words, "everything will live right there in the code right where it belongs."

## Is it fast, and should you rewrite?

On performance he points to the TechEmpower benchmarks, where FastAPI ranks among the fastest Python frameworks, and is honest about what that means: it runs on Uvicorn and is built on Starlette, so the bare server underneath should always win, and the exact ranking within that cluster matters less than being in it.

He is just as honest about when not to use it. A stable Django app that isn't an API and needs no new features should stay as it is; the gentler path is putting a FastAPI layer in front for new endpoints. He closes with the dependency injection system (auth, database sessions), WebSockets, background tasks, Typer for command-line apps built the same way, and Thinc, a deep learning library that uses the same type-annotation approach.

## Who should watch

Python developers who build or consume HTTP APIs and haven't tried FastAPI yet, and anyone who wants a crisp argument for type hints in Python. Seasoned FastAPI users can skip to the validation and `Query` sections.

Title: Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020: practise being wrong, on purpose
Description: Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020 roundup - the first Conf42, in London - on adoption, JVM and SQL Server experiments, Kubernetes chaos and the humans in the loop
Body:
Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020 was the very first Conf42: one day in London on January 23, 2020, with 11 talks. Its running argument was that the hard part of chaos engineering isn't breaking things. It's getting an organisation to want to know how it breaks, and treating every finding as a lesson rather than a blame. Speakers kept referring to each other's talks during the day, and the posts below follow those threads.

All the talks are on the [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020 event page](https://www.conf42.com/ce2020) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrD9gbDVOMwa2tAud9SfJjmk).

## Being wrong is the job

[Russ Miles](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Russ_Miles_how_to_be_wrong), CEO of ChaosIQ, opened by rewriting the vocabulary. Fire drills are a terrible analogy because they make you complacent. Don't say incident, say surprise. Every system is wrong, all the time, and blame points the wrong way. His reframe stuck with the rest of the day: "chaos engineering could be better phrased as deliberately practicing being wrong," Russ Miles said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020. He also gave the business case in one number, about $100,000 for an hour of downtime for 95% of enterprise systems, and pointed sceptics of the speed-versus-reliability trade-off to the book *Accelerate*.

## How do you get an organisation to adopt it?

Three talks took on adoption from different sides. [Vilas Veeraraghavan](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Vilas_Veeraraghavan_resilience_adoption) of Walmart Labs described the ramp at Walmart scale: price every incident, do the observability and playbook homework first, gate experiments behind a five-level maturity model, and avoid vanity positions like a designated chaos practitioner. [Adrian Hornsby](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Adrian_Hornsby_getting_out_of_the_starting_blocks) of AWS started with "don't call it chaos engineering", argued that good intentions fail where mechanisms (tool, adoption, audit) work, and recommended starting with a middle team, tracking MTTR, and having everyone write down their hypothesis before saying it out loud. [Joyce Lin](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Joyce_Lin_who_is_responsible_for_chaos) of Postman asked who owns chaos. Her answer: whoever gets paged starts it, and testers are starting to automate the experiments SREs design.

[Luka Kladaric](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Luka_Kladaric_quality_software_hostile_environments) of Sekura supplied the cautionary tale: a startup in tech bankruptcy, with a ten-gigabyte monorepo and an hour and a half per deploy, rescued by a rebel infrastructure team over a year and a half. His conclusion was to stop calling it tech debt and budget sustainability work instead.

## Chaos inside the code and the database

The hands-on talks went below the infrastructure. [John Fletcher and Manuel Wessner](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_John_Fletcher_Manuel_Wessner_chaos_monkey_for_spring_boot) of Codecentric AG live-coded Chaos Monkey for Spring Boot: latency and exception assaults on annotated beans, runtime control through Actuator, a Chaos Toolkit experiment that found a missing fallback (fixed with Titanic). [Long Zhang](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Long_Zhang_jvm) of KTH Royal Institute of Technology brought the research version, injecting exceptions through bytecode instrumentation with ChaosMachine, TripleAgent and POBS to sort try-catch blocks into resilient, fragile and silent ones.

[Andrew Pruski](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Andrew_Pruski_sql_server) of Channel Advisor showed that DBAs are natural chaos engineers. Stopping the primary of an Always On availability group failed over once, then failed, because of the clustered role's default limit of one failure in six hours. He found the same setting on some of his production instances. Then he played KubeInvaders against SQL Server pods.

## Kubernetes, the cloud-native way

[Uma Mukkara](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Uma_Mukkara_cloud_native) of Chaos Native argued that if you deploy with YAML, chaos should be YAML too, reviewed through GitOps. Litmus models it as ChaosExperiment, ChaosEngine and ChaosResult custom resources, with pluggable libraries like Pumba and PowerfulSeal and a Chaos Hub where developers publish application-specific experiments for SREs. He pointed to Pruski's demo to make the point: pods coming back doesn't prove SQL Server works.

## The humans in the loop

The day ended where it kept heading. [Yury Nino](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Yury_Nino_postmortem_culture) of Aval Digital Labs found that 60% of the 45 engineers she surveyed in Colombia had never written a postmortem. Her answer: chaos game days, which end with a postmortem by design, plus Gaveta, a tool to cut down the 90 days a game day can take to plan. [Matty Stratton](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Matty_Stratton_psychology) of PagerDuty closed on the psychology of it all: say contributing factor rather than root cause, mind how people perceive the word chaos, don't use game days to put people under stress, and "never surprise anybody with your chaos experiment." Behind every graph, he reminded the room, there are people.

## Sponsors and what came next

Thanks to gold sponsors [PagerDuty](https://www.pagerduty.com/) and [ChaosIQ](https://chaosiq.io), who also each had a speaker on stage.

The series came back as [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021](https://www.conf42.com/ce2021) and has run every year since. Hopefully without fire drills.

Title: If you deploy with YAML, you should break things with YAML
Description: Uma Mukkara (Chaos Native) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020 on cloud-native chaos engineering as Kubernetes CRDs, GitOps and a shared hub of experiments
Body:
Killing a pod by hand proves the pod came back. It doesn't prove the application works, and it leaves no record of who killed it. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020, [Uma Mukkara](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Uma_Mukkara_cloud_native), CEO of Chaos Native and co-creator of the Litmus project, defined cloud-native chaos engineering as chaos declared in a Kubernetes manifest: custom resources, an operator, results you can scrape, and experiments developers publish for SREs to reuse.

The talk is explicitly about practice rather than preaching. It's also, inevitably, an introduction to Litmus, the open-source project his team built and the talk's worked example.

## Why does cloud native need its own kind of chaos?

Mukkara's picture of a cloud-native stack is the argument. Linux is about 17 million source lines, Kubernetes about 35 million, Node.js about 12 million, libraries another 2.5 million, and your own code maybe 50,000 lines on top. Linux upgrades every 12 to 18 months; Kubernetes, and the microservices around your app, change far more often, and you control almost none of it.

So the job isn't verifying your code, it's verifying the 99% you depend on, continuously. You can't assume your cloud provider's managed Kubernetes is hardened. Don't assume, verify, as several speakers said that day.

The second difference is operational: in Kubernetes everything is YAML, applied with `kubectl apply` and kept in Git. A chaos experiment is an infrastructure change. "I'm killing a pod. Who gave you permission?" he asks, which is why chaos needs to go through GitOps like everything else. His definition fits in one line: if you put chaos engineering as an intent into a YAML manifest, you're practising cloud-native chaos engineering.

## Four principles

From building chaos tests for the storage project OpenEBS, where users needed proof their data would survive, his team distilled the principles:

1. **Open source**, because generalised tooling only spreads that way, as Kubernetes itself did.
2. **Chaos APIs as CRDs**, so chaos is defined like a pod or a service.
3. **Pluggable chaos logic**, so you can bring the tools you already use, such as Pumba, which came up earlier in the day.
4. **Community driven**, so experiments are built and shared together.

He wrote them up on the CNCF blog.

## How does Litmus model an experiment?

Litmus, Apache 2.0 licensed, had just reached general availability, with 50+ contributors and 600+ GitHub stars. Three custom resources do the work:

- **ChaosExperiment**: the smallest unit of chaos, such as deleting a pod.
- **ChaosEngine**: binds experiments to an application, with the service account and permissions for who can kill what.
- **ChaosResult**: where the outcome lands, so Prometheus or another tool can pull it.

An operator runs the engine. Chaos libraries are pluggable: PowerfulSeal and Pumba were built in, and adding your own means wrapping your chaos logic in a Docker image that does the damage when you `docker run` it, then pointing a new experiment CR at it. "Think litmus as a way to use your chaos experiments with a more acceptable Gitops way," Uma Mukkara said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020.

## Generic versus application-specific chaos

The Chaos Hub is to chaos experiments what Helm charts are to applications. Developers push experiments; SREs pull the ones they need, install Litmus from its Helm chart, and create a ChaosEngine.

Generic experiments cover Kubernetes resources: pod delete, container kill (one container in a multi-container pod), CPU hog, network latency, loss and packet corruption, plus cloud-specific infrastructure faults like node loss, disk loss and disk fill. The interesting ones are application-specific. Mukkara points back to Andrew Pruski's KubeInvaders demo from the same day: pods came back, but did SQL Server actually work? An application experiment encodes the pre-checks, the attack and the post-checks. For OpenEBS that means killing a storage controller target or a replica, with the expected behaviour written by the OpenEBS developers, so a user doesn't need to know the internals to verify it.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE teams on Kubernetes who have run a few `kubectl delete pod` experiments and want them reviewable, repeatable and in Git. Also a useful snapshot of where Litmus started.

Title: Good intentions don't scale chaos engineering. Mechanisms do
Description: Adrian Hornsby (Amazon Web Services) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020 on the mechanisms, first team and hypothesis habits that get chaos engineering adopted
Body:
The first thing to fix about chaos engineering is the name. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020, [Adrian Hornsby](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Adrian_Hornsby_getting_out_of_the_starting_blocks), Principal Technologist for architecture at Amazon Web Services, gave eight tips for teams stuck at the start, numbered from zero: don't call it chaos, build mechanisms instead of asking people to try harder, start with the middle team, measure MTTR, and make the hypothesis the main event.

It's an adoption talk, not a failure-injection talk. His own open-source failure-injection tools only get a brief mention at the end.

## Tip zero: don't call it chaos engineering

Hornsby asked on Twitter what was stopping wide adoption, and the top answer was that there's enough chaos in prod already. The follow-up showed why: teams spend their time fighting fires, so chaos engineering looks like extra work on top.

Every customer he's seen struggle had the same blocker: leadership hears "chaos" and stops listening. So call it engineering. He numbers this one zero because it's a requirement, not a tip.

## Why do good intentions fail?

His favourite internal Amazon story: Jeff Bezos shadowing a customer service rep who glances at a ticket and predicts, correctly, that the customer wants to return a table. They'd had thousands of those in two weeks. Telling everyone to care more and try harder changed nothing, because people were already trying their best.

What worked was an Andon cord, borrowed from Toyota's 1902 silk looms and later its car lines, where anyone who spots a defect can stop production and gets thanked for it. Amazon gave customer service reps the equivalent: pull a listing with a known defect. For one item wrongly listed as including a recharge cable, contacts per unit fell from 33% to 3.7%.

If chaos engineering is stalling, Hornsby argues, you're missing a mechanism, and a mechanism has three parts: a tool, adoption, and audit.

## Start from data about your own fires

Ask a team for its five most painful outages of the last two years and, in his experience, nine companies out of ten answer from gut feeling and recent memory. His usual suspects: it's always DNS, configuration drift, SSL certificate expiry, deployment failures and third-party links. None of those is about coding skill.

He's candid about operator error: he deleted a production database twice and wasn't fired, because the real causes were no guardrails, an identical terminal for test and prod, and being interrupted every few seconds during a fire. Amazon's postmortem process, Correction of Errors (COE), asks what happened, the customer impact and blast radius, the contributing factors, the data behind them, lessons learned, and corrective actions with a due date (two weeks by default). Never stop at operator error.

The audit is a weekly operational review with leadership where a weighted wheel of fortune picks which service team presents its metrics and COE follow-ups. Adoption comes through a policy engine that codifies best practices into checks, scores every team, and puts the scores in front of leadership. He calls it a tool to amplify social pressure.

## Pick a Trojan horse and one metric

You never go from zero to 100 across a company. Don't start with the best team, because they're already doing well and nothing visibly changes. Don't start with the worst, who still need infrastructure as code and to shut port 22. Start in the middle.

Measure one thing: mean time to recovery. Outages make smart people sweat, swear and get temporarily stupid; practice reduces the fear, and less fear means faster recovery. "For me, the essence of chaos engineering is training the team to be confident," Adrian Hornsby said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020.

## Over-index on the hypothesis

His most practical tip costs nothing. Put everyone connected to the service in a room (engineers, project managers, designers, the CTO), state a hypothesis such as "what happens if my database goes down", and have each person write their prediction on paper without talking. Discussion produces convergence towards the loudest voice; writing produces divergence. In every meeting he's run, people disagreed, which exposes stale specifications and assumptions before any experiment runs.

## Break things early, locally, and with people

Chaos belongs early in the journey, like security. New hires on his old teams built a small API with a health check and made it as resilient as they could in Docker, using tools like `docker stop`, `wrk` to DDoS their own health endpoint, `stress-ng`, `tc` for latency and `iptables` to block DNS. Should a saturated box answer the API or the health check? Get it wrong and the load balancer pulls the instance.

Keep a blast-radius mindset, and assume anything unverified is broken: backups, auto scaling, multi-AZ (AZs do fail), self-healing, and people. In one experiment he sent a key engineer home; six hours later they had to bring him back, because only he knew how to get the database back up.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers whose chaos programme has a tool but no momentum.

Title: The SQL Server failover setting a chaos experiment caught
Description: Andrew Pruski (Channel Advisor) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020 on chaos experiments for SQL Server availability groups, backups and SQL on Kubernetes
Body:
Failing over an availability group with T-SQL proves very little. Switching off the primary does. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020, [Andrew Pruski](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Andrew_Pruski_sql_server), SQL Server DBA at Channel Advisor and Microsoft Data Platform MVP, ran exactly that experiment live in an Azure lab, watched it fail the second time, and found a default cluster setting he then went and fixed in his own production instances.

His argument is that DBAs are natural chaos engineers already: they don't just take backups, they verify them and practise restores against an RPO and RTO. Chaos engineering is that habit applied to everything else.

## Where do you find the failures worth testing?

Pruski recommends two starting points. A past incident analysis (or, borrowing Russ Miles' term from earlier in the day, a past surprise analysis) finds failures that have happened and the mitigations put in place, so you test something that will actually come up. A likelihood-impact map ranks every failure you can think of. People tend to be overly optimistic or overly pessimistic, so if everything clumps at one end, do it again until three or four candidates sit in the red.

His SQL Server candidates come with war stories:

- **High availability.** A two-node Always On availability group with automatic failover. The realistic test isn't `ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP ... FAILOVER`; it's killing the primary.
- **Monitoring.** A runaway query filling the transaction log stops all writes. You know what SQL Server will do; the experiment is whether you got a growth warning before the full-log alert.
- **Restores.** Years ago, on SQL Server 2005, a third-party compression tool's "instant restore" on a three-terabyte database sat at 99% for five hours and then failed. He hadn't tested restores with that feature. Now he runs the dbatools PowerShell module on a separate server to restore random databases from backup and flag problems.
- **User error.** A friend's `UPDATE` without a `WHERE` clause applied a 15% discount to every transaction the company made for about half an hour. The fix tested the process, not the database: read-only access for everyday accounts, separate SQL logins for changes, and SSMSBoost warning about unqualified updates (until everyone learned to click OK).
- **Disaster recovery.** Unlikely, high impact, and real: an ex-colleague's data centre lost power about two months earlier, there was no DR plan, and they were down for four hours.

His last item is the strange one: is there anything else you haven't thought of? The way to answer it is to ask sysadmins, network admins, database developers and end users.

## The experiment that failed

The hypothesis: if the primary node fails, the availability group listener, the endpoint applications connect to, stays online. The method: stop the database engine service on the primary rather than a polite T-SQL failover. The steady state check is a PowerShell `Test-NetConnection` against the listener wrapped in a Pester test. Rollback in a real environment would be point-in-time restores; in the demo, restarting the service.

The first run passed: the group failed over to the second node. The run back failed. The listener stayed offline because of the clustered role's failover settings: a maximum of one failure in a period of six hours, after which the role is left in a failed state. Those are the defaults. Raising the limit to ten made the next run pass.

"I can't really remember the last time I checked that setting for my production SQL instances. And I went and checked and guess what, a couple of them had those default settings," Andrew Pruski said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020. He calls the experiment a little contrived. It still turned up a production fix from a lab.

## SQL Server on Kubernetes, with Space Invaders

To finish, he shows SQL Server 2019 (RC1 at the time) on Kubernetes. On MicroK8s on his laptop he deletes the pod, and Kubernetes notices the running state no longer matches the desired state, starts a new pod with a new IP, and the service still answers. Then, because his boss asked for a GUI with more wow factor, he moves to a ten-pod cluster in Azure and plays KubeInvaders, where the aliens are your pods. It has an automatic mode, and it fires little Kubernetes logos.

In the Q&A he explains it isn't a toy for them: they were running a proof of concept on their own Kubernetes cluster backed by a Pure Storage array, with persistent volumes for system databases and transaction logs, and had already corrupted quite a few databases by killing pods under heavy transactions. That feeds straight back into how fast they can restore.

## Who should watch

DBAs and anyone who owns a stateful service and has only ever failed it over on purpose, in a maintenance window. Also the fastest proof that chaos engineering isn't just for stateless microservices.

Title: Stop calling it tech debt. Call it sustainability work
Description: Luka Kladaric (Sekura) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020 on digging a startup out of tech bankruptcy and budgeting sustainability work over tech debt sprints
Body:
Tech debt is a bad name, because debt comes with a balance you can check. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020, [Luka Kladaric](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Luka_Kladaric_quality_software_hostile_environments), chaos manager at Sekura Collective, told the story of a startup in what he calls tech bankruptcy, the year and a half his team spent fixing it mostly in secret, and why the fix should have been a standing budget for sustainability work.

The chaos in this talk isn't injected. It's the organic kind, grown over eight years of "just this once".

## What makes an environment hostile?

Kladaric's definition: anywhere engineering is treated as the implementing workforce for ideas from outside, with little or no autonomy. Product owns 100% of engineering time, and engineers claw back time for the foundations.

His definition of tech debt is the classic one, the implied cost of an easy solution over a slower and better approach, accumulated over time. His examples are more fun: the API with no pagination that started at 20 results and three years later returns thousands, at ten megabytes a response; the module where a ticket about user messaging makes everyone back away from their desks and stare at the floor. That reaction, he says, is a measurable cue.

## How bad can it get?

The case study is one company, and he left out "the more esoteric stuff":

- A ten-gigabyte monolithic Git repository hosted in the office. Fast on the office network, a bad day for the remote engineer on DSL who needs to re-clone.
- No concept of stable: any change rolled out everything, so one commit took an hour and a half to deploy. Four commits were the deploy pipeline for the day, and a fix for a noon breakage waited in the same queue.
- A handcrafted Jenkins box in the office with no record of how it was configured, and three white-label Android builds that each built differently.
- No local dev environments, no database schema versioning (changes went straight to the master database "with honor system accounting"), half the servers not deployable from scratch, self-hosted abandonware for code review, and a VPN needed for everything, even by support.

Outages were daily. His favourite: the main production API server going down because a product manager committed an iOS translation string change, on a Friday at 7pm on the other side of the planet, 2am for him.

## The fix, done in the shadows

The infrastructure team was "staffed with rebels" with the blessing of a small part of leadership. Every terrible thing became a ticket in a hidden project called Monsters under the bed, attacked in the half hours between meetings. It took over a year and a half. What changed:

- The build server was rebuilt from scratch with Ansible in the cloud, with build and deploy jobs defined in code.
- The monorepo was split into 40 smaller repositories, one team at a time, pausing a single team for an hour and keeping its history. Earlier proposals had all been all-or-nothing. Only affected projects built, and commit to live went from hours to seconds. Holdout teams joined months later.
- About 80 servers in 20 roles were rebuilt with Ansible, under the cover story of an upgrade to Ubuntu 16. Nobody asked how long that would take.
- Code moved to GitHub, local dev environments arrived, the VPN shrank to read access on the master database, and schema changes became code-reviewed SQL scripts.

"The moral of the story is, don't wait for permission to do your job right," Luka Kladaric said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020. If you see something broken, fix it; if you don't have time, write it down and come back when you can steal a minute.

Then he turns on his own story. A team subverting the process with a manager saying "pretend I didn't know" is not a success. It's a symptom.

## Why tech debt is the wrong metaphor

Debt suggests control: like a credit card, you check the balance and pay down 10% this month, 20% next. Tech debt has no number. In his words, it's a pain index with no upper bound that can double by the next time you check your balance. And nobody explicitly asks for it to be fixed, so it always loses to features with measurable outcomes.

His alternative comes from Gojko Adzic's article *Sprints, marathons and root canals*: software development has no finish line, so basic hygiene shouldn't need a calendar slot, any more than brushing your teeth does. Rename the work to sustainability work. Give each team or engineer a regular percentage of time for it, tune it over time, let engineers pick what they stumble over, and lend it back to product during crunch, rather than fighting for occasional tech debt sprints.

## Who should watch

Engineers at startups who recognise more than three items on that list, and the engineering managers who need a better pitch than asking for yet another refactoring sprint.

Title: Want a postmortem culture? Run a game day and write one
Description: Yury Nino (Aval Digital Labs) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020 on using chaos game days to build a blameless postmortem habit, and a tool to plan them
Body:
Teams that never write postmortems won't start because someone sends a template. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020, [Yury Nino](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Yury_Nino_postmortem_culture), DevOps Engineer at Aval Digital Labs in Colombia, argued for a different on-ramp: run a chaos game day, which ends with a postmortem by design, and automate the planning so the game day actually happens.

It's a short talk in two halves: why postmortems don't happen, then a walkthrough of Gaveta, the game day tool her team was building.

## A town that already does postmortems

Nino opens with her hometown, Garagoa in the Boyacá department. Every 16 December, people there mark the end of the year with a ceremony called the death of sadness: they review what they did over the year and make resolutions for the next. So if a town can hold a yearly postmortem, why don't software engineers hold one after an incident?

She has data from her country. In a survey of 45 software engineers, 18 (40%) had written a postmortem and 27 (60%) had not. And 55% said they didn't know what a postmortem was. Another group thought postmortems were a job for DevOps and operations engineers, not developers.

## Why blame keeps postmortems unwritten

Nino's working definition is the plain one: a postmortem answers what went wrong and how we learn from it. She points to the well-known public ones, GitLab's account of an engineer dropping a production database and AWS's write-up of the S3 outage in Virginia in February 2017.

The barrier is culture. Lack of accountability goes with a blameful culture, and she singles out the five whys, citing John Allspaw's critique: asking why so easily turns into asking who, and the postmortem ends with a human tagged as the root cause. Her closing note borrows from Sidney Dekker's *The Field Guide to Understanding Human Error*: "If something goes wrong and a human is involved, it is a symptom of a deeper trouble," Yury Nino said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020.

## How a chaos game day works

A game day has three roles. The master of disaster picks a failure, often in secret, declares the start of the incident and launches the attack. The first on-call person sees, triages and tries to mitigate. The team then analyses the failure and fixes it, and the game day only ends when they write the postmortem. You get the habit of writing postmortems without the fear, because nobody caused the outage except the person whose job it was to cause it.

The catch is the planning: an agenda, roles, communications, an experiment designed like a scientific one, provisioned hardware and software, a chaos tool such as Chaos Toolkit or Gremlin, and observability so you can see what happens. On average, she says, a person spends 90 days planning a game day.

## Gaveta: the toolbox for game days

To cut that down, her team at Aval Digital Labs designed Gaveta (the name, she explains, means toolbox). It's written in Go with a hexagonal architecture: a core that orchestrates handlers for planning, communications, infrastructure, documentation and backlog, with adapters so each can use a different tool.

In the mockups she shows, the master of disaster:

- writes the agenda, which becomes Google Calendar events, and sets the roles so Slack or push notifications can remind participants;
- uploads a Terraform file that provisions the cloud provider (AWS or GCP), the chaos agent (Gremlin or Chaos Toolkit) and the observability tool (Datadog in the demo, New Relic works too);
- designs the experiment: application, hypothesis (in the demo, whether a Hystrix circuit breaker configuration holds up), a ten-minute attack and the blast radius;
- and gets a pre-filled postmortem, inspired by ChaosIQ's template, with the next actions pushed to Confluence and Jira.

Mobile matters too, she notes, because a good game day comes with food and music.

## Who should watch

Engineering leads in organisations where postmortems are rare or punitive, and anyone who has to run their first game day and wants the checklist of what goes into planning one. Gaveta was a work in progress at the time, so watch it for the design, not a download link.

Title: Who owns chaos? Whoever gets paged, and soon the testers
Description: Joyce Lin (Postman) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020 on which roles start chaos programs, and why testers are starting to run chaos experiments
Body:
Chaos programs get started by the people who feel production pain, which is why testers were missing from them. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020, [Joyce Lin](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Joyce_Lin_who_is_responsible_for_chaos), Developer Advocate Lead at Postman, looked at who actually does chaos engineering across the community and spotted a new pattern: SREs design the experiments, testers run and automate them.

It's a short talk (Postman, she says up front, is not the subject) built from conversations at community days and conferences. Think of it as a field survey of job titles, with a few quotes worth stealing.

## Who does chaos today?

Start with the community's own map of well-known chaos engineers and tools. Most of the names have "engineer" in the job title: dedicated chaos engineers, which Lin calls vanity roles after Vilas Veeraraghavan's talk earlier that day, plus site reliability engineers. About a third come from security, ops or R&D.

The motivation is simple, and she lets Kolton Andrus, CEO at Gremlin, say it: it boils down to who gets paged. If that's an SRE or ops team, they have the most incentive to make their own lives better. It's how Andrus himself started at Netflix.

## Responsibilities, not titles

Lin maps the responsibilities that pull people into chaos work:

- **Chaos specialists**: a dedicated team where resilience is a core competency.
- **Deployment and uptime**: SREs, production engineers, a DevOps department, or, as at Postman with its microservices, the developers who build the services.
- **Incident management**: the shift from the postmortem to the pre-mortem, preventing failures instead of analysing them.
- **Domain experts**: data, storage and networking teams.
- **Testing in production**: about seven hands went up in the room. Production has the most information for recreating real failures, but regulated industries like finance and healthcare often can't touch it.

## Why aren't testers doing chaos?

Before chaos engineering there was chaos testing: when Netflix introduced Chaos Monkey, it pitched it to the test community under that name. Shift-left logic says resilience belongs early in the lifecycle, where bugs are cheapest. But testers aren't on call and don't push hotfixes, so SREs and ops pioneered the practice instead.

Lin's example of the exception is Abby Bangser, Platform Test Engineer at MOO in London, who argued that the biggest limitation to delivering software faster is the focus on adding more pre-release testing, and that chaos engineering is about building confidence that we aren't fragile. At a few very large companies, Lin found the hand-off already formalised: engineers come up with the chaos experiments, testers run and automate them.

## How does a chaos program start?

Whoever starts one needs three things: insight into the likely vulnerabilities and how to structure an experiment, access to pull the plug and roll back, and the organisational pull to get management and neighbouring teams on board. The third is the hardest, and a catastrophe makes it easy. Lin met a director of testing whose CTO ordered a chaos program after the company lost $600 million in 22 minutes.

You shouldn't wait for that. Her advice comes from Casey Rosenthal, CEO at Verica: assemble bits and pieces from the resilience engineering frameworks that appeal to you, build a practice around them, and expect not to get it right the first or second time.

Her closing point is the one that ties the event together. "A valuable chaos test will not only teach you about your systems, but also your team," Joyce Lin said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020. So build resilience into the organisation too, and celebrate the failures instead of sweeping them under the rug.

## Who should watch

QA and test engineers wondering whether chaos is their job (it can be), and engineering leads deciding where a new chaos program should live. It's a quick watch.
