Title: Every outage is a chaos exercise you didn't schedule
Description: Vilas Veeraraghavan (Walmart Labs) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020 on the homework, maturity model and mistakes behind chaos engineering adoption at Walmart
Body:
Getting teams to run chaos experiments is harder than running them. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020, [Vilas Veeraraghavan](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Vilas_Veeraraghavan_resilience_adoption), Director of Engineering at Walmart Labs, explained how Walmart built the ramp: price every incident, do the observability and playbook homework first, gate experiments behind a five-level maturity model, and stop appointing designated chaos practitioners.

This is not a tooling talk. It's a field report on adoption, including the parts that went wrong, from someone whose blast radius is very large.

## Why does scale change the conversation?

Veeraraghavan opens with the numbers that make any disruption expensive: more than 11,000 stores running on Walmart software, annual revenue above half a trillion dollars, and 270 million people transacting across stores and the website in a week.

Walmart set some truths before any experiment. Reliability is no longer a function of redundancy and over-scaled hardware. In a hybrid cloud, the cloud provider is an external dependency and a reliability risk, whatever its guarantees. Scheduled downtime is no longer acceptable. And users can lose trust in a brand after one bad experience, sometimes for good.

## Start with the outages you already had

The sales pitch to teams was simple: you're already doing chaos engineering, just badly. "We realized that every outage was essentially a chaos exercise that was completely unintentional, but was happening nonetheless and was causing people to be reactive," Vilas Veeraraghavan said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020.

So they calculated a cost per incident, walked through the whole path (page, ticket, triage, escalation to a subject matter expert, fix, deploy), and broke it down by quarter to see trends. The target is to stop incidents at the third step: give the on-call engineer enough information to resolve it at initial triage, before it becomes an escalation.

## The homework comes before the first experiment

Two prerequisites, both non-negotiable in his view:

- **Observability.** Logging alone, Splunk and Kibana dashboards included, isn't enough. You need second-level metrics that show deltas and trends, plus alerts. His test: can an on-call engineer narrow down an issue within the SLA of a P1?
- **On-call playbooks.** A disaster recovery failover playbook, each service's critical dependencies defined, a playbook or automated fallback for every critical dependency failure, and non-critical dependencies listed with the thresholds where they start to hurt (an async log shipper slowly filling the disk, say). "Having a playbook is not the answer. Testing a playbook continuously is the answer."

He notes that doing the homework surfaces gaps on its own, before anyone injects a fault.

Then production-like load generation, build or buy with no preference, because a failure injection test is pointless if you can't characterise behaviour under real traffic. Do no harm: rehearse in pre-prod with production-shaped load and move to prod once you're confident. And invest in CI/CD, including a profiling stage and an inference layer that feeds production signals back into the pipeline.

## A maturity model, not a free-for-all

Walmart didn't let teams just turn up and run chaos tests. A maturity model from level one to level five sets requirements per level, which builds the team's confidence and management's confidence in the team. The payoff he describes is support cost: at level one, a five-digit dollar figure per minute of incident; at level five, a few hundred dollars per minute, with a couple of engineers reading good observability instead of a crowd guessing what to shut down.

They also built their own tooling, Resiliency Doctor, because the ecosystem hadn't produced the killer product yet. And they invested in people: training, certifications, brown bag sessions, blameless postmortems, and "carrots, not sticks".

## What went wrong

The most useful section is the don'ts:

- **Vanity positions.** A designated chaos practitioner or resiliency expert shifts the responsibility to one person. Every engineer needs to feel empowered to run exercises.
- **Partial participation.** Exercises need the team's dependencies and the SRE and support teams signed up, not just the team itself.
- **Assuming instead of verifying.** Ask a team whether they can find an issue in 15 minutes and they will say yes. No team, he says, is as well instrumented as it thinks.
- **Imposing one resilience metric.** Goals differ per team and application. A central metric that meant nothing to teams was, in his words, a painful learning.

And teams are never ready at first. Let them fail, but not in prod.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and platform or SRE leads trying to take chaos engineering from one enthusiastic team to a whole organisation. If you need a slide of reasons to convince finance, the incident-cost framing is the one to borrow.

- [Chaos Engineering: Getting out of the Starting Blocks](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Adrian_Hornsby_getting_out_of_the_starting_blocks) by Adrian Hornsby at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020, on the same adoption problem from the AWS side.

Title: Your catch blocks are a hypothesis. Test them in production
Description: Long Zhang (KTH Royal Institute of Technology) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020 on injecting exceptions into running JVM code to find fragile try-catch blocks
Body:
Most chaos engineering kills machines. Long Zhang's research kills `try` blocks. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020, [Long Zhang](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Long_Zhang_jvm), a PhD student in computer science at KTH Royal Institute of Technology, presented three research tools that inject exceptions into running Java code through bytecode instrumentation, so you can see which of your catch blocks actually recover and which only look like they do.

It's a research talk, and an unusually practical one: the papers, source code and experiment data are all public in the [Royal Chaos repository on GitHub](https://github.com/KTH/royal-chaos).

## Why aim chaos at exception handling?

Zhang starts from a research finding he cites: almost 90% of failures are somehow related to exception handling. Then he admits the relatable part: he often writes bad catch blocks himself, ones that catch the exception without giving the system a real way to recover. Catching an exception is not the same as recovering from it, and the catch block is the code path your tests are least likely to exercise.

Infrastructure-level chaos (killed regions, network latency, maxed-out CPU) tells you how the system copes. Application-level chaos tells you which line of your code coped badly.

## ChaosMachine: short-circuit the try block, live

The first tool, ChaosMachine, was published in IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering. It takes an idea from testing called short-circuit testing (throw an exception at the start of a `try` block so the whole block is skipped and the catch runs) and moves it into a production-like environment. No source code needed: a Java agent instruments the bytecode at runtime, with a monitoring sidecar and a perturbation injector per JVM, steered by a chaos controller.

Each try-catch block gets judged against four hypotheses:

- **Resilience**: the catch path behaves like the try path did without the exception.
- **Observability**: the exception causes a user-visible effect.
- **Debug**: the exception leaves an explicit message in the logs.
- **Silence**: none of the above. It fails, and neither users nor developers find out.

On ttorrent, a Java BitTorrent client, the experiment found 52 try-catch blocks, of which 27 were covered by the workload, 6 looked resilient and 3 were silent. Zhang frames this as falsification rather than verification: an abnormal behaviour is the useful result, because you learn something from it.

## TripleAgent: fault injection plus failure-oblivious computing

The second system, TripleAgent, combines monitoring, perturbation and failure-obliviousness. It injects exceptions at the start of methods that declare `throws`, then tries catching and ignoring the exception earlier in the call chain instead of letting it propagate to the developer's handler, and compares the two behaviours.

The perturbation points fall into three buckets: fragile (one exception crashes or wedges the system), sensitive (one is fine, a stream of them is not) and immune (the catch handles any number). In the ttorrent evaluation, TripleAgent identified 238 perturbation points whose resilience could be improved with failure-oblivious handling. Zhang is careful that these are suggestions for developers, not something to switch on blindly: "as a research prototype you can't directly use it in production. I think it's even more dangerous," Long Zhang said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020.

The inspiration is a nice touch: Zhou Botong's ambidexterity technique from the novel *The Legend of the Condor Heroes*, attack with one hand and defend with the other, each hand training the other. Chaos engineering attacks, self-healing defends, and monitoring lets you score the fight.

## POBS: observability via the base image

The third idea fixes the obvious pain: the `java -javaagent` command line for these experiments is long and tedious. POBS (automatic observability for Dockerized Java applications) moves it into the base image. An empirical study of 1,952 Dockerfiles across 589 Java projects on GitHub found the most popular bases (Java 8 and OpenJDK 8 at the top), so POBS augments those with TripleAgent and the Glowroot monitoring dashboard. A developer changes one `FROM` line to the augmented image and gets monitoring plus switchable fault injection. Run a normal and an augmented container side by side and you have a built-in control group.

## Who should watch

Java engineers who own critical services and suspect their error handling is mostly empty catch blocks with good intentions, and anyone curious where chaos engineering research was heading beyond killing pods. The live demo is short; the ideas are the point.

Title: Chaos Monkey for Spring Boot: one dependency, then break things
Description: John Fletcher and Manuel Wessner (Codecentric AG) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020 on chaos experiments for Spring Boot apps without installing anything
Body:
If your service runs on Spring Boot, your first chaos experiment is one Maven or Gradle dependency away. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020, [John Fletcher and Manuel Wessner](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_John_Fletcher_Manuel_Wessner_chaos_monkey_for_spring_boot), two maintainers of Chaos Monkey for Spring Boot at Codecentric AG, live-coded latency, exceptions and a downed database into a toy movie recommender, then fixed it with a fallback called Titanic.

It's mostly a live demo, with the usual live-demo honesty: one experiment fails before it starts because an old assault is still switched on. That's a feature of the talk, not a bug.

## What does the plugin actually attack?

The demo app has one REST endpoint that recommends a random movie from a database. Add the `chaos-monkey-spring-boot` dependency, activate the `chaos-monkey` Spring profile, enable it, and pick two things in `application.properties`:

- **Watchers**: which beans to hit, by annotation. Controllers, REST controllers, services, repositories and components.
- **Assaults**: what to do to them. Latency (by default a random one to three seconds, or a fixed range you set), exceptions, killing the app, and filling memory.

The assault level sets how often it fires. Level 1 hits every request; level 5 hits roughly one in five, chosen at random rather than every fifth. Point it at the service layer with a latency assault and the endpoint goes from milliseconds to two or three seconds, straight away.

Restarting the app for every experiment gets old fast, so the pair switch on Spring Boot Actuator. The `/actuator/chaosmonkey` endpoints let you enable, disable and reconfigure assaults at runtime from Postman or any HTTP client. Set an exception assault on the REST controller at level 2, and about every second request comes back as a 500 with a Chaos Monkey runtime exception.

## From clicking around to an experiment

Clicking in Postman is fun but it's not an experiment. For that they use the Chaos Toolkit, which has a Chaos Monkey for Spring Boot integration, so the experiment JSON can call the Actuator URL directly. The steady state hypothesis is concrete: a movie comes back in under a second with HTTP 200. The method enables Chaos Monkey, throws a `ConnectException` with the message `connection timed out` on every repository call to fake a dead database, and the rollback disables it again.

First run: steady state deviated, weakness found, no movies. The fix is a one-line fallback using Vavr's `Try` (the functional library under Resilience4j): if fetching a recommendation throws, return a movie everybody likes. Second run: steady state met with the database still down, and everyone gets Titanic. Arguably a weakness of a different kind.

For CI, they note the Chaos Toolkit didn't hand back a clean pass/fail exit code at the time, so they grep its output for the result and let grep supply the return code.

## Why a plugin and not a platform?

The project's history explains the design. It was started by their Codecentric colleague Benjamin Wilms, who was building circuit breakers and fallbacks and wanted to know whether they worked. Fletcher has seen that gap before.

"I've been, by the way, in various places where they're building this stuff, and nobody ever tested whether any of these things actually worked," John Fletcher said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2020.

Because it lives inside the app, there is nothing to install on servers and no permissions to ask for. You don't even need the dependency in your POM: the jar can go on the classpath from the command line, so production builds stay clean.

## What's new, and what was next

Recent additions covered runtime assaults scheduled by cron, for example `0 0 * * * *` with `killApplicationActive` to kill the app every hour, in the spirit of Netflix's original Chaos Monkey. The memory assault fills 5% of memory every second up to 95% and holds it for 40 seconds, to see how your app handles running out. They warn it's flaky, because different JVMs and Java versions garbage-collect differently.

The roadmap: assaults on outgoing HTTP calls through `RestTemplate` and `WebClient`, and working out what chaos means for reactive Spring applications.

## When the plugin isn't enough

The last stretch is a quick tour of the wider toolbox: `tc` with `netem` for kernel-level network delay, `stress` for CPU and memory load, Pumba for killing, pausing and delaying Docker containers (it can run as a DaemonSet on Kubernetes), KubeInvaders for shooting pods as Space Invaders aliens, Alibaba's ChaosBlade, and chaos-as-a-service platforms for teams that would rather click than memorise `tc` flags.

## Who should watch

Java and Spring developers who have Resilience4j or Hystrix-style fallbacks in production and have never seen them fire. It's a practical first chaos talk: no platform team, no tickets, about half an hour.
